claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA supplemental BLA approval letter, Herceptin (trastuzumab) BLA 103792/5250, October 20, 2010, approving trastuzumab for HER2-overexpressing metastatic gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. The pivotal trial behind it was ToGA (Bang YJ et al., Lancet 2010;376:687-97, PMID 20728210).
outcome_summary: Zanidatamab (ZW25), a bispecific antibody against two HER2 epitopes, entered industry-sponsored Phase 2 for biliary tract cancer with HERIZON-BTC-01 (NCT04466891). This was a single-arm Phase 2b trial sponsored by Zymeworks, now Jazz, with BeiGene as a collaborator. ClinicalTrials.gov gives its actual start as 2020-10-01. Its primary endpoint was confirmed ORR by independent central review. In cohort 1 (HER2 IHC 2+/3+), 33 of 80 patients responded: ORR 41.3% (95% CI 30.4-52.8), median duration of response 12.9 months (Harding et al., Lancet Oncol 2023). The trial was the basis for approval, so the endpoint is treated as met. The Phase 3 confirmatory trial HERIZON-BTC-302 (NCT06282575) started on 2024-07-19 and is still recruiting. That start is inside the 4-year window, so the program advanced. On 2024-11-20 the FDA granted accelerated approval to Ziihera (zanidatamab-hrii) for previously treated, unresectable or metastatic HER2-positive (IHC 3+) BTC. That approval rested on 62 IHC 3+ patients from HERIZON-BTC-01 (ORR 52%, DoR 14.9 months). It came about 7 weeks after the 4-year mark. The drug is approved for this disease today. Caveat: an earlier Jazz Phase 2 basket trial that included BTC patients (NCT03929666, start 2019-08-29) exists. Measured from that date, the Phase 3 start would fall outside 4 years. This answer uses the entry date provided, 2020-10-01.

evidence.earliest_source: FDA supplemental BLA approval letter, Herceptin (trastuzumab) BLA 103792/5250, October 20, 2010, approving trastuzumab for HER2-overexpressing metastatic gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma. The pivotal trial behind it was ToGA (Bang YJ et al., Lancet 2010;376:687-97, PMID 20728210).
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: zanidatamab (ZW25) is a biparatopic bispecific antibody against HER2/ERBB2. It binds ECD2 and ECD4 and blocks HER2 signalling, which fits the recorded "ERBB2 inhibitor". The CT.gov record, first posted 2020-07-10, lists HER2, bispecific and biparatopic antibody as keywords, and Weisser et al. 2023 (Nat Commun, PMID 36914633) describes the mechanism.
(2) Disease: NCT04466891 (HERIZON-BTC-01, ZWI-ZW25-203) is a Phase 2b single-arm study of ZW25 monotherapy in HER2-amplified biliary tract cancer (intrahepatic or extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer). Actual start 2020-10-01, which matches the recorded entry date. Lead sponsor is now listed as Jazz Pharmaceuticals, with BeiGene as a collaborator.
(3) Claim: only partly true. An ERBB2-targeted drug, trastuzumab, was FDA-approved for HER2+ gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma on 2020-10-20 minus ten years, i.e. 2010-10-20 (sBLA 103792/5250 letter), well before the Phase 2 entry. No HER2-directed drug was FDA-approved for biliary tract cancer itself before October 2020. A January 2021 Cancers paper (PMC7825072) states "The role of HER2-targeted therapy in BTC is unknown". Gastric cancer and BTC are both GI adenocarcinomas, but they arise in different organs, so calling gastric "closely related" is a judgement call. That is why the answer is partial rather than yes.
DATA ERROR: the evidence row dates the gastric approval to 1998-09-25. That date is Herceptin's original BLA approval (Drugs@FDA, ORIG-1), which was for breast cancer. The gastric indication was approved on 2010-10-20. Both dates still predate the Phase 2 entry.
(5) The key source is a Genentech/Roche approval for trastuzumab, and ToGA was Roche-sponsored. Neither comes from zanidatamab's sponsor (Zymeworks/Jazz/BeiGene).

The FDA then granted accelerated approval on 2024-11-20, about 4.1 years after entry, so the approval itself falls just outside the 4-year window.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA accelerated approval of IRESSA (gefitinib), NDA 21-399, AstraZeneca, 5 May 2003, for locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC after failure of platinum-based and docetaxel chemotherapy. The 2003 label describes gefitinib as an inhibitor of the EGFR tyrosine kinase (EGFR-TK).
outcome_summary:
Aumolertinib (HS-10296/almonertinib; Hansoh) entered industry-sponsored Phase 2 in NSCLC through the Phase 1/2 APOLLO trial NCT02981108, which started 2017-05-08. That trial's Phase 2 part had ORR as its primary endpoint and enrolled 244 T790M+ patients. Within 4 years the program reached Phase 3: AENEAS (NCT03849768) started 2019-02-01. It met its primary endpoint of investigator-assessed PFS versus gefitinib: 19.3 vs 9.9 months, HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.36-0.60, P<.0001 (JCO 2022, PMID 35580297). China's NMPA approved Ameile on 2020-03-17 for T790M+ NSCLC after prior EGFR-TKI therapy, and the drug remains marketed in China. Many further Phase 3 trials are listed, including adjuvant, post-chemoradiation and combination studies.

Outside China the path was rockier, but these setbacks were regulatory or partner decisions, not efficacy or safety findings. EQRx licensed ex-China rights in July 2020. In November 2022 it said the FDA would not accept an interim monotherapy comparison and pushed a US filing to 2027, contingent on a Phase 3b against osimertinib (NCT05493501). EQRx terminated that trial and gave notice on 2023-08-01 that it was ending the license as part of a pipeline wind-down tied to its merger with Revolution Medicines. The CT.gov record says the trial was stopped for corporate reasons, "not related to any efficacy or safety issues."

The EU granted approval (Aumseqa) on 2026-02-12 for first-line EGFR ex19del/L858R and for T790M+ NSCLC, according to Hansoh's press release. Secondary reports say the European Commission revoked that authorisation on 2026-09-25 on a procedural, data-exclusivity issue (referencing osimertinib data) and that Hansoh resubmitted in late September 2026; this was not checked against a primary EC/EMA document.

The FDA has not approved the drug. Overall the program advanced and is approved for this disease in China, so this is not a failure.

evidence.notes:

This confirms EGFR as the target and inhibition as the action. That paper was published after Phase 2 entry, but it is only used here to confirm the mechanism.

(2) Disease: the ClinicalTrials.gov record for NCT02981108 is a Phase 1/2 open-label study sponsored by Jiangsu Hansoh Pharmaceutical. Its condition is "Nonsmall Cell Lung Cancer" (locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC that progressed after a prior EGFR TKI). The actual start date is 2017-05-08, which matches the recorded Phase 2 entry date. The record includes a "Phase 2 Extension" arm at the 110 mg RP2D. Disease mapping to MONDO:0005233 is correct.

(3) Claim: true. openFDA Drugs@FDA lists these ORIG approvals of EGFR-acting drugs for NSCLC, all before 2017-05-08:
- IRESSA (gefitinib, NDA021399): 2003-05-05
- TARCEVA (erlotinib, NDA021743): 2004-11-18
- GILOTRIF (afatinib, NDA201292): 2013-07-12
- TAGRISSO (osimertinib, NDA208065): 2015-11-13, for EGFR T790M+ NSCLC after EGFR TKI therapy. This is the same population as the aumolertinib entry trial.
- PORTRAZZA (necitumumab, BLA125547, anti-EGFR antibody): 2015-11-24, squamous NSCLC.

The FDA approval letter for IRESSA confirms the NSCLC indication. The 2003 label confirms EGFR-TK inhibition. The Tagrisso 2015 approval letter and label confirm the EGFR T790M+ NSCLC indication and that it is a kinase inhibitor. I did not separately check the breast cancer row (2007-03-13, presumably lapatinib) or the 2016-04-15 squamous row. Neither is needed, because the NSCLC approvals support the claim directly.

(4) The earliest source (2003) predates Phase 2 entry (2017-05-08) by about 14 years.

(5) The key evidence is FDA approvals held by other sponsors (AstraZeneca, OSI, Boehringer Ingelheim, Lilly), not Hansoh. So it is not sponsor-authored.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA accelerated approval of Lynparza (olaparib, AstraZeneca), NDA 206162, approval letter dated 12/19/2014: monotherapy for deleterious or suspected deleterious germline BRCA-mutated advanced ovarian cancer after three or more prior lines of chemotherapy. The 2014 label says olaparib inhibits PARP enzymes "including PARP1, PARP2, and PARP3".
outcome_summary:
The Phase 2 entry is confirmed. NCT02354586 (QUADRA) is a Phase 2 trial sponsored by Tesaro (industry) in ovarian cancer, and it started on 2015-03-23 (ACTUAL). QUADRA met its primary objective: 13 of 47 patients (28%) in the HRD-positive, platinum-sensitive primary efficacy population responded, one-sided p=0.00053 (Lancet Oncol 2019).

The program advanced within 4 years in two ways:
- **FDA approval:** on 2017-03-27, under NDA 208447 (Type 1 NME, priority review, orphan), Zejula capsules were approved for maintenance treatment of recurrent epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube or primary peritoneal cancer in complete or partial response to platinum-based chemotherapy.
- **New Phase 3:** PRIMA (NCT02655016) started on 2016-07-11.

The decisive trial was the Phase 3 ENGOT-OV16/NOVA study (NCT01847274), which began in 2013. It met its primary endpoint of progression-free survival:
- gBRCA cohort: 21.0 vs 5.5 months, HR 0.27
- non-gBRCA HRD-positive: HR 0.38
- overall non-gBRCA cohort: 9.3 vs 3.9 months, HR 0.45
- P<0.001 for all three comparisons (NEJM 2016)

Niraparib is still approved for ovarian cancer today. The current Zejula tablet label (NDA 214876, effective 2026-07-28) covers:
- first-line maintenance in HRD-positive advanced disease
- maintenance in germline BRCA-mutated recurrent disease

So the recurrent-disease indication has been narrowed to gBRCA-mutated patients and the first-line indication is limited to HRD-positive disease, but the drug remains approved for this disease. This is not a failure.

evidence.notes: (1) Target and action: Jones et al., J Med Chem 2009 (PMID 19873981), from IRBM/Merck Research Labs Rome, describes MK-4827 (niraparib) as a PARP1 and PARP2 inhibitor with IC50 of 3.8 nM and 2.1 nM. (2) Entry trial: NCT02354586 (QUADRA, sponsor Tesaro) is a Phase 2 single-arm study of niraparib in advanced, relapsed high-grade serous epithelial ovarian, fallopian tube or primary peritoneal cancer after three or four prior chemotherapy regimens. Its actual start date, 2015-03-23, matches the recorded Phase 2 entry date, and its conditions are Ovarian Neoplasms and Ovarian Cancer, so mapping it to MONDO:0008170 ovarian cancer is correct. (3) Claim: the FDA granted olaparib accelerated approval on December 19, 2014 for germline BRCA-mutated advanced ovarian cancer after three or more prior lines of chemotherapy. Three sources confirm this: the approval letter (NDA 206162, dated 12/19/2014), the AstraZeneca press release of 19 Dec 2014, and the FDA approval summary by Kim et al., Clin Cancer Res 2015 (PMID 26187614). The 2014 label, section 12.1, states that olaparib inhibits PARP1, PARP2 and PARP3. So the same targets, PARP1 and PARP2, were hit in the same direction (inhibition) for the same disease. Olaparib's approved population (gBRCAm, three or more prior lines) also closely overlaps QUADRA's (three or four prior regimens). (4) The approval on 2014-12-19 came about 3 months before Phase 2 entry on 2015-03-23, and it matches the date recorded in our database. (5) The key evidence is AstraZeneca's approval and the FDA's review. Niraparib's sponsor at Phase 2 entry was Tesaro, and the compound came from Merck, so the key source was not written by the drug's sponsor.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA accelerated approval of Lynparza (olaparib) capsules, NDA 206162, AstraZeneca, signed 12/19/2014. Indication: monotherapy for deleterious germline BRCA-mutated advanced ovarian cancer after 3 or more prior lines of chemotherapy. The 2014 label (section 12.1) describes olaparib as an inhibitor of PARP1, PARP2 and PARP3.
outcome_summary: The program reached Phase 2 and advanced to approval. The entry trial was GALAHAD (NCT02854436), a Janssen Phase 2 trial of single-agent niraparib in mCRPC with DNA-repair gene defects, which started on 2016-08-31. Its primary endpoint was objective response rate in measurable BRCA-mutated patients, reported at 34.2% (95% CI 23.7-46.0) on ClinicalTrials.gov and published in Lancet Oncol 2022. Within four years of that start, Janssen began the Phase 3 MAGNITUDE trial (NCT03748641, start 2019-01-25) of niraparib plus abiraterone acetate and prednisone versus placebo plus abiraterone acetate and prednisone. MAGNITUDE met its primary endpoint, rPFS by blinded central review. In the BRCA1/2 subgroup the hazard ratio was 0.53 (P=.001); in the HRR+ cohort it was 0.73 (P=.022). Futility was declared in the HRR- cohort (JCO 2023). The FDA approved Akeega (niraparib/abiraterone acetate, NDA 216793) with prednisone on 2023-08-11 for BRCA-mutated mCRPC. A supplemental approval on 2025-12-12 added BRCA2-mutated mCSPC, per the current label; that indication rests on the second Phase 3, AMPLITUDE (NCT04497844, start 2020-09-23). Two caveats on scope: the approval is for the fixed-dose combination with abiraterone, not niraparib alone, and only for the BRCA- or BRCA2-mutated subsets.

Indication: monotherapy for deleterious germline BRCA-mutated advanced ovarian cancer after 3 or more prior lines of chemotherapy. evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action are confirmed. In the Merck discovery paper (Jones et al., J Med Chem 2009, PMID 19873981), niraparib (MK-4827) inhibits PARP1 with an IC50 of 3.8 nM and PARP2 with an IC50 of 2.1 nM.

(2) The entry trial is NCT02854436 (Galahad), a Phase 2 study of niraparib monotherapy in men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer and DNA-repair anomalies. Its condition is listed as "Prostatic Neoplasms", its sponsor is Janssen R&D, and its actual start date is 2016-08-31, which matches the recorded Phase 2 entry date. So the disease mapping to prostate cancer is correct.

(3) The claim is only partly supported:
- **What holds:** an FDA-approved drug acting on the same targets (PARP1/PARP2) existed before Phase 2 entry. This was olaparib, approved for germline BRCA-mutated advanced ovarian cancer. openFDA gives the original approval status date as 20141219, and the letter's electronic signature is dated 12/19/2014, which matches the evidence rows' 2014-12-19.
- **What fails:** that approval was for ovarian cancer, not prostate cancer. Ovarian cancer is a different organ and sex-specific cancer, not a closely related disease. The only link is the shared BRCA/homologous-recombination-deficiency biomarker logic.
- No PARP inhibitor was approved for prostate cancer before entry. openFDA shows rucaparib's prostate efficacy supplement on 2020-05-15 and olaparib's on 2020-05-19 (FDA mCRPC letter, 208558 S-014). Rucaparib's first approval was 2016-12-19 and niraparib's was 2017-03-27, both after entry.
- If the benchmark counts ovarian cancer as "closely related" to prostate cancer, the claim holds. Otherwise the same-target approval exists, but the disease part of the claim is not met.

(4) The approval (2014-12-19) predates Phase 2 entry (2016-08-31) by about 20 months.

(5) The approval belongs to AstraZeneca, the olaparib sponsor. The niraparib entry trial was sponsored by Janssen, and niraparib originated at Merck. So the key evidence was not authored by the drug's sponsor.

On 2023-08-11 the FDA approved Akeega (a fixed-dose combination of niraparib and abiraterone acetate, NDA 216793) with prednisone for BRCA-mutated mCRPC, based on MAGNITUDE.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA supplemental BLA approval letter STN 103792/5250, Herceptin (trastuzumab, Genentech), dated October 20, 2010. It approved Herceptin for HER2-overexpressing metastatic gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma in patients with no prior treatment for metastatic disease. The approval rested on the ToGA phase 3 trial (Bang YJ et al., Lancet 2010;376:687-697, PMID 20728210, NCT01041404).
outcome_summary: The program advanced and the drug is approved for this disease. The entry trial, DESTINY-Gastric02 (NCT04014075), was a Daiichi Sankyo single-arm Phase 2 in Western patients that started 2019-11-26 (actual start per ClinicalTrials.gov) and is completed. It met its primary endpoint of ORR by independent central review: 38% at the primary analysis and 42% at the update (Lancet Oncology 2023). The FDA approved Enhertu for HER2-positive gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma after a prior trastuzumab-based regimen on 2021-01-15. That approval was based on the randomized Phase 2 DESTINY-Gastric01 (NCT03329690; ORR primary endpoint; confirmed ORR 40.5% vs 11.3%; OS 12.5 vs 8.4 months versus irinotecan or paclitaxel). The global Phase 3 DESTINY-Gastric04 (NCT04704934) started 2021-05-21. Its primary endpoint was OS against ramucirumab plus paclitaxel, and it met it: median 14.7 vs 11.4 months, HR 0.70, P=0.004 (NEJM 2025). Both the Phase 3 start and the approval fell within four years of Phase 2 entry. The program is not a failure. The main safety signal was adjudicated drug-related ILD or pneumonitis, in about 14% of patients in DESTINY-Gastric04.
key_trial: NCT03329690 (DESTINY-Gastric01, randomized Phase 2 that supported the FDA approval). The entry trial was NCT04014075 (DESTINY-Gastric02) and the confirmatory Phase 3 was NCT04704934 (DESTINY-Gastric04).

It enrolled patients with HER2-positive unresectable or metastatic gastric or GEJ adenocarcinoma whose disease progressed on or after trastuzumab. Its actual start date, 2019-11-26, matches the recorded entry date, and the population maps to gastric cancer (MONDO:0001056). claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA approval letter NDA 022465/S-010 (Votrient/pazopanib, GlaxoSmithKline), dated 04/26/2012, approving pazopanib "for the treatment of patients with advanced soft tissue sarcoma (STS) who have received prior chemotherapy". Supporting trial: PALETTE, van der Graaf et al., Lancet 2012 (PMID 22595799).
outcome_summary:
Lilly's CAMPFIRE trial (NCT04145700) was a randomized, open-label Phase 1/2 study in pediatric and young-adult patients with relapsed or refractory synovial sarcoma. It compared ramucirumab plus gemcitabine and docetaxel against gemcitabine and docetaxel alone. The trial started on 2020-03-04 and enrolled 23 patients (16 on ramucirumab, 7 on control).

It was terminated on 2023-02-23 because it met the protocol's futility criteria; that is the "why stopped" wording on the ClinicalTrials.gov record.

**Primary endpoint (progression-free survival) not met:**
- Median PFS was 2.10 months with ramucirumab and 2.03 months on control.
- The Bayesian posterior mean hazard ratio was 2.62 (80% credible interval 1.19 to 4.46), pointing against ramucirumab. Success required a posterior probability above 99% that the HR was below 1.
- Overall response rate was 6.3% versus 0%.

**Exposure was achieved:**
- Ramucirumab Cmax was 231 µg/mL, and the trough on Cycle 2 Day 1 was 55.4 µg/mL. Both exceed the adult-derived efficacy target of a trough of at least 50 µg/mL (Pilbeam et al., Pediatr Blood Cancer 2024).
- The FDA label's pediatric section says PK in these trials was within the adult range, safety and effectiveness in children were assessed but not established, and no new safety signals were seen.

This means the drug reached exposure judged adequate, and adding VEGFR2 blockade to chemotherapy gave no clinical benefit. VEGFR2 target engagement itself was not measured, so the engagement claim rests on PK as a proxy. A preclinical paper showing xenograft responses in synovial sarcoma models did not carry over to patients. That is why the failure code is F2 rather than F1 (no exposure) or F5/F6 (toxicity).

No Phase 3 trial or FDA approval for synovial sarcoma followed within four years or since. Ramucirumab is approved only for adult gastric/GEJ adenocarcinoma, NSCLC, colorectal cancer and HCC.

One limitation: my web search budget was used up, so I could not find a peer-reviewed results paper or a Lilly press release for this trial. A 2023 review (PMC10618684) said results were not yet available.

failure_second.reasoning:
The program is Lilly's ramucirumab (anti-VEGFR2/KDR antibody) in relapsed, recurrent or refractory synovial sarcoma in children and young adults. The entry trial was CAMPFIRE, NCT04145700 (J1S-MC-JV02), a randomized open-label Phase 1/2 study. It compared ramucirumab 9 mg/kg plus gemcitabine and docetaxel against gemcitabine and docetaxel alone, with 23 patients randomized 16 to 7. It started on 2020-03-04 and ended on 2023-02-23 with status TERMINATED. The registry gives the reason as: "Study terminated for meeting protocol specified futility criteria."

Posted results:
- **Primary endpoint:** median PFS was 2.10 months with ramucirumab versus 2.03 months without it.
- **Bayesian analysis:** the posterior mean HR was 2.62 (80% credible interval 1.19-4.46), pointing toward harm. The posterior probability that HR < 1 was 0.051, far below the ≥99% needed to claim success.
- **Response:** ORR was 6.3% versus 0%, with no complete responses.

Exposure was shown. Ramucirumab Cmin was 73.3 µg/mL on C1D8 and 55.4 µg/mL on C2D1 (geometric means), and no treatment-emergent anti-drug antibodies were seen. Those troughs are at or above the ≥50 µg/mL target that adult population PK and exposure-efficacy analyses set for ramucirumab (Pilbeam et al., Pediatr Blood Cancer 2024, PMID 38189770). The trial measured no pharmacodynamic marker of VEGFR2 blockade.

The preclinical rationale came from mouse models: anti-VEGFR2 (DC101) plus chemotherapy gave stable disease and partial regressions in synovial sarcoma xenografts (Lowery et al., Oncotarget 2019, PMID 31565186). This did not carry over to patients.

So adequate drug exposure was shown, but anti-angiogenic VEGFR2 blockade added nothing to chemotherapy in synovial sarcoma. That is the F2 pattern: the drug reached its exposure target, but the biology did not translate.

Alternatives considered:
- **F1 rejected:** exposure targets were met.
- **F5/F6 rejected:** the stopping reason is futility, not toxicity. Serious adverse events were more frequent with ramucirumab (8/16 vs 2/6), but no source names them as the cause.
- **F7 considered but secondary:** the sponsor lists as a limitation that matched historical controls did much better than the randomized control arm, which made the hazard-ratio estimates highly variable. The trial was also small. Even so, the randomized comparison itself showed no PFS difference, so lack of efficacy, not design, is the main explanation.

No later ramucirumab synovial sarcoma trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov. No peer-reviewed CAMPFIRE results paper or Lilly press release was found. PubMed has no record citing NCT04145700, and the web search budget ran out before a broader search. Confidence is moderate, because no publication gives the investigators' own reading of why it failed.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: The FDA approved Genentech's Trastuzumab (Herceptin, BLA 103792) on September 25, 1998 (approval letter ref. 98-0369), for metastatic breast cancer whose tumors overexpress HER2. The 1998 label says trastuzumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds the extracellular domain of HER2.
outcome_summary:
Disitamab vedotin (RC48), an anti-HER2 ADC with an MMAE payload, first entered industry-sponsored Phase 2 for breast cancer on 2016-12-23 in RemeGen's Phase 1b/2 C003 CANCER trial (NCT03052634) in HER2-positive and HER2-low advanced breast cancer. That trial set the RP2D at 2.0 mg/kg every two weeks. At that dose the objective response rate was 42.9% in HER2-overexpressing disease and 33.3% in HER2-low disease (Cancer Commun 2024, PMID 38940019).

The program advanced within the 4-year window. The Phase 2/3 trial RC48-C006 (NCT03500380) started 2018-04-24 and compared the drug with lapatinib plus capecitabine. The Phase 3 trial RC48-C012 (NCT04400695) in HER2-low metastatic breast cancer started 2020-09-29 and is still recruiting, with primary completion estimated for 2027-12.

The Phase 3 stage of RC48-C006 enrolled HER2-positive breast cancer with liver metastases after trastuzumab and taxanes (n=104). It met its primary endpoint: blinded independent review PFS was 9.9 vs 4.9 months, HR 0.56 (95.48% CI 0.35-0.91), p=0.01. Grade 3 or worse treatment-related adverse events were similar between arms (37.7% vs 36.0%) (Nat Commun 2026, PMID 42802176).

On that basis China's NMPA approved disitamab vedotin on 2025-04-30 for HER2-positive breast cancer with liver metastases after trastuzumab and taxanes. RemeGen's pipeline page lists HER2-positive and HER2-low breast cancer with liver metastasis as "China Launched". There is no FDA approval for breast cancer. Pfizer/Seagen are running a US Phase 1/2 trial in HER2-expressing breast cancer (NCT06966453).

The status "approved_for_disease" therefore reflects a China (NMPA) approval, not an FDA one. The program did not fail.

- Tykerb (lapatinib), NDA022059, 2007-03-13
- Perjeta (pertuzumab), BLA125409, 2012-06-08
- Kadcyla (T-DM1), BLA125427, 2013-02-22; this one is also a HER2-directed ADC.
I did not check the 2013-07-12 NSCLC row (probably afatinib, which is mainly an EGFR drug), and the claim does not depend on it.
(5) The key evidence is FDA approvals held by Genentech and Novartis, not RemeGen work. I did not look into the clinical outcome, as instructed.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA accelerated approval letter, NDA 21-399, IRESSA (gefitinib, an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor), to AstraZeneca, signed 5/5/03. It covers monotherapy for locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC after failure of both platinum-based and docetaxel chemotherapies.
outcome_summary:
Rezivertinib (BPI-7711) is a third-generation EGFR TKI from Beta Pharma. Its Phase 2 entry is confirmed: NCT03386955 is an industry-sponsored Phase I/IIa trial (Beta Pharma Shanghai) in EGFR-mutant / T790M-positive NSCLC with an actual start date of 2017-08-16, and 215 patients were enrolled.

Phase 2 results:
- Phase 2b T790M trial (NCT03812809, n=226): blinded central review (BICR) objective response rate (ORR) was 64.6% (J Thorac Oncol 2022).
- First-line Phase IIa cohort of NCT03386955: BICR ORR was 83.7% (BMC Med 2023).

The program advanced within 4 years. The Phase 3 REZOR trial (NCT03866499, double-blind, rezivertinib versus gefitinib first line, n=369) began enrolling on 2019-07-15 per the published paper. ClinicalTrials.gov gives an actual start of 2021-04-30. Either date falls before the 2021-08-16 cutoff. REZOR met its primary endpoint: median PFS by blinded central review was 19.3 versus 9.6 months (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.36-0.63, p<0.0001), with no new safety signals (Lancet Respir Med 2025). A 2026 analysis also found better CNS PFS (HR 0.58).

Current status: per a 2026 Chin Med J review, China's NMPA approved rezivertinib on 2024-05-15 for EGFR T790M-positive NSCLC that progressed on or after an EGFR-TKI, and on 2024-10-29 for first-line EGFR-mutant advanced NSCLC. I found no FDA approval, so 'approved_for_disease' here means a Chinese approval. The program did not fail.

Data caveat: the case record lists 'SH-1028' as a code name, but a 2022 J Thorac Oncol editorial lists rezivertinib and SH-1028 as separate drugs (SH-1028 is a different company's compound). That alias looks mis-mapped, though it does not change this outcome.

evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: rezivertinib (BPI-7711) is described as "a novel third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor selective for EGFR-sensitizing and T790M mutations" in the published Phase 1 report of the entry trial NCT03386955 (Shi et al., J Thorac Oncol 2022, PMID 35181498). That paper has authors from Beta Pharma Inc. and Beta Pharma (Shanghai), the sponsor. So EGFR (inhibitor) is correct.

(2) Disease: the ClinicalTrials.gov record for NCT03386955 is sponsored by Beta Pharma Shanghai (org study ID BPI-7711-2015-001). It is a Phase I/IIa trial titled "BPI-7711 Capsule in Patients With EGFR Mutation T790M Positive Non-small Cell Lung Cancer" with condition "Non-small Cell Lung Cancer". The Phase IIa part enrolls treatment-naive patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC. Its actual start date, 2017-08-16, matches the recorded Phase 2 entry date. The NSCLC mapping (MONDO:0005233) is correct.

(3) and (4) Claim: verified from the FDA approval letters (text pulled from the accessdata PDFs) and from openFDA Drugs@FDA original approval dates. Several EGFR-targeting drugs were FDA-approved for NSCLC before 2017-08-16:
- gefitinib (IRESSA), NDA 21-399, accelerated approval 2003-05-05 (letter signed 5/5/03)
- erlotinib (TARCEVA), NDA 21-743, 2004-11-18, for locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC after at least one prior chemotherapy regimen
- afatinib (GILOTRIF), NDA 201292, 2013-07-12 (date from openFDA)
- osimertinib (TAGRISSO), NDA 208065, accelerated approval 2015-11-13, for metastatic EGFR T790M-positive NSCLC that progressed on or after EGFR TKI therapy. This is the same indication and mechanism class as rezivertinib.
- necitumumab (PORTRAZZA), BLA 125547, 2015-11-24 (date from openFDA)
- gefitinib re-approval, NDA 206995, 2015-07-13 (from openFDA)

The 2003, 2004, 2013 and 2015 NSCLC dates in our evidence rows all match the FDA sources. The breast cancer and squamous cell carcinoma rows are not needed for the claim, and I did not verify them individually.

(5) Sponsor: the key evidence is FDA regulatory action on other companies' drugs (AstraZeneca, OSI, Boehringer Ingelheim). None of it was authored by Beta Pharma.

Data-quality flag: our record lists "SH-1028" and "[14C]SH-1028" as code names for rezivertinib. PubMed shows SH-1028 is a different third-generation EGFR TKI (oritinib) from Nanjing Sanhome Pharmaceutical (Han et al., Front Pharmacol 2021, PMID 33986687). Lau & Ou (J Thorac Oncol 2022, PMID 36192074) list rezivertinib and SH-1028 as separate agents. Both drugs inhibit EGFR, so this claim is unaffected, but the code-name mapping should be fixed. The WebSearch budget was used up, so all checks used direct curl and WebFetch to primary sources.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA Purple Book: BLA 103174, Prolastin (Alpha-1-Proteinase Inhibitor (Human)), current holder Grifols Therapeutics, original approval December 2, 1987. The current Prolastin-C Liquid label gives the indication as augmentation therapy in adults with emphysema due to severe hereditary alpha1-PI (alpha1-antitrypsin) deficiency.
outcome_summary: Fazirsiran (ARO-AAT/TAK-999) is a GalNAc-siRNA from Arrowhead that silences SERPINA1 to treat liver disease from alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ). It entered industry Phase 2 on 2019-08-07 with SEQUOIA (NCT03945292, AROAAT2001). This was a placebo-controlled trial with 40 patients, sponsored by Arrowhead. It met its primary endpoint: at week 16, serum Z-AAT changed by -62%, -85% and -93% at 25, 100 and 200 mg versus +4.6% on placebo (CT.gov results; all p<0.0001). Liver Z-AAT fell by a median of 93%, globule burden dropped, and no adverse event led to discontinuation (Clark et al., Gastroenterology 2024, PMID 38964420). In the open-label Phase 2 AROAAT2002 (NCT03946449), total liver Z-AAT fell by about 80–90% (Strnad et al., NEJM 2022, PMID 35748699). Takeda licensed the program in October 2020. Takeda started the Phase 3 REDWOOD trial (NCT05677971; primary endpoint: at least one stage of METAVIR fibrosis improvement at week 106 in F2–F3 patients) on 2023-03-06, within the 4-year window. Takeda later started a second Phase 3 (NCT06165341, start 2024-03-01) and a Phase 3 extension (NCT05899673, start 2023-08-08). The drug is not approved. No stop has occurred, so this is not a failure.

evidence.earliest_source: FDA Purple Book: BLA 103174, Prolastin (Alpha-1-Proteinase Inhibitor (Human)), current holder Grifols Therapeutics, original approval December 2, 1987. The current Prolastin-C Liquid label gives the indication as augmentation therapy in adults with emphysema due to severe hereditary alpha1-PI (alpha1-antitrypsin) deficiency.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and direction: confirmed from a pre-entry source. Arrowhead's FY2018 10-K (filed 2018-12-11) describes ARO-AAT as an RNAi therapeutic "designed to knock down the Alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) gene transcript and reduce the hepatic production of the mutant AAT protein". That matches SERPINA1 with gene_expression_reduction. Wooddell et al., JCI Insight 2020 (PMID 32379724; authors from Arrowhead and Saint Louis University) also reports that ARO-AAT reduces serum AAT. ChEMBL CHEMBL5095435 (fazirsiran) has no mechanism record.

(2) Entry trial: NCT03945292 (AROAAT2001, SEQUOIA) is a Phase 2 trial sponsored by Arrowhead. Its condition is Alpha 1-Antitrypsin Deficiency and its actual start date was 2019-08-07, the same as the phase2_entry date. The disease mapping is correct.

(3) Claim: only partly true. The FDA-approved drugs for AATD before 2019-08-07 are all plasma-derived alpha1-proteinase inhibitor augmentation products. The Purple Book lists Prolastin (BLA 103174, 1987-12-02), Aralast (BLA 125039, 2002-12-23), Zemaira (BLA 125078, 2003-07-08) and Glassia (BLA 125325, 2010-07-01). The disease is the same, and the active substance is the SERPINA1 gene product itself: UniProt P01009 (gene SERPINA1) is alpha-1-antitrypsin / alpha-1 protease inhibitor. These are replacement therapies, though; they do not act on SERPINA1. ChEMBL CHEMBL4297879 gives the mechanism as "Leukocyte elastase inhibitor", with ELANE (CHEMBL248) as the target. Open Targets lists no drugs or clinical candidates under SERPINA1 (ENSG00000197249). The direction is also opposite: augmentation raises AAT protein, mainly to protect the lung, while fazirsiran lowers SERPINA1 expression to reduce liver Z-AAT. The claim is right if "same target" means the same gene product. It is wrong under a ChEMBL or Open Targets definition of the pharmacological target, and under a same-direction reading.

(4) Date: the evidence row's approval_date_used of 2014-12-31 is not the earliest approval. The earliest is Prolastin on 1987-12-02, and every approval listed above predates Phase 2 entry. ChEMBL gives this molecule a first_approval of 2015, which may be where the 2014/2015 date came from.

(5) Sponsor: Prolastin is held by Grifols, and the other products by Takeda and CSL Behring. None of these approvals came from Arrowhead, the sponsor at Phase 2 entry. Takeda holds the Aralast and Glassia BLAs and is named on fazirsiran's code name TAK-999. I did not verify when Takeda's involvement with fazirsiran began, and it does not concern the earliest source, Prolastin.

outcome.advance_event: Takeda started the Phase 3 REDWOOD trial (NCT05677971, TAK-999-3001) of fazirsiran in AATD-associated liver disease with METAVIR F2–F3 fibrosis on 2023-03-06 (actual start date). That is about 3.6 years after the Phase 2 entry on 2019-08-07 (NCT03945292, AROAAT2001/SEQUOIA). Arrowhead's SEC filings confirm a $40.0M milestone paid when Takeda began the Phase 3 REDWOOD study in March 2023.
outcome.summary: Fazirsiran (ARO-AAT/TAK-999) is a GalNAc-siRNA from Arrowhead that silences SERPINA1 to treat liver disease from alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (PiZZ). It entered industry Phase 2 on 2019-08-07 with SEQUOIA (NCT03945292, AROAAT2001). This was a placebo-controlled trial with 40 patients, sponsored by Arrowhead. It met its primary endpoint: at week 16, serum Z-AAT changed by -62%, -85% and -93% at 25, 100 and 200 mg versus +4.6% on placebo (CT.gov results; all p<0.0001). Liver Z-AAT fell by a median of 93%, globule burden dropped, and no adverse event led to discontinuation (Clark et al., Gastroenterology 2024, PMID 38964420). In the open-label Phase 2 AROAAT2002 (NCT03946449), total liver Z-AAT fell by about 80–90% (Strnad et al., NEJM 2022, PMID 35748699). Takeda licensed the program in October 2020. Takeda started the Phase 3 REDWOOD trial (NCT05677971; primary endpoint: at least one stage of METAVIR fibrosis improvement at week 106 in F2–F3 patients) on 2023-03-06, within the 4-year window. Takeda later started a second Phase 3 (NCT06165341, start 2024-03-01) and a Phase 3 extension (NCT05899673, start 2023-08-08). As of June 30, 2026, Arrowhead's 10-Q (filed 2026-08-04) still lists fazirsiran as Phase 3, partnered with Takeda. REDWOOD is still recruiting, with primary completion estimated for 2029-01. The drug is not approved. No stop has occurred, so this is not a failure.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA approval of troglitazone (Rezulin, NDA 020720, Parke-Davis/Warner-Lambert, now listed under Pfizer; companion NDA 020719 Prelay, Sankyo) on 1997-01-29 for type 2 diabetes. Its label says it acts by binding PPAR nuclear receptors. The evidence row's date, 1999-05-25, is the approval of rosiglitazone (Avandia, NDA 021071), whose original label calls it a "highly selective and potent agonist" of PPARγ and indicates it for type 2 diabetes.
outcome_summary:
KDT501 is a hops-derived isohumulone made by KinDex Pharmaceuticals. It is a modest partial PPARγ agonist, and later work showed it also acts on the Tas2r108 bitter taste receptor. Its first industry Phase 2 was NCT02444910. That trial was open-label and single-arm, with 9 obese insulin-resistant or prediabetic patients. It ran from April to November 2015 with the University of Kentucky, and its registered condition is type 2 diabetes.

The FDA had capped dosing at 28 days per patient, with a limit on drug exposure (AUC) set from rodent toxicology. Doses were escalated from 600 to 1000 mg twice daily.

The primary endpoint was the change in 2-hour OGTT glucose at day 28. It fell from 171 to 162 mg/dL, which was not significant. Fasting glucose, HbA1c, fructosamine, HOMA-IR, Matsuda index, clamp insulin sensitivity and insulin secretion also did not change.

Some biomarkers did move. Total and high-molecular-weight adiponectin rose, TNF-α fell, and triglycerides 4 hours after a fatty meal fell. The drug was well tolerated, with mostly mild GI events (Kern et al. 2017, J Endocr Soc).

No later trial of KDT501 in diabetes was registered. KinDex's current pipeline lists KDT501 only for PCOS and NASH, with the next goal being a PCOS study. Patsnap Synapse lists type 2 diabetes as inactive at Phase 2.

No company statement explains why diabetes development was dropped. Stop reason = efficacy is my inference: the primary endpoint was missed and insulin sensitivity did not improve, and the company then moved the drug to other indications. That pivot also has a business/strategic side (F8).

F4 is the best code because the adipose and inflammation markers improved but the glucose and insulin sensitivity outcomes did not. F7 is a strong alternative: the authors attribute the null result to the tiny sample, the 28-day FDA-capped treatment and a possibly suboptimal dose.

Its label says it acts by binding PPAR nuclear receptors. The evidence row's date, 1999-05-25, is the approval of rosiglitazone (Avandia, NDA 021071), whose original label calls it a "highly selective and potent agonist" of PPARγ and indicates it for type 2 diabetes.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action. KDT501 is a modest partial PPARγ agonist. Konda et al., PLoS One 2014 (PMID 24498211), reports "only modest, partial PPARγ agonist activity" and a gene-expression profile different from rosiglitazone's. The NCT02444910 record also describes a "modest, partial agonist effect" at PPARγ. Both describe the mechanism as pleiotropic: the CT.gov record names GPR120 agonism first, and Lum et al. 2017 (PMID 28930429) later found PTGR2 as a target. PPARG partial agonist is therefore a correct annotation but probably not the main mechanism. The PPARγ annotation rests on a sponsor-authored paper: all Konda 2014 authors worked for or consulted for KinDex, which funded the study.
(2) Disease. NCT02444910 (KinDex with the University of Kentucky, Phase 2, start 2015-04, n=9, single arm) lists "Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2" as its condition. Its eligibility criteria, however, require IGT, IFG or metabolic syndrome with HbA1c <7.0% and fasting plasma glucose <126 mg/dL, and the title says "Insulin Resistant Subjects". So it enrolled non-diabetic, insulin-resistant or prediabetic people, not patients with type 2 diabetes. Mapping to MONDO:0005148 is therefore not strictly correct, but the actual population is closely related to type 2 diabetes.
(3) Claim. It holds for type 2 diabetes, and through the claim's "closely related" wording for the insulin-resistant population. Three PPARγ-agonist thiazolidinediones were FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes before 2015-04-01 (dates from openFDA and Drugs@FDA): troglitazone 1997-01-29, rosiglitazone 1999-05-25 (the date in the evidence row) and pioglitazone 1999-07-15. Lehmann et al. 1995 (PMID 7768881) shows that thiazolidinediones are selective PPARγ activators. Troglitazone was later withdrawn, but its approval happened.
(4) Timing. Every approval came 15 or more years before Phase 2 entry.
(5) Sponsor authorship. The key evidence is FDA approvals held by other companies (Warner-Lambert/Sankyo, SmithKline Beecham, Takeda), not KinDex.

outcome.advance_event: None. Within four years of the 2015-04 Phase 2 start, no Phase 3 trial started and there was no FDA approval. A ClinicalTrials.gov search for KDT501 / KDT-501 returns only NCT02444910. The type 2 diabetes program never went past this one small Phase 2 study.

failure_second.reasoning:
Code F1, with moderate-to-low confidence. No company statement, press release or SEC filing says why KDT501 stopped. KinDex was private, and I found no discontinuation notice. The code comes from the trial data and the publications that followed, not from a stated reason. My web-search budget had run out, so I could check only ClinicalTrials.gov, PubMed/PMC and the Wayback Machine (which was mostly unreachable).

What the primary sources show:
(1) There was only one Phase 2 trial, NCT02444910 (KinDex with the University of Kentucky). It was open-label and single-arm, enrolled 9 insulin-resistant prediabetic or metabolic-syndrome subjects, started in April 2015 and was completed in November 2015. No results are posted. A ClinicalTrials.gov search for KDT501 or KinDex finds no other trial and no Phase 3.
(2) Kern et al., J Endocr Soc 2017 (PMID 29264518):
- An agreement with FDA limited dosing to 28 days and capped exposure at an AUC0-12 of 22,500 ng·h/mL. The Phase 1 cap was set to match exposure in the most sensitive toxicology species (rodents).
- Exposure was reached: the mean AUC0-12 at day 28 was 14,047 ng·h/mL.
- The primary endpoint, 2-hour OGTT glucose, did not change significantly. HbA1c, fructosamine, HOMA-IR, the Matsuda index and clamp insulin sensitivity did not change either.
- Plasma adiponectin and HMW adiponectin rose, TNF-alpha fell, and postprandial triglycerides fell.
- The drug was well tolerated, with only mild or moderate GI side effects, so toxicity is not the explanation.
(3) Finlin et al., Front Endocrinol 2017 (PMID 29033896), which analysed adipose biopsies from the same trial, states directly: "we found no evidence of KDT501 PPARgamma agonism in humans. Direct PPARgamma target genes such as adiponectin, LPL, CD36, PNPLA2, and FABP4 were not induced." The authors attribute the adiponectin rise to a post-transcriptional, non-PPARgamma mechanism. They add that "longer treatment or higher blood levels of KDT501" may be needed.
(4) Later sponsor-linked papers changed the proposed mechanism. Kok et al., Mol Metab 2018 (PMID 30120064) says KDT501 signals through the bitter taste receptor Tas2r108. Wu et al., Endocrinology 2019 (PMID 30418546) moved to a mouse model of PCOS. Lum et al., ACS Chem Biol 2017 (PMID 28930429) identifies PTGR2 as a target. None of these reports further T2D clinical development.

Why F1: the program's stated target is PPARG, as a partial agonist. Exposure was shown in humans, but engagement of PPARgamma was explicitly not found in human adipose tissue, and no glycemic effect followed. Dose and duration were held below what might have been needed by the FDA exposure cap.

Alternatives:
- F4: some biomarkers moved (adiponectin, TNF-alpha, postprandial triglycerides) while glucose and insulin sensitivity did not.
- F7: the trial was tiny, 28 days long and uncontrolled, and the authors blame the null result on its short duration and small size.
- unknown: no source states the reason for stopping.

The reason the program stopped is unclear. The best-supported mechanistic explanation is the absence of PPARgamma engagement.

adjudication.reasoning:
ADVANCEMENT. The KDT501 program did not advance within 4 years.
- The CT.gov API record for NCT02444910 shows KinDex as sponsor with the University of Kentucky. It is Phase 2, single-group and open-label, with n=9. It started 2015-04, finished 2015-11 (COMPLETED) and has no posted results.
- CT.gov searches for "KDT501", "KDT-501" and sponsor "KinDex" each return only this one trial. There is no Phase 3 and no FDA approval.
- KinDex's pipeline page now lists KDT501 only for PCOS and NASH, framed around TAS2R modulation. It says the "next goal is to study KDT501 in PCOS patients". Diabetes is no longer an indication for KDT501.
- The pipeline's s4=0 is therefore correct. Its stop reason ("completed, no results posted, no reason stated") matches the registry. One small labelling issue: the event is recorded as "suspended", but the trial was completed. That does not change the outcome.

DISEASE MAPPING (minor, does not change the outcome). The registered condition is "Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2". But the eligibility criteria require IGT, IFG or metabolic syndrome, with HbA1c <7.0% and FPG <126 mg/dL. Exclusion criterion 1 is "Prior or current history of T2DM". Kern 2017 describes the population as nondiabetic, insulin-resistant prediabetic subjects. So MONDO:0005148 is imprecise, though the population is closely related to type 2 diabetes.

CLAIM. The claim holds and predates entry. Drugs@FDA/openFDA dates:
- Troglitazone (Rezulin, NDA020720): approved 1997-01-29.
- Rosiglitazone (Avandia, NDA021071): approved 1999-05-25. Its 1999 label calls it "a highly selective and potent agonist for the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-gamma (PPARγ)" and indicates it for type 2 diabetes.
- Pioglitazone (Actos, NDA021073): approved 1999-07-15.

All three were approved more than 15 years before the 2015-04 Phase 2 entry, for type 2 diabetes, which is the mapped disease and closely related to the actual prediabetic population.

The PPARG partial-agonist annotation comes only from sponsor-authored in vitro work. Konda 2014 (all authors KinDex employees or consultants) reports "only modest, partial PPARγ agonist activity". This weakens the target annotation but not the claim as worded.

FAILURE CODE: F1. No source states why the type 2 diabetes program stopped, so the code comes from the trial results.
- Exposure was reached. Mean AUC0-12 was 14,047 ng·h/mL, under an FDA-agreed cap of 22,500. Dosing was limited to 28 days.
- Finlin et al. 2017 analysed adipose biopsies from this same trial and states: "we found no evidence of KDT501 PPARγ agonism in humans. Direct PPARγ target genes such as adiponectin, LPL, CD36, PNPLA2, and FABP4 were not induced". It says the data are "not consistent with KDT501 directly stimulating PPARγ transcriptional activity". It attributes the adiponectin rise to a post-transcriptional mechanism.
- Kern et al. 2017 reports no significant change in the OGTT primary endpoint (2-h glucose 171 to 162 mg/dL), HOMA-IR, the Matsuda index or clamp insulin sensitivity.
- The company later reframed KDT501's mechanism around TAS2R bitter-taste receptors (pipeline page), which fits with the PPARγ hypothesis having been abandoned.

So engagement of the annotated target (PPARG) was looked for in humans and not found, and the glycemic efficacy expected from a TZD-like mechanism did not appear. That is F1 for this target-based rule.

Alternatives considered:
- F4: adiponectin, TNF-α and postprandial triglycerides moved but glycemia did not. I rate it weaker because the authors say these markers moved through a non-PPARγ mechanism, and the primary endpoint was itself a glycemic surrogate.
- F7: n=9, 28 days, uncontrolled. The authors cite the small sample, short duration and possibly suboptimal dose.
- F8: the company's pivot to PCOS/NASH.

Confidence is moderate because the stop reason is never stated.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA approval of Eulexin (flutamide), NDA 018554 (Schering), approved 1989-01-27. Its label indication is use with LHRH agonists for metastatic (Stage D2) carcinoma of the prostate, and it acts as an antiandrogen that inhibits androgen uptake and nuclear binding. Later prostate-cancer approvals of AR antagonists, all before the 2016-04-12 entry: Casodex (bicalutamide), NDA 020498, 1995-10-04; Nilandron (nilutamide), NDA 020169, 1996-09-19; Xtandi (enzalutamide), NDA 203415, 2012-08-31, for mCRPC after docetaxel, the same castration-resistant setting as the entry trial.
outcome_summary: Rezvilutamide (SHR3680) is Jiangsu Hengrui's oral second-generation AR antagonist. It entered prostate cancer through the industry-sponsored Phase I/II trial NCT02691975 in mCRPC, which started 2016-04-12; the Phase 2 portion's primary endpoint was rPFS. The program advanced within four years. The randomized Phase 3 CHART trial (NCT03520478, n=654, vs bicalutamide, both with ADT, in high-volume mHSPC) started 2018-05-30. CHART met both co-primary endpoints at preplanned interim analyses: BICR-assessed rPFS HR 0.44 (95% CI 0.33-0.58, p<0.0001) and OS HR 0.58 (0.44-0.77, p=0.0001) (Lancet Oncol 2022). China approved rezvilutamide in June 2022 for mHSPC with high tumour burden (Drugs 2023, "Rezvilutamide: First Approval"). Hengrui keeps developing it in prostate cancer, including a newer Phase 3 in mHSPC (NCT07241416, started 2025-12). Drugs@FDA lists no US approval (openFDA query returned no matches), so the approval is Chinese, not FDA. Some combination studies were terminated, such as NCT04102124 and NCT03741712, but the monotherapy program was not stopped and this is not a failure.

It enrolled patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, its listed conditions are Hormone Refractory Prostate Cancer and Metastatic Prostate Carcinoma, and its actual start date is 2016-04-12, the same as the recorded Phase 2 entry. So the prostate cancer mapping is correct. (3) Claim: Drugs@FDA/openFDA shows several original approvals of AR antagonists for prostate cancer well before 2016: flutamide NDA018554 on 1989-01-27, bicalutamide NDA020498 on 1995-10-04, nilutamide NDA020169 on 1996-09-19, and enzalutamide NDA203415 on 2012-08-31. The 2012 Xtandi label says "XTANDI is indicated for the treatment of patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer who have previously received docetaxel", and its section 12.1 says "Enzalutamide is an androgen receptor inhibitor ... competitively inhibit androgen binding to androgen receptors". The Casodex label calls bicalutamide "a non-steroidal androgen receptor inhibitor" indicated with an LHRH analog for Stage D2 metastatic prostate carcinoma. The three prostate-cancer evidence rows (1989-01-27, 1995-10-04, 2012-08-31) match these approval dates exactly. The two hypogonadism rows (1953, 2014) are presumably testosterone products. Facts were checked with ClinicalTrials.gov API v2, the openFDA drugsfda and label endpoints (which mirror Drugs@FDA), the 2012 Xtandi label PDF on accessdata.fda.gov, and PubMed E-utilities. Clinical outcome was not researched.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA approval letter, BLA 125370 (Benlysta/belimumab), March 9, 2011. It approves belimumab for adult patients with active, autoantibody-positive SLE who are receiving standard therapy. The 2011 label says belimumab is specific for soluble BLyS, "also referred to as BAFF and TNFSF13B", and blocks it from binding its receptors on B cells.
outcome_summary: Phase 2 entry is confirmed. NCT04058028 is an Amgen-sponsored Phase 2b dose-ranging trial of rozibafusp alfa at 70, 280 or 420 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks against placebo in active SLE with inadequate response to standard of care. It started on 2020-02-19 (actual), used response-adaptive randomization, enrolled 244 patients and ended on 2023-07-25. The decision came from Amgen's Q1 2023 earnings release (8-K, 2023-04-27), which says the Phase 2b study "was stopped for futility". The Q4 2022 release had still described it as enrolling. The posted results back this up. The primary endpoint was SRI-4 response at week 52: placebo 26/43 (60%), 70 mg 29/51 (57%), 280 mg 21/35 (60%) and 420 mg 35/48 (73%). There was no dose-response, the placebo response was high, and no statistical test was posted. The analysis counted only patients who could reach the visit before the termination decision, and 53 patients left the study by 'Decision by Sponsor'. Serious adverse events were similar across arms (placebo 6/62, 420 mg 3/87), so safety was not the reason for stopping. No Phase 3 trial was ever registered. Rozibafusp alfa stopped appearing in Amgen's later SEC filings; the last filing found that names it is the Q1 2023 release that reports the futility stop. That supports 'stopped' as its status today. Phase 1 studies had shown target engagement: dose-related, reversible blockade of both targets, more than 90% ICOSL receptor occupancy at 210 mg or more every 2 weeks, and lower naive B-cell counts, which shows BAFF was being blocked (ACR Open Rheumatol 2022; Clin Pharmacol Ther 2023). Since the drug hit both targets but showed no clinical benefit in SLE, the best code is F2. The high placebo response could also point to a trial-design problem (F7), but no source makes that argument.

evidence.earliest_source: FDA approval letter, BLA 125370 (Benlysta/belimumab), March 9, 2011. It approves belimumab for adult patients with active, autoantibody-positive SLE who are receiving standard therapy. The 2011 label says belimumab is specific for soluble BLyS, "also referred to as BAFF and TNFSF13B", and blocks it from binding its receptors on B cells.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and direction: Amgen's preclinical paper (Zhang et al., Clin Exp Rheumatol 2019, PMID 30789152, published online 15 Feb 2019) describes AMG 570 as "an ICOSL and BAFF bispecific inhibitory molecule" that "inhibits human and cynomolgus monkey ICOSL and BAFF". Monkeys treated with it lost B cells, which fits BAFF blockade. The Phase 1b paper (Abuqayyas et al., ACR Open Rheumatol 2022, PMID 35899378) calls rozibafusp alfa a "first-in-class bispecific antibody-peptide conjugate targeting ICOSL and BAFF", with PK/PD reflecting "dual ICOSL and BAFF blockade". So both recorded targets, TNFSF13B (BAFF) and ICOSLG, and the binder/neutralizer action are confirmed.
(2) Disease: NCT04058028 (Amgen study 20170588) is "A Phase 2b Dose Ranging Study to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Rozibafusp Alfa (AMG 570) in Subjects With Active Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)". outcome.summary: Phase 2 entry is confirmed. NCT04058028 is an Amgen-sponsored Phase 2b dose-ranging trial of rozibafusp alfa at 70, 280 or 420 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks against placebo in active SLE with inadequate response to standard of care. The decision came from Amgen's Q1 2023 earnings release (8-K, 2023-04-27), which says the Phase 2b study "was stopped for futility". The Q4 2022 release had still described it as enrolling. The posted results back this up. The primary endpoint was SRI-4 response at week 52: placebo 26/43 (60%), 70 mg 29/51 (57%), 280 mg 21/35 (60%) and 420 mg 35/48 (73%). There was no dose-response, the placebo response was high, and no statistical test was posted. The analysis counted only patients who could reach the visit before the termination decision, and 53 patients left the study by 'Decision by Sponsor'. Serious adverse events were similar across arms (placebo 6/62, 420 mg 3/87), so safety was not the reason for stopping. No Phase 3 trial was ever registered. The high placebo response could also point to a trial-design problem (F7), but no source makes that argument.

The Q4 2022 release (filed 2023-01-31) still said the study "continues to enroll patients". Rozibafusp does not appear in any Amgen SEC filing after the Q1 2023 release (EDGAR full-text search). The ClinicalTrials.gov results also refer to "the study termination decision being communicated to sites". In participant flow, "Decision by Sponsor" accounts for 35 of 88 in the 420 mg arm and 13 of 62 on placebo. The Amgen-authored design paper (Lupus Sci Med 2023) describes a Bayesian adaptive design with response-adaptive randomisation. Futility was assessed against SRI-4 at interim analyses run by an independent DMC, which tells the sponsor only when stopping for futility is recommended.

Efficacy, from posted results among patients who could reach the visit:
- SRI-4 at week 52 (primary): placebo 26/43 (60%), 70 mg 29/51 (57%), 280 mg 21/35 (60%), 420 mg 35/48 (73%).
- SRI-4 at week 24: 33/54, 30/58, 20/36, 46/66.
- BICLA at week 52: 21/43, 20/51, 15/35, 29/48.
- Moderate/severe flare rates were not better than placebo (0.34, 0.52, 0.46, 0.34).
There is no clear dose response, and the low and middle doses did no better than placebo.

- Phase 1a/1b (CPT 2023, PMID 37150935; ACR Open Rheumatol 2022, PMID 35899378): dose-related, reversible engagement of both targets. 1. No study measured target engagement directly in SLE. The registry posts only drug levels, so engagement in SLE is inferred from the Phase 1 exposure-response data.

- The trial was small (40 randomized, 80% CI, exploratory), so F7 is a plausible secondary contributor.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA (CBER) approval letter for Remicade (infliximab, Centocor), BLA 103772, dated August 24, 1998, approving it for moderately to severely active and fistulizing Crohn's disease. The 1998 label says infliximab binds human TNFα and neutralizes both its soluble and transmembrane forms.
outcome_summary:
V565 is VHsquared's oral, enteric-coated, protease-resistant llama single-domain anti-TNF antibody (a "Vorabody"). The record lists it as a monoclonal antibody, but it is not a conventional mAb.

**Decisive trial.** The Crohn's Phase 2 was HarbOR (NCT02976129; EudraCT 2016-002939-15). It was a double-blind, placebo-controlled 2:1 study of 6 weeks' oral V565 three times daily, given as add-on therapy, in 125 patients with active Crohn's disease. It ran from Dec 2016 to 8 Mar 2019 and finished without early termination.

**Primary endpoint not met.** The primary endpoint was response at Day 42: a CDAI drop of at least 70 points or CDAI below 150, plus at least a 40% fall in CRP or FCP.
- Results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov: 29/82 on V565 (35.4%) versus 16/43 on placebo (37.2%).
- The EU CTR lists a pre-specified logistic-regression superiority analysis with p>0.05.
- The secondary endpoint (CDAI drop of at least 100 plus at least a 50% CRP/FCP fall) was 20/82 versus 9/43, also p>0.05.
- Exploratory signals favoured V565 on some measures. Blinded central endoscopy readers judged the mucosa improved in 18/32 on V565 versus 3/10 on placebo. CRP normalised in 11/58 versus 4/31. FCP normalised in 7/23 versus 3/10.
- Safety did not differ: serious adverse events were 3.66% versus 4.65%.

**Status.** There was no Phase 3 or approval within four years, and there is none to date. A 2024 review states there are no ongoing Phase 3 trials of V565 (Ther Adv Gastroenterol 2024). No new V565 Crohn's trial has been registered since 2019.
- The sponsor later published, with authors listing both VHsquared and Sorriso Pharmaceuticals affiliations, that it had folded V565 into a bispecific TNF/IL-23p19 molecule, V56B2 (Sci Rep 2021).
- An independent 2026 commentary on SOR102 cites the V56B2 paper as the source for SOR102. Sorriso is developing SOR102, a TNF/IL-23 bispecific, in ulcerative colitis.
- Sorriso's pipeline lists an oral anti-TNF Vorabody, SOR101, only for checkpoint-inhibitor colitis. No source I could reach confirms that SOR101 is V565. No anti-TNF monotherapy program in Crohn's disease remains.
- There was no explicit discontinuation announcement. The stop is inferred from the missed primary endpoint, no further Crohn's trials, and the pipeline pivot.

**Stop reason and failure code.** I classed the stop reason as efficacy, since the decisive trial missed its primary endpoint. The sponsor's only comment was that "improvements in key measures of clinical efficacy were observed".

I chose F4, with low confidence. The pattern fits: an exploratory endoscopic signal (56% vs 30%, small subset, no statistics) without a clinical response, while TNF itself is clinically validated in Crohn's. No source states why the trial failed.
- F1 is a plausible alternative. Target engagement in tissue (lower phosphoprotein, V565 found in the lamina propria) was shown only in 5 ulcerative colitis patients. In Crohn's patients only stool and serum levels were measured: V565 was found in stool and not in serum. An ileostomy study found mini-tablets only partly dissolved.
- F7 is another alternative: a 6-week add-on design with a 37% placebo response.

I used PubMed and Europe PMC searches in place of WebSearch, because the session's search budget was used up.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: V565 (VHsquared Ltd, later Sorriso Pharmaceuticals), an oral, gut-restricted anti-TNFa single-domain antibody in enteric-coated mini-tablets. The Phase 2 HarbOR trial (NCT02976129) tested it in active Crohn's disease.

Why it did not advance: its only Phase 2 efficacy trial in Crohn's missed its primary endpoint, and there was no safety problem.

1. Trial result (ClinicalTrials.gov posted results). The trial was double-blind, randomized 2:1, with 125 patients dosed three times daily for 6 weeks. It ran from Dec 2016 and completed 2019-03-08.
   - Primary endpoint at Day 42: CDAI response plus a reduction of at least 40% in CRP or faecal calprotectin. V565 29/82 (35.4%) vs placebo 16/43 (37.2%), so no separation.
   - Secondary endpoint (stricter response): 20/82 vs 9/43.
   - Exploratory endpoints:
     - Endoscopic "better than baseline": 18/32 vs 3/10.
     - CRP normalised: 11/58 vs 4/31.
     - Faecal calprotectin normalised: 7/23 vs 3/10.
   - Safety: serious adverse events 3/82 vs 2/43, no deaths, no signal.
   - An independent 2024 review (PMID 39711916) reports the same result: response did not differ significantly (35.4% vs 37.2%), and there were no Phase III trials.
2. After the trial. ClinicalTrials.gov lists no later V565 trial; the only other V565 records are the earlier Phase 1 studies NCT03010787 and NCT03705117. The sponsor's archived HARBOR page and press materials never announced the results. In 2021 the sponsor described "improvements in key measures of clinical efficacy" (Sci Rep 2021, PMC8484351) and moved to a bispecific: V565 combined with an anti-IL-23p19 domain antibody (V56B2). That paper pitches the bispecific as giving efficacy "in a greater proportion of patients". The later SOR102 is described as the same two-domain TNF/IL-23 construct (commentary PMID 42291178 cites the V56B2 paper for it) and was developed in ulcerative colitis (PMID 41242336). Sorriso's current anti-TNF monomer, SOR101, is repositioned to colitis caused by immune checkpoint inhibitors, not Crohn's disease. No source gives an explicit reason for stopping.

Why F2 and not the other codes:
- Not F1. Exposure and target engagement were shown in humans:
  - Micromolar V565 in ileostomy fluid and in the stool of Crohn's patients.
  - In 4 of 5 ulcerative colitis patients, V565 in the lamina propria on T cells and macrophages, with about a 50% drop in tissue phosphoproteins after 7 days (Nurbhai 2019, PMID 31575982; NCT03705117).
- TNF itself is clinically validated in Crohn's: systemic anti-TNF antibodies are the most effective approved therapy (cited in PMC8484351 and PMID 39711916). So the failure points to the local, partial, luminal neutralisation not carrying over to clinical response in transmural or ileal Crohn's disease. That is F2's "partial inhibition / wrong tissue".
- Not F7. The V565 point estimate was numerically below placebo, so there is no trend that a larger trial would rescue.
- Not F8. The pivot to a bispecific came after the failed readout and was framed as needing more efficacy.

Caveats:
- No sponsor statement gives the reason, so this is inferred from the results.
- Plausible alternatives are F3 (the sponsor moved to colonic disease, ulcerative colitis and checkpoint-inhibitor colitis) and F1 (tissue engagement was shown in ulcerative colitis but never in Crohn's tissue).
- Confidence is moderate to low.

OUTCOME: did not advance within 4 years.
- The entry trial is HarbOR (NCT02976129), a Phase 2 study of V565 in Crohn's disease sponsored by VHsquared. It started in Dec 2016, so the 4-year window closed on 2020-12-01.
- Searching ClinicalTrials.gov for V565 returns only three studies: HarbOR and two Phase 1s (NCT03010787, NCT03705117). None is a Phase 3, and V565 has no FDA approval.
- HarbOR completed on 2019-03-08 without stopping early (EU CTR: "Was the trial ended prematurely? No").
- Results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov: the primary responder endpoint at Day 42 was 29/82 on V565 versus 16/43 on placebo (35.4% vs 37.2%). The EU CTR reports a pre-specified logistic-regression superiority test with p>0.05.
- An independent 2024 review (PMC11660281) reports the same result and says there are no ongoing Phase 3 trials.

PIPELINE RECORD IS CORRECT.
- s4=0 is right, and so is the reason "efficacy: primary endpoint not met".
- years_to_event 2.26 matches the 2019-03-08 completion date.
- One nit, not an error: the event label "suspended" is loose. The trial completed, and the program was quietly dropped rather than formally suspended. The sponsor moved V565 into the bispecific V56B2 / SOR102 (Sci Rep 2021, PMC8484351). Sorriso's current pipeline lists the oral anti-TNF SOR101 only for colitis caused by checkpoint inhibitors, not Crohn's disease.

CLAIM (rule B1): supported, and it predates entry.
- The CBER approval letter dated August 24, 1998 approves infliximab (Remicade, Centocor) for moderately to severely active and fistulizing Crohn's disease. openFDA confirms BLA103772 ORIG-1 approved 19980824.
- That is 18 years before Phase 2 entry. The target matches: both drugs neutralize TNF-alpha (Crowe 2018, PMID 29563546).

  - Our record labels V565's modality "monoclonal_antibody". It is a llama single-domain antibody (Vorabody).
  - The evidence agent found that some evidence rows carry the drug's first-approval date instead of the date of the indication they name. Examples are the infliximab UC row and the Humira rows.

FAILURE CODE: F2, moderate-to-low confidence.
- The target is clinically validated: systemic anti-TNF antibodies work in Crohn's disease.
- Human exposure and engagement were shown:
  - Micromolar V565 in ileostomy fluid and in Crohn's patients' stool.
  - In 4 of 5 ulcerative colitis patients, V565 in the lamina propria with about a 50% drop in tissue phosphoproteins (Nurbhai 2019, PMID 31575982).

- F4 is weak. The biomarker parts did not clearly move: FCP normalised in 7/23 vs 3/10 (30% vs 30%) and CRP in 11/58 vs 4/31. The only signal was an exploratory endoscopic subset (18/32 vs 3/10) with no statistics.

- F1 is the main alternative: tissue engagement was never shown in Crohn's tissue itself.
- No source states the reason for stopping.

claim: Before the program entered Phase 2, the FDA had approved a drug acting on the same target for this disease or a closely related one.
evidence_source: FDA approval of Eulexin (flutamide) capsules, NDA 018554 (Schering), original approval 1989-01-27; flutamide is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen whose label indication is metastatic carcinoma of the prostate. The FDA approval letters for Casodex (bicalutamide, NDA 020498, 1995-10-04) and Xtandi (enzalutamide, NDA 203415, 2012-08-31, for mCRPC after docetaxel) also support the claim. The Xtandi approval is the closest match.
outcome_summary:
TRC253 (JNJ-63576253) is an androgen receptor antagonist that Janssen discovered. It was designed to block the wild-type receptor and ligand-binding-domain mutants, especially F877L. TRACON licensed it in September 2016, with Janssen keeping an option to take it back. TRACON ran the open-label Phase 1/2a trial NCT02987829 (start 2017-05-23; 72 patients with mCRPC who had progressed on enzalutamide (Xtandi) or apalutamide (Erleada)).

The trial's primary endpoint was a descriptive count of dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs), with no efficacy hypothesis, so met/not met does not apply. Only one DLT occurred, at 320 mg, and 280 mg daily became the recommended Phase 2 dose. The drug reached the target concentration of 335 ng/mL at doses of 240 mg and above. Grade 1 QTc prolongation was the most common adverse event.

Efficacy was poor. In November 2019 TRACON disclosed a lower-than-expected response rate and that F877L was rarer than expected, and enrollment was capped at about 70 patients. By the April 2020 press release, the PSA response rate was 8% in 63 evaluable patients, and 27% had stable disease for more than 5 months. On April 20, 2020 Janssen declined to opt back in after reviewing the Phase 2 data. TRACON's CEO said the F877L mutation was "far less common than predicted" and that the drug "was not highly active" in patients with acquired resistance to Xtandi or Erleada. TRACON's FY2020 10-K said US commercialization was "not viable." TRACON then looked for a partner in China, did not find one, and returned all rights to Janssen in May 2021.

I chose F3 (wrong population or subtype) because the drug reached exposure but its target subgroup, F877L-mutant mCRPC, turned out to be rare. Most patients in the post-enzalutamide/apalutamide population it was tested in did not respond, and it was never tested in earlier-line patients. F8 (commercial) is a secondary factor, since the final termination was framed as commercial non-viability that followed from this finding.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: TRC253 (JNJ-63576253), an oral androgen receptor antagonist built to block the F877L ligand-binding-domain mutation as well as wild-type AR. Janssen discovered it and licensed it to TRACON. It was tested in men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) who had progressed on enzalutamide (Xtandi) or apalutamide (Erleada). The only Phase 2 study was NCT02987829, a Phase 1/2a trial that started 2017-05-23. It enrolled 72 patients and was completed, and no Phase 3 followed.

What the primary sources show:
1) Results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov: 5 of 72 patients had a confirmed PSA50 response (1 at 160 mg, 3 at the 280 mg recommended Phase 2 dose, 1 at 320 mg). Median time to progression at 280 mg was 4.64 months (n=44). There was 1 dose-limiting toxicity, at 320 mg. The drug reached the target concentration of 335 ng/mL in 4/7 patients at 240 mg, 4/4 at 280 mg and 5/6 at 320 mg. FDHT-PET uptake in tumours fell by 34% to 46% at some doses (n=1 to 2 per dose). So drug exposure was reached and there is partial evidence the drug bound its target; F1 does not fit.
2) TRACON 8-K, Nov 2019: the interim Phase 2 data showed "a lower than expected initial response rate and prevalence of the F877L mutation."
3) TRACON 8-K and press release, April 24, 2020: on April 20, 2020, after reviewing the Phase 2 data, Janssen declined its option to take the drug back. The CEO said "the F877L androgen receptor mutation TRC253 was designed to treat was far less common than predicted, and the product candidate was not highly active in prostate cancer patients with acquired resistance to Xtandi or Erleada." The release reports a PSA response rate of 8% in 63 evaluable patients and calls the 280 mg dose well tolerated (grade 1 QTc prolongation was the most common side effect), so F5 and F6 do not fit. TRACON argued the drug might work in an earlier line of treatment and sought a partner in China.
4) TRACON 10-Q (Q2 2021) and 10-K (FY2021): after the Phase 1/2 trial, TRACON "determined commercialization of TRC253 in prostate cancer in the United States was not viable." In May 2021 it returned all rights to Janssen.

Coding: the final steps (Janssen not opting in, no China partner, rights returned) were business decisions, but each one followed from the efficacy result. The drug was active in cells and animal models and reached its exposure targets. It failed because the patients it was tested in did not match what it was designed for: the F877L mutation was rare in post-enzalutamide/apalutamide patients, and the drug had little effect on their other resistance mechanisms. The sponsor itself pointed to a different disease stage (earlier line) as where the drug might work. That is a wrong population/subtype/stage failure, so the code is F3. Runner-up codes: F2 (target engaged but no clinical benefit), and F8 as the immediate trigger for stopping. The trial had no randomised comparison, so its overall efficacy is uncertain, but the sponsor's stated reason is clear.

error_source: disease mapping (evidence step only: memantine's Alzheimer's dementia approval was counted as a 'closely related' disease to MDD). The outcome step has no error: s4=0 is correct.

outcome_summary:
Entry confirmed. NCT03756129 is a Novartis-sponsored Phase 2 proof-of-concept study in treatment-resistant depression (TRD) that started on 2019-02-08 (IV infusion, n=70). It met its primary endpoint: change in MADRS at 24 h versus placebo was -8.25 for pooled 0.16 mg/kg (p=0.0013) and -5.71 for pooled 0.32 mg/kg (p=0.0196). It was published in J Clin Psychiatry 2025 (PMID 40767837).

No Phase 3 trial and no approval followed. Novartis instead ran a second Phase 2, NCT04722666, an IV add-on to comprehensive standard of care in MDD with acute suicidal ideation with intent (start 2021-07-20, n=199). At 24 h the drug did not separate from placebo: MADRS change was -17.5 on placebo versus -16.4, -17.2, -17.7 and -12.7 across the four MIJ821 doses. No formal test was posted, so "not met" is my reading of the descriptive results. ClinicalTrials.gov records the trial as "Terminated by Novartis" (primary completion 2023-09-26). Novartis also started a subcutaneous TRD Phase 2, NCT05454410 (start 2023-03-13, completed 2023-11-28). There, 10 mg gave a nominal -5.2 (90% CI -9.6 to -0.7) versus placebo; 4 mg and 1 mg showed no effect.

Novartis's Q2 2023 investor presentation still listed MIJ821 for TRD and for MDD with suicidality, with submission planned for 2026 or later. The Q3 2023 interim financial report (6-K, 2023-10-24) says: "MIJ821 (onfasprodil) Depression, Phase 2 – Program discontinued following strategic review, including a benefit risk assessment of acute MDD with suicidality." MIJ821 is absent from the Q3 2023 and later investor presentations and from the current Novartis pipeline page.

Coding: the stated reason leads with a strategic review, and the TRD indication was dropped despite a positive proof-of-concept, so I used business_or_strategic and F8. The trigger was clearly the failed acute-suicidality trial, where the placebo response under intensive standard of care was very high. Efficacy with F3 (population) or F7 (trial design) is therefore a defensible alternative reading. Target engagement and a clinical signal were shown in TRD, and the healthy-volunteer study showed a dose-related EEG effect plus dissociative adverse events (PMID 37817426). That argues against F1 or F2.

evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action are confirmed. Onfasprodil (MIJ821) is described as a "highly potent and novel selective NR2B subunit negative allosteric modulator" (GluN2B = GRIN2B) in the Novartis Phase 2 paper (PMID 40767837) and in the review PMID 38868733.
(2) Disease is confirmed. NCT03756129 (Novartis, CMIJ821X2201, Phase 2) studied treatment-resistant depression, with MDD keywords and a MADRS endpoint. Its actual start date of 2019-02-08 matches the recorded entry date.
(3) The claim is not supported. The only evidence row is memantine (Namenda, NDA 21-487), approved 2003-10-16 (openFDA ORIG submission date and FDA approval letter). Its indication is moderate to severe dementia of the Alzheimer's type. That is a neurodegenerative dementia, not major depressive disorder or a closely related mood disorder, so the "this disease or a closely related one" condition fails.
The target link is also weak. The 2003 label calls memantine a low-to-moderate affinity uncompetitive open-channel NMDA receptor antagonist. That is a non-subunit-selective pore block, not GluN2B-selective negative allosteric modulation. Kotermanski & Johnson 2009 (PMID 19261873) report that at physiological Mg2+, therapeutic memantine concentrations have negligible effects on NR1/2B receptors.
No FDA-approved NMDA-receptor drug for depression existed before entry. Esketamine (Spravato, NDA 211243) was approved for treatment-resistant depression on 2019-03-05, 25 days AFTER the 2019-02-08 Phase 2 entry, so it cannot support the claim.
(4) The memantine approval (2003) does predate entry, but it does not support the disease part of the claim.
(5) The approval was held by Forest Laboratories (now AbbVie), not by Novartis, the onfasprodil sponsor.
