failure_second.reasoning:
Program: derazantinib (ARQ 087 / BAL087), an oral FGFR1-3 inhibitor, in HER2-negative gastric adenocarcinoma with FGFR2 aberrations. The entry trial was FIDES-03 (NCT04604132), a Phase 1b/2 study sponsored by Basilea that started on 2020-10-06. Its ClinicalTrials.gov status is TERMINATED, with primary completion on 2022-11-21 and 47 patients treated. The stated reason is "Terminated prematurely for administrative reasons not related to patient safety." No Phase 3 trial of derazantinib in any indication is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Why it stopped, from the sponsor's own releases:
(1) On 2022-02-15 Basilea announced it would separate anti-infectives from oncology and look for transactions for its oncology assets. In that release it still listed FIDES-03 in gastric cancer as a study it would keep running in 2022.
(2) On 2022-06-27 Basilea said it had "decided to terminate the license agreement and return the rights to Merck & Co, Inc. by the end of the year." The CFO said "the changing competitive landscape and the evolving clinical data from our open-label studies led us to conclude that a transaction could not be closed at the terms and within the timelines required."
(3) On 2023-01-11 Basilea said it had decided in February 2022 to "exit oncology by the end of 2022." It added that for "oncology assets which were not transacted, Basilea decided to transfer the rights for the FGFR inhibitor derazantinib back to Merck & Co."
I found no later derazantinib trial in gastric cancer by Merck or anyone else.

Efficacy data that contributed: the posted ClinicalTrials.gov results show monotherapy produced no responses. Confirmed ORR by blinded central review was 0/13 in cohort 1.1 (FGFR2 fusion or amplification, 300 mg once daily), 0/8 in cohort 1.2 (FGFR1-3 mutations) and 0/13 in cohort 1.3 (200 mg twice daily). PFS at 4 months in cohort 1.3 was 7.7%, median PFS was 1.7 months, and median OS was 3.3 months. The combination with paclitaxel and ramucirumab gave ORRs of 2/5 and 4/7 in small, non-randomized cohorts, and the recommended Phase 2 dose was 200 mg. Hyperphosphataemia, an on-target sign of FGFR inhibition, was reported in a few patients. The urothelial sister study (FIDES-02, PMID 38627238) concluded the drug "did not show sufficient efficacy to warrant further development."

Coding: the program stopped because the sponsor exited oncology, could not find a partner, and handed the license back. The trial record calls the termination administrative. That makes F8 (commercial/strategic) the best single code. Weak gastric monotherapy efficacy is a real contributing factor. Basilea cites "evolving clinical data" and the competitive landscape as why no partner deal closed, but it never names a scientific reason such as F2 or F3 as the cause. The efficacy contribution is shown only by the posted results, not by any sponsor explanation.

evidence_source: Crotty PL, Braun SE, Anderson RA, Whitley CB. "Mutation R468W of the iduronate-2-sulfatase gene in mild Hunter syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type II) confirmed by in vitro mutagenesis and expression." Hum Mol Genet 1992 Dec;1(9):755-7 (PMID 1284597). This is the oldest paper cited by Reactome reactions R-HSA-9036046 and R-HSA-2262743. Both reactions were created 2012-05-20 (B. Jassal) and released 2012-09-18.
outcome_summary: Tividenofusp alfa (DNL310, Denali Therapeutics) is an IDS enzyme replacement engineered to cross the blood-brain barrier. Its first industry-sponsored Phase 2 trial in MPS II was the open-label Phase 1/2 study NCT04251026 (DNLI-E-0002, 47 patients). ClinicalTrials.gov confirms it started on 2020-07-16. The program advanced within the four-year window: the Phase 2/3 COMPASS trial (NCT05371613, DNLI-E-0007, 65 patients, randomized and double-blind against idursulfase) started on 2022-07-21. Its primary endpoints are CSF heparan sulfate (HS) at 24 weeks and Vineland-3 at 96 weeks. Primary completion is estimated for 2027-12, so COMPASS has no results yet. A Phase 2/3 extension study (NCT06075537) started on 2023-09-20. Denali submitted the BLA on 2025-05-05. A major amendment pushed the goal date back three months. FDA granted accelerated approval on 2026-03-24 under the brand name AVLAYAH (tividenofusp alfa-eknm, BLA 761485), with priority review, orphan status and a rare pediatric disease priority review voucher. The approved use is the neurologic manifestations of Hunter syndrome (MPS II) in pediatric patients weighing at least 5 kg, started before advanced neurologic impairment. Approval rested on reduced CSF HS in Trial 1 (NCT04251026). At Week 24, CSF HS fell by a mean of 91% (95% CI 89-92%) in 44 patients, and 93% of them were below the upper limit of normal. Urine HS fell by 86% and urine DS by 91%. The registered primary outcomes of NCT04251026 are safety and urine total GAG. No results are posted on ClinicalTrials.gov, so the 'met' call rests on the label's PD data and the approval itself. FDA requires a confirmatory double-blind, randomized, standard-of-care-controlled trial (PMR 4953-1), which matches COMPASS's design. The label carries a boxed warning for anaphylaxis, plus warnings for anemia and membranous nephropathy. The program did not fail.

Its first industry-sponsored Phase 2 trial in MPS II was the open-label Phase 1/2 study NCT04251026 (DNLI-E-0002, 47 patients). ClinicalTrials.gov confirms it started on 2020-07-16. The program advanced within the four-year window: the Phase 2/3 COMPASS trial (NCT05371613, DNLI-E-0007, 65 patients, randomized and double-blind against idursulfase) started on 2022-07-21. Its primary endpoints are CSF heparan sulfate (HS) at 24 weeks and Vineland-3 at 96 weeks. Primary completion is estimated for 2027-12, so COMPASS has no results yet. A Phase 2/3 extension study (NCT06075537) started on 2023-09-20. Denali submitted the BLA on 2025-05-05. A major amendment pushed the goal date back three months. FDA granted accelerated approval on 2026-03-24 under the brand name AVLAYAH (tividenofusp alfa-eknm, BLA 761485), with priority review, orphan status and a rare pediatric disease priority review voucher. The approved use is the neurologic manifestations of Hunter syndrome (MPS II) in pediatric patients weighing at least 5 kg, started before advanced neurologic impairment. Approval rested on reduced CSF HS in Trial 1 (NCT04251026). At Week 24, CSF HS fell by a mean of 91% (95% CI 89-92%) in 44 patients, and 93% of them were below the upper limit of normal. Urine HS fell by 86% and urine DS by 91%. The registered primary outcomes of NCT04251026 are safety and urine total GAG. evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action. Donanemab (LY3002813) is an IgG1 antibody against an N-terminal pyroglutamate amyloid-beta epitope (AβpE3-42) that is found only in brain amyloid plaques. It lowers plaque amyloid, so recording it as an APP depleter is reasonable. Two sources show this. Lilly's 2012 Neuron paper (DeMattos et al., PMID 23217740) used the murine parent antibody to clear existing plaques. The Lilly Phase 1b paper (Lowe et al. 2021, PMID 34585215) describes the antibody and shows rapid reduction of amyloid on PET. One caveat: the drug binds a modified Aβ fragment derived from APP, not the APP protein itself.

(2) Disease. The entry trial NCT03367403 (TRAILBLAZER-ALZ) is a Phase 2 trial sponsored by Eli Lilly, with condition "Alzheimer Disease" in early symptomatic AD. Its actual start date is 2017-12-18, which matches the recorded Phase 2 entry date. Reactome tags the reaction with DOID:10652, Alzheimer's disease, which matches MONDO:0004975.

(3) Claim. Reactome R-HSA-8863009 "Influx of extracellular calcium" is a disease reaction (isInDisease=true, disease Alzheimer's disease). It is positively regulated by APP(672-713), which is Aβ1-42 (regulation R-HSA-8867561). The summation reads "Beta amyloid increases influx of extracellular calcium ... mechanism has not been completely elucidated (Lee et al. 2000, Abramov et al. 2004)". It is a black-box ('omitted') reaction, and the regulator is Aβ1-42 rather than the pyroglutamate AβpE3-42 that donanemab binds. Still, the reaction does link the APP gene product to AD. The database year of 2000 matches the earliest cited paper, Lee et al., Nature, 2000. That paper shows Aβ1-42 inducing calpain-mediated p35 to p25 conversion, which is downstream of calcium influx. The Abramov 2004 paper is the more direct evidence for Aβ-induced calcium signals.

(4) Timing. Both cited papers (2000 and 2004) and the reaction's Reactome release date (2016-09-19) are before the 2017-12-18 Phase 2 entry.

(5) Sponsor. Lee et al. were at HHMI and Harvard Medical School. Abramov, Canevari and Duchen are academic authors. Neither paper has Eli Lilly authors. The mechanism papers for the drug itself (DeMattos 2012, Lowe 2021) are Lilly-authored, but they are not the evidence behind this claim.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: efzofitimod (ATYR1923), aTyr Pharma. The Phase 2 trial in COVID-19 is NCT04412668. Single IV dose of 1 or 3 mg/kg versus placebo in hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19 pneumonia who were not on mechanical ventilation. It started 2020-06-04, completed 2020-10-23 and enrolled 36 (the company says 32). Its primary endpoint was safety (TEAEs/SAEs), and its posted results include no efficacy p-values.

What happened:
(1) On 2021-01-04 aTyr announced "positive topline results" in an 8-K (EX-99.1). The trial met its primary safety endpoint, with no drug-related SAEs. On time to recovery, the 3 mg/kg arm had a median of 5.5 days versus 6 days on placebo, and 83% versus 56% recovered by day 6. The release says the study "was not powered for statistical significance".
(2) The FY2020 10-K (filed 2021-03-24) says: "Future development plans in COVID-19 are being assessed in light of the evolving pandemic and therapeutic landscape and availability of non-dilutive financing." It also says the company "will move the program forward based upon the competitive landscape and the availability of non-dilutive financing", and that the COVID data would be leveraged for its interstitial lung disease (ILD) programs. The same filing names dexamethasone and Actemra (tocilizumab) as competing immunomodulators in COVID-19.
(3) By the FY2021 10-K (filed 2022-03-15), all forward plans for COVID were gone. The trial is described only as data "for our mechanistic understanding of efzofitimod and for its application in ILD."
(4) ClinicalTrials.gov lists no further COVID trial of efzofitimod. The molecule went on to a Phase 3 in pulmonary sarcoidosis (NCT05415137, started 2022-09) and a Phase 2 in SSc-ILD (NCT05892614).

The sponsor's only stated reason for not advancing in COVID-19 is strategic: a fast-moving therapeutic landscape and competition, plus dependence on non-dilutive funding, followed by a pivot of the asset to ILD. So the code is F8.

Caveats:
- The efficacy signal was weak, which plausibly fed into the decision.
- The posted CT.gov results show placebo recovering faster than the 3 mg/kg arm: median time to recovery 4.5 days on placebo versus 5.5 days on 3 mg/kg. That conflicts with the 6-day placebo figure in the press release.
- The 1 mg/kg arm had 5 participants with SAEs versus 0 on placebo, including 2 deaths that the safety monitoring board judged unrelated to the drug.
- No source says efficacy or safety was the reason the program stopped, and no peer-reviewed paper on this trial turned up on PubMed.
- Record discrepancy: our record lists the target as "NRP1 (agonist)". The sponsor's filings call efzofitimod a "selective modulator of neuropilin-2" (NRP2), so the target field looks wrong.

adjudication.reasoning:
Outcome. NCT04412668 is aTyr's Phase 2 of ATYR1923 (efzofitimod) in severe COVID-19 pneumonia. It started 2020-06-04, which matches the recorded entry date, and completed 2020-10-23. Its CT.gov status is COMPLETED, not suspended, and it has no whyStopped entry. ClinicalTrials.gov lists four efzofitimod trials in total. The only Phase 3 is NCT05415137, in pulmonary sarcoidosis. There is no COVID-19 Phase 3 from any sponsor and no FDA approval for COVID-19. So the drug did not advance within 4 years, and the pipeline's s4=0 is correct.

The pipeline's event and reason are wrong. 'Suspended / safety' at 0.39 years is just the trial completion date. The 2021-01-04 8-K press release says the trial met its primary safety endpoint, with no drug-related SAEs. The posted results do show 5 SAEs and 2 deaths in the 1 mg/kg arm and none in the 3 mg/kg or placebo arms, but aTyr reported none of these as drug-related. No source says the program was stopped for safety.

Why it stopped: the FY2020 10-K says 'Future development plans in COVID-19 are being assessed in light of the evolving pandemic and therapeutic landscape and availability of non-dilutive financing.' It also says aTyr 'will move the program forward based upon the competitive landscape and the availability of non-dilutive financing.' By the FY2021 10-K the COVID data appears only as input for 'mechanistic understanding' and for interstitial lung disease (ILD), and the asset has moved to sarcoidosis and SSc-ILD. The stated reason is strategic: competition, funding, and portfolio, so F8. The efficacy signal was weak and the study was unpowered: CT.gov reports median time to recovery of 4.5 days on placebo versus 5.5 days on 3 mg/kg. That may have contributed, but no source names efficacy as the reason.

Evidence claim. Reactome does now link NRP1 to COVID-19. R-HSA-9699007 (FURIN-mediated) and R-HSA-9694661 (TMPRSS2-mediated) both carry 'Positive regulation by NRP1' (dbId 9768874). However:
- Both reactions have releaseDate 2020-09-15.
- The NRP1 regulation instance's creation edit is 'Stephan, Ralf, 2022-03-15'.
- The primary NRP1/SARS-CoV-2 evidence is Daly et al., bioRxiv, posted 2020-06-05, the day after entry (Science version PMID 33082294, epub 2020-10-20).
- The '2010' date matches the oldest PMID on the Open Targets row, 21068237 (Shulla et al., epub 2010-11-10). That paper is about TMPRSS2 and SARS-CoV-1 and does not mention NRP1.

So nothing predates entry. The target mapping is also wrong: aTyr's 8-K and 10-Ks describe ATYR1923 as a 'selective modulator of neuropilin-2', not an NRP1 agonist. The claim fails on timing and on target identity.

claim: Reactome curates a pathway reaction linking the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), dated before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Costa PP, Figueira AS, Bravo FR. "Amyloid fibril protein related to prealbumin in familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy." Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 1978;75(9):4499-503 (PMID 279930). This is the earliest TTR-specific paper cited by Reactome reaction R-HSA-977136, "Amyloid precursor proteins form ordered fibrils", which Reactome released on 2011-06-14. The earliest cardiac-relevant TTR citation in that reaction is Bergström et al., BBRC 2001 (PMID 11467836), on senile systemic ATTR amyloid in heart tissue.
outcome_summary: Acoramidis (AG10/BBP-265/ALXN2060) is a small-molecule TTR stabilizer. Its Phase 2 entry record, NCT03536767, is an industry-sponsored (Eidos Therapeutics, a BridgeBio company) open-label long-term safety/PK/PD study in amyloid cardiomyopathy. It started on 2018-08-08 and ended with status 'Terminated', and the stated reason is 'Study ended by the sponsor due to meeting Study Objectives', not failure. The program advanced fast: the Phase 3 ATTRibute-CM trial (NCT03860935) started on 2019-03-19, well within 4 years. That trial randomized 632 patients 2:1 to acoramidis 800 mg twice daily or placebo for 30 months. It met its four-step hierarchical primary endpoint (all-cause death, CV hospitalization, NT-proBNP, 6MWD) with a win ratio of 1.8 (95% CI 1.4-2.2, P<0.001), and adverse events were similar in the two arms (NEJM 2024, PMID 38197816). The FDA approved Attruby (NDA216540, Type 1 NME) on 2024-11-22 for adult wild-type or variant ATTR-CM, to reduce CV death and CV-related hospitalization. The drug is approved for this disease, so it is not a failure.

evidence.earliest_source: Costa PP, Figueira AS, Bravo FR. "Amyloid fibril protein related to prealbumin in familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy." Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 1978;75(9):4499-503 (PMID 279930). This is the earliest TTR-specific paper cited by Reactome reaction R-HSA-977136, "Amyloid precursor proteins form ordered fibrils", which Reactome released on 2011-06-14. evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: confirmed. Penchala et al., PNAS 2013 (PMID 23716704) describes AG10 as "a potent and selective kinetic stabilizer of TTR" that prevents V122I and wild-type TTR tetramer dissociation. The entry-trial record also uses TTR-stabilization PD assays (FPE, Western blot). "Other" (stabilizer) is the right action.

(2) Trial and disease: NCT03536767 (AG10-202, Eidos) is a Phase 2 open-label extension in symptomatic transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM), condition "Amyloid Cardiomyopathy", actual start 2018-08-08. "Cardiomyopathy" (MONDO:0004994) is a correct but broad parent. The parent Phase 2 study AG10-201 (NCT03458130, ATTRm-CM/ATTRwt-CM) started earlier, on 2018-04-27; that could be taken as the real Phase 2 entry, but it does not change the timing verdict.

(3) Claim: partly supported. TTR (TTR(21-147), UniProt P02766) is a member of the "Systemic amyloid fibril monomers" set (R-HSA-977105). That set feeds reactions R-HSA-977136 and R-HSA-976734 in the pathway "Amyloid fiber formation" (R-HSA-977225). Both reactions were released 2011-06-14, before Phase 2 entry. However:
- Reactome tags both reactions only with generic "Amyloidosis" (DOID:9120), not cardiomyopathy or ATTR-CM.
- Open Targets mapped that tag to Orphanet_85443 / MONDO_0019438, "AL amyloidosis". AL amyloidosis is immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis and has nothing to do with TTR, so the evidence_disease label is a mapping error.
- Both reactions are generic multi-protein reactions covering about 11 systemic and many localized amyloid precursors. They are not a curated TTR-cardiomyopathy link.
- The years in our DB do not concern TTR. 1976 is Rosenthal et al. on SAA (PMID 1270801); 1979 is Pepys et al. on SAP binding (PMID 118839). The earliest TTR-specific citation is Costa 1978 (FAP, a neuropathy). The cardiac-relevant one is Bergström 2001 (wild-type TTR amyloid from heart tissue in senile systemic amyloidosis).

Judged leniently, amyloidosis covers ATTR amyloidosis, the parent condition of ATTR-CM, so the link holds in substance. As recorded, though, the evidence disease (AL amyloidosis) is wrong.

(4) Timing: every cited source (1976-2010 literature, 2011 Reactome release) predates 2018.

(5) Sponsor: the Reactome curation and the papers it cites are not sponsor-authored. Separately, the 2013 PNAS AG10 paper establishing the mechanism was co-authored by Isabella Graef and Mamoun Alhamadsheh, whom Eidos's 2018 IPO prospectus names as company founders. That paper is the target-action evidence, not the claim's evidence.

Not checked: clinical outcome, which was deliberately left out.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: afuresertib (LAE002), an oral pan-AKT inhibitor, given with weekly paclitaxel versus paclitaxel alone in platinum-resistant ovarian cancer (PROC). The entry trial was PROFECTA-II/GOG-3044 (NCT04374630), sponsored by Laekna. It started 2020-07-07, was open-label and randomized 150 patients 2:1 (99 to the combination, 51 to paclitaxel). Laekna called it a "Phase II registrational/pivotal" trial and said it would discuss an NDA "should the topline data meet the NDA criteria" (2023 interim results release).

What happened:
(1) The trial missed its primary endpoint in the unselected intent-to-treat (ITT) population. Median PFS was 4.3 vs 4.1 months. The paper gives HR 0.7 (95% CI 0.50-1.10; P=0.139); Laekna's announcement gives HR 0.744 (0.502-1.102). Overall survival was numerically worse with the combination: 11.2 vs 13.1 months, HR 1.2 (0.77-1.81). Sources: ClinicalTrials.gov posted results; Herzog et al., Gynecol Oncol 2025, PMID 40221173; HKEX announcement of 2024-01-28.
(2) The only signal came from an exploratory biomarker subgroup: phospho-AKT IHC>1, 37% of patients. In that subgroup median PFS was 5.4 vs 2.9 months, HR 0.352 (0.125-0.997). Both the authors and the sponsor framed the next step around that subgroup. The paper's conclusion: "did not significantly improve PFS/OS in patients with PROC. However, exploratory biomarker findings suggest potential efficacy in phospho-AKT positive patients." Laekna said it would "identify a registration path for PROC patient populations that may benefit from afuresertib."
(3) What followed: the 2024 interim report pipeline listed PROC as "In preparation for Phase III." The 2024 annual report (April 2025) and the 2025 interim report changed this to "We plan to pursue strategic partnerships to support further development of this program." PROC was still on the pipeline chart in the 2025 annual report (April 2026). It is gone from the 2026 interim report (September 2026) and from the current website pipeline. No reason is given for removing it. Meanwhile the company put its resources into the HR+/HER2- breast cancer program. That Phase III (AFFIRM-205) enrolled patients selected for PIK3CA/AKT1/PTEN alterations and met its primary endpoint. ClinicalTrials.gov lists no Phase 3 afuresertib trial in ovarian cancer.

Coding: the direct cause of failure was no efficacy in an all-comer, biomarker-unselected PROC population. Both the investigators and the sponsor attribute any benefit to a pAKT-defined subgroup, which makes F3 (wrong population/subtype) the best single code.

Alternatives considered:
- F7 (power/design): the trial was small, open-label and missed with HR about 0.74. But the OS HR above 1 argues against simple underpowering, and no source names design as the cause.
- F8 (commercial): the later move to partnering and the removal from the pipeline are commercial steps. They came after the efficacy miss and no source gives a strategic reason.
- F5/F6 (toxicity): serious TEAEs were 34.3% vs 25.5%, including GI perforations. Both sources call this consistent with the AKT-inhibitor class and manageable, and neither cites it as a reason.
- F1/F2: target engagement was not reported in this trial. The posted results include only pharmacokinetics.

Caveats: the pAKT subgroup result is exploratory and post hoc, with a CI that reaches 0.997. The paper abstract also calls the subgroup "AKT mutation biomarker+ (IHC>1)". Whether PROC was dropped mainly for efficacy reasons or for strategic/funding reasons is not stated by any source ("unclear"). Confidence in F3 is moderate.

outcome_summary:
The industry-sponsored Phase 2 entry is confirmed. NCT04693520 is an open-label biomarker study by Alzheon of ALZ-801 in APOE4 carriers with early Alzheimer's disease. It started on 2020-09-30 (actual), and ClinicalTrials.gov lists it as COMPLETED.

The program advanced within four years. Alzheon's Phase 3 APOLLOE4 trial (NCT04770220; 325 APOE4/4 patients with early Alzheimer's disease; 265 mg twice daily vs placebo for 78 weeks) started on 2021-05-19 and completed in 2024.

APOLLOE4 missed its primary endpoint, ADAS-Cog13 (the cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale). The posted results give a least-squares mean difference of -0.51 with p=0.6058. Alzheon's topline release of 2025-04-10 says the primary endpoint was 'not met' (11% slowing, p=0.607). The key secondary clinical outcomes also showed no effect in the overall population. Hippocampal atrophy slowed significantly (18%, p=0.017). In the prespecified MCI subgroup (MMSE above 26, N=125) results were only nominally significant: ADAS-Cog13 p=0.041, DAD p=0.016, CDR-SB p=0.053. The full results were published in Drugs in 2025. The common adverse events were gastrointestinal, and there was no increase in ARIA (the brain swelling and bleeding seen with amyloid antibodies). Plasma p-tau217 fell significantly in the overall population (Drugs, 2026).

The Phase 3 long-term extension (NCT06304883) was TERMINATED in March 2026, with the reason given as 'Sponsor business decision'.

Current status: the drug is not approved and no marketing application has been filed. As of October 2026, ClinicalTrials.gov lists no new Phase 3 trial. Alzheon's press releases still describe the drug as 'currently in Phase 3 development' (April 2026). In February and September 2026 the company said it is 'moving forward with plans for the next Phase 3 study', which appears to focus on APOE4/4 patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). The program has not been formally stopped.

On the coding: because the program advanced to Phase 3 within the window, the failure code is not_a_failure. However, the advancing Phase 3 itself failed its primary endpoint. If that trial were coded as a failure, the best code would be F3 (wrong disease stage, with benefit limited to MCI). status_now is a judgment call: the program is in Phase 3 by the company's own description, but no Phase 3 trial is active and nothing has been filed.

claim: Reactome curates a pathway reaction linking the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), dated before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Usharani P, Warn-Cramer BJ, Kasper CK, Bajaj SP. Characterization of three abnormal factor IX variants (Bm Lake Elsinore, Long Beach, and Los Angeles) of hemophilia-B. Evidence for defects affecting the latent catalytic site. J Clin Invest 1985;75(1):76-83 (PMID 3965513). This is the earliest literature reference on Reactome reaction R-HSA-9670874, "FIXa variant:FVIIIa does not convert FX to the active FXa", which Reactome annotates with the disease hemophilia B.
outcome_summary:
The entry trial is NCT03995784 (DLZ-201), an open-label Phase 2b sponsored by Catalyst Biosciences. It started 2019-06-18 in 6 men with severe hemophilia B, giving 100 IU/kg of dalcinonacog alfa under the skin every day for 28 days. The primary endpoint was reaching a FIX activity level of at least 12%. All 5 patients who completed the study reached it by Day 29: 3 by Day 7 and 4 on Days 14 to 28 (CT.gov posted results; Mahlangu et al., Haemophilia 2021, PMID 33960073). Catalyst's FY2020 10-K reports FIX levels up to 27%, no bleeds, no neutralizing antibodies and no serious adverse events. One patient withdrew on Day 7 because of injection-site reactions, and one non-neutralizing anti-drug antibody was seen. In the earlier Phase 1/2, two cousins with the same rare FIX mutation developed neutralizing antibodies specific to DalcA.

Catalyst then called the program "Phase 3 Ready". In 2021 it moved its focus to complement and stopped developing its own hemostasis programs. Its FY2021 10-K (March 2022) says it was "actively seeking a partner", had FDA guidance on the design of a registrational Phase 3 and the data to start it, and was "exploring opportunities to license or sell DalcA". In May 2022 Catalyst sold its complement portfolio to Vertex and then merged with a fibrosis company. Its FY2022 10-K says that on 2023-02-27 GC Biopharma bought the legacy bleeding-disorder programs (MarzAA, DalcA and CB 2679d-GT) for $6.0M in total.

ClinicalTrials.gov shows no later trial of DalcA from any sponsor, and no Phase 3 ever started. A 2023 pharmacokinetic modelling paper (PMID 37341915) found that no every-other-day regimen met the target, so dosing would have to be daily. That may have hurt its commercial appeal, but no source names it as the reason. The program met its Phase 2 endpoint and then stopped for portfolio, funding and partnering reasons, so the code is F8. I could not confirm GC Biopharma's current plans for the drug: its pipeline page returned 404.

So "F9 (replacement)" is correct.

(2) Entry trial: NCT03995784 (DLZ-201, Catalyst Biosciences) is Phase 2 ("Phase 2b"). Its only listed condition is Hemophilia B and it enrolled adult males with severe congenital hemophilia B. The actual start date is 2019-06-18, which matches the recorded Phase 2 entry date. Disease mapping is correct.

(3) Claim: All four Reactome reactions in the hemophilia B rows exist and Reactome annotates each with disease "hemophilia B":
- R-HSA-9670874: earliest literature is 1985 (PMID 3965513).
- R-HSA-9673223: earliest literature is 1986 (Bentley et al., Cell, PMID 3009023, defective propeptide processing in FIX).
- R-HSA-9673231: earliest literature is 1987 (Rabiet et al., JBC, PMID 3667614).
- R-HSA-9670888: earliest literature is 1997 (Kurachi et al., Biochemistry, PMID 9100030).
The year stored in our database for each row matches its reaction's earliest literature reference. The fifth row (R-HSA-9668365, FVIIIa variant) is annotated by Reactome as "factor VIII deficiency" (hemophilia A), not hemophilia B. It is an F8-variant reaction that involves FIXa and only supports the claim under the "very similar disease" allowance.

(4) Timing caveat: The underlying literature predates Phase 2 entry by decades. The Reactome curation itself does not: every one of these reactions, and their parent pathway R-HSA-9673202 "Defective F9 variant does not activate FX", has Reactome releaseDate 2020-06-10, about a year AFTER the 2019-06-18 Phase 2 entry. (5) Sponsor authorship: None. The 1985 JCI paper's authors are academic hemophilia researchers (Usharani, Warn-Cramer, Kasper, Bajaj). failure_second.reasoning:
I coded this F8 (commercial or strategic). The Phase 2b worked, and the sponsor says it was ready for Phase 3. The program stopped because Catalyst Biosciences left hemophilia, could not find a partner and sold the assets.

**The Phase 2b met its goal.** NCT03995784 (DLZ-201) ran from 2019-06-18 to 2020-04-30 and has posted results.
- **Efficacy:** 6 men with severe hemophilia B received 100 IU/kg of dalcinonacog alfa (DalcA) under the skin every day for 28 days. All 5 who finished reached factor IX activity of at least 12% by day 29.
- **Safety:** there were no serious adverse events and no thrombotic events. 2 participants had antibodies to the drug, but neither had neutralizing antibodies.
- **Dropout:** one participant left on day 7 because of injection-site reactions.
- The paper (Mahlangu 2021, Haemophilia) concludes that the drug raised factor IX into the mild-hemophilia range.

So the drug clearly reached and raised its target, which rules out F1, F2 and F4.

**The company said it was ready for Phase 3 but did not run it itself.**
- The 2020 10-K described DalcA as having shown efficacy and safety in Phase 2b. Its plans for DalcA were limited to "Complete formulation studies of DalcA."
- On 2021-11-12, Catalyst made a "strategic decision" to stop developing MarzAA, its other bleeding-disorder drug. It said it would focus only on complement drugs and sell or license its hemophilia portfolio, DalcA included.
- The 2021 10-K, filed 2022-03-31, says Catalyst had "received guidance from the FDA on the design of the registrational Phase 3 clinical trial, have the necessary data to support its initiation, and are exploring opportunities to license or sell DalcA." It describes the move as "pivoting from hemophilia" to complement, and says the company was then exploring strategic alternatives.
- In 2022, Catalyst sold its complement programs to Vertex and kept offering DalcA for partnering.
- On 2023-02-27, GC Biopharma bought the bleeding-disorder programs (MarzAA, DalcA and CB 2679d-GT) for $6M.
- ClinicalTrials.gov lists no Phase 3 under any of the drug's names. The only trials are NCT03186677 (Phase 1/2a) and NCT03995784.

**Factors I considered but did not choose:**
- In the earlier Phase 1/2a, two cousins developed neutralizing antibodies that were specific to DalcA, and the 10-Ks list this as a risk. But the company said its root-cause investigation found the drug's immunogenic potential was low.
- Daily injections were a burden: a 2023 dosing-model paper found that no every-other-day regimen reached the target level.

Either of these may have made partners less interested, but no primary source names them as the reason. The stated reasons are portfolio and funding choices, so F8 is the best code.

claim: Reactome curates a pathway reaction linking the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), dated before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Weng AP et al., 'Activating mutations of NOTCH1 in human T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia', Science 2004;306:269-71 (PMID 15472075). It is cited by Reactome pathway R-HSA-2644603 'Signaling by NOTCH1 in Cancer' (released 2013-03-12) and is the source of the NOTCH1 HD/PEST-mutant entities in the six reactions where DLL4 appears.
outcome_summary:
Dilpacimab (ABT-165) is AbbVie's DVD-Ig bispecific antibody against DLL4 and VEGF. Its first industry Phase 2 trial, NCT03368859, was a randomized open-label study of ABT-165 plus FOLFIRI versus bevacizumab plus FOLFIRI in second-line metastatic colorectal cancer. It started on 2018-03-20 and enrolled 70 patients. The sponsor terminated it and its primary completion date was 2019-12-18. The CT.gov whyStopped field gives no usable reason ("Study may continue"). The participant-flow table counts 18 and 23 patients as "Study terminated by Sponsor".

The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS), and the dilpacimab arm did worse. Median PFS was 3.78 months (95% CI 2.07-7.20) with dilpacimab versus 7.36 months (95% CI 5.68-10.55) with bevacizumab, a stratified hazard ratio of 3.57 (95% CI 1.57-8.11) against dilpacimab. Objective response was 5.6% versus 14.7%. Median overall survival was 7.95 months with dilpacimab and not reached with bevacizumab. Four dilpacimab patients (11.8%) had serious treatment-related adverse events, including one fatal intestinal perforation; the bevacizumab arm had none. The paper reporting the trial (Strickler et al., Future Oncol 2022) concluded the combination was "not well tolerated and did not provide clinical benefit". The Phase 1 paper (Gordon et al., Mol Cancer Ther 2021) states the Phase 2 study "was discontinued after interim analysis showed lack of improved efficacy beyond bevacizumab".

evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: confirmed. AbbVie's preclinical paper (Li et al., Mol Cancer Ther 2018, PMID 29592882) calls ABT-165 a DVD-Ig built 'based on its ability to bind and inhibit both DLL4 and VEGF'. That matches DLL4 and VEGFA as binder/neutralizer. The paper says 'VEGF'; reading that as VEGF-A is a small inference.

(2) Disease: entry trial NCT03368859 (AbbVie M14-064, Phase 2, actual start 2018-03-20) compared ABT-165+FOLFIRI with bevacizumab+FOLFIRI in previously treated metastatic colorectal adenocarcinoma. CT.gov lists the condition as 'Cancer'. Mapping it to MONDO:0004992 'cancer' is correct but very broad.

(3) Claim: technically true, but weak. All six reactions exist in Reactome:
- R-HSA-2730752
- R-HSA-2220944
- R-HSA-2769007
- R-HSA-2900765
- R-HSA-2737728
- R-HSA-2220976

Each is annotated with disease 'cancer' and 'T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia'. DLL4 (UniProt Q9NR61) is a participant in each, but only as one member of the generic DLL/JAG ligand set (DLL1, DLL4, JAG1, JAG2). The disease entity is gain-of-function NOTCH1 HD/PEST mutants in T-ALL, not DLL4:
- Two reactions are explicitly 'irrespective of ligand binding'.
- The three ubiquitination reactions say this 'has not been investigated but is assumed to occur' from wild-type NOTCH1.

So Reactome gives no DLL4-specific causal link to cancer, and nothing about colorectal cancer.

Dating: the years in our database (1997, 2001, 2006) are the years of literature cited on the reactions, not curation dates:
- 1997: Pan & Rubin, Drosophila Kuzbanian (PMID 9244301), no cancer content.
- 2001: Lai et al., Drosophila neuralized (PMID 11740940), no cancer content.
- 2006: Malecki et al., leukemia NOTCH1 HD mutants (PMID 16738328).

The first source that ties these reactions to cancer is Weng et al. 2004. The parent pathway also cites Ellisen 1991 (PMID 1831692) for the NOTCH1 translocation in T-ALL, but not for the HD/PEST mutants. Reactome curation: created Nov 2012 to Jan 2013 (Orlic-Milacic), reviewed Feb 2013, pathway released 2013-03-12. Separately, R-HSA-2730752 lists a bad reference, PMID 2691227, a 1989 trypanosomiasis review.

(4) Timing: every source (1997-2006 papers; Reactome curation 2013) predates the 2018-03-20 Phase 2 entry.

(5) Sponsor: no. Weng et al. are from Brigham and Women's/Harvard; Pan & Rubin is a Drosophila academic paper. The only AbbVie-authored paper (PMID 29592882) supports the target and action, not the Reactome claim.

I did not research the clinical outcome.

failure_second.reasoning:
Dilpacimab (ABT-165) is AbbVie's DVD-Ig bispecific that blocks both DLL4 and VEGF. It stopped because adding DLL4 blockade to VEGF blockade did not make it better than bevacizumab alone. In patients it did worse, even though Phase I had shown that it bound both targets.

Program: Phase 2 trial NCT03368859 (M14-064), dilpacimab + FOLFIRI versus bevacizumab + FOLFIRI in second-line metastatic colorectal cancer. Randomized, open label, n=70. It started 2018-03-20 and ended 2019-12-18 with status TERMINATED. Every patient who had not already left the trial was taken off it with the reason "Study terminated by Sponsor" (18 dilpacimab, 23 bevacizumab). The registry's stop reason, "Study may continue", explains nothing. Only two dilpacimab trials are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (this Phase 2 and the Phase I NCT01946074), so no Phase 3 was ever started.

Why it stopped (primary source): the Phase I paper (Gordon et al., Mol Cancer Ther 2021, PMC9398147) says the Phase 2 study "was discontinued after interim analysis showed lack of improved efficacy beyond bevacizumab." The same paper notes that AbbVie had already decided to "terminate further monotherapy development."

Phase 2 results (ClinicalTrials.gov results section; Strickler et al., Future Oncol 2022, PMID 35920133):
- Median PFS 3.78 months with dilpacimab versus 7.36 months with bevacizumab (HR 3.57, 95% CI 1.57-8.11).
- Response rate 5.6% versus 14.7%.
- Median OS 7.95 months versus not reached.
- Deaths 12/34 versus 6/32.
- Serious treatment-related adverse events 11.8% versus 0, including one fatal intestinal perforation.
- Authors' conclusion: dilpacimab + FOLFIRI "was not well tolerated and did not provide clinical benefit" compared with bevacizumab + FOLFIRI.

Target engagement was shown, which rules out F1. In Phase I, free plasma VEGF fell significantly within 2 hours at every dose, and total soluble DLL4 rose in a dose-dependent way, consistent with the drug binding it. Preclinically, dilpacimab plus chemotherapy had beaten anti-VEGF treatment in mouse tumour models (Li et al. 2018, PMID 29592882). That benefit did not carry over to patients, which fits F2.

Why not the other codes:
- F5 (on-target toxicity) is the runner-up. Hypertension, GI perforation and pulmonary hypertension are known class effects of blocking VEGF and DLL4, and the dilpacimab arm tolerated treatment worse. But the stated reason for stopping was the efficacy result at the interim analysis, not safety.
- F7 does not fit: the PFS hazard ratio was clearly worse, so a small trial does not explain the result.
- F3 is not supported: no source says the wrong population was chosen.
- F8: no source points to a business reason. AbbVie still listed ABT-165 for solid tumours in its June 2019 pipeline slides.

Could not verify ("unclear"):
- The interim analysis details (its stopping boundary, the Phase 2 dilpacimab dose, dose intensity) and how much toxicity contributed to the worse PFS. The publisher blocked access to the Future Oncology full text (HTTP 403 bot protection), so I worked from its abstract.
- The Phase 2 dose itself: one review (PMC11544561) lists 2.5 mg/kg for NCT03368859 but labels it a Phase 1b with 16 patients, which conflicts with the registry.
- Any company press release about the discontinuation: none found, and an SEC full-text search for "dilpacimab" returned no hits.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Suzuki T et al., 'Familial pulmonary alveolar proteinosis caused by mutations in CSF2RA', J Exp Med 2008;205:2703-10 (PMID 18955570, epub 27 Oct 2008). A companion paper in the same issue also reports it: Martinez-Moczygemba M et al., PMID 18955567. Earlier, weaker report for CSF2RB: Dirksen U et al., J Clin Invest 1997 (PMID 9410898). Definitive CSF2RB papers: Tanaka et al., J Med Genet 2011, epub Nov 2010 (PMID 21075760), and Suzuki et al., Eur Respir J 2011 (PMID 21205713).
outcome_summary:
Molgramostim is Savara's inhaled recombinant GM-CSF (Molgradex, now branded MOLBREEVI). Its first industry Phase 2 trial in autoimmune PAP was IMPALA (NCT02702180), a three-arm randomized placebo-controlled trial with 138 to 139 patients that started on 2016-03-21. The registry lists it as Phase 2, but Savara called it a pivotal Phase 3.

IMPALA missed its primary endpoint. The company's June 2019 topline said the change in A-aDO2 at week 24 was -4.6 mmHg versus placebo for continuous dosing (p=0.17). ClinicalTrials.gov results agree (LS mean -4.6, 95% CI -11.1 to 2.0, p=0.1688). Savara put the miss down to a stronger-than-expected placebo effect. Some secondary endpoints were positive: SGRQ improved by 7.6 points (p=0.01) and DLCO by 7.9% predicted (p=0.007). The later NEJM paper (2020; PMID 32897035) imputed invalid A-aDO2 values and reported p=0.03 for the primary endpoint. In October 2019 the FDA said in a Type C response that the data were not sufficient to support a BLA.

The Phase 3 extension IMPALA-X (NCT03482752) started on 2018-04-16, inside the 4-year window, and was terminated in January 2021 after the IMPALA results and regulator advice. Savara then ran a new pivotal Phase 3, IMPALA-2 (NCT04544293). It started on 2021-05-19 and switched the primary endpoint to DLCO. It met that endpoint in June 2024: +6.0% predicted at week 24 (p=0.0007), with SGRQ also significant.

Today the BLA is under FDA review. The FDA filed it in February 2026 with Priority Review, and the PDUFA date was extended to 2026-11-22 after a major amendment. The EMA validated the MAA in March 2026, and the UK MHRA validated an MAA in April 2026. A pediatric Phase 3 (NCT06431776) started on 2025-10-22. There is no approval yet: openFDA has no molgramostim record, and Savara has filed no approval 8-K. The program is still advancing, so the answer is not_a_failure. The IMPALA miss and the FDA feedback that followed (an endpoint and trial-design issue) delayed the pivotal Phase 3 by about two years. The program did not stop.

evidence.earliest_source: Suzuki T et al., 'Familial pulmonary alveolar proteinosis caused by mutations in CSF2RA', J Exp Med 2008;205:2703-10 (PMID 18955570, epub 27 Oct 2008). A companion paper in the same issue also reports it: Martinez-Moczygemba M et al., PMID 18955567. Earlier, weaker report for CSF2RB: Dirksen U et al., J Clin Invest 1997 (PMID 9410898). Definitive CSF2RB papers: Tanaka et al., J Med Genet 2011, epub Nov 2010 (PMID 21075760), and Suzuki et al., Eur Respir J 2011 (PMID 21205713).
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02702180 names the drug as molgramostim (rhGM-CSF), 300 mcg, inhaled. GM-CSF signals through a receptor made of a binding alpha subunit (GM-CSF-Ralpha, encoded by CSF2RA) and an affinity-enhancing beta subunit (encoded by CSF2RB), as stated in the abstract of PMID 18955570. ChEMBL target CHEMBL2364169 is this CSF2RA/CSF2RB complex. ChEMBL has no mechanism row for molgramostim itself (CHEMBL2109134), but it lists sargramostim (CHEMBL1201670), also recombinant GM-CSF, as an AGONIST of the same complex. Since the drug is the receptor's natural ligand, 'agonist' is the right direction.

(2) Disease: the entry trial NCT02702180 (IMPALA, MOL-PAP-002, Phase 2, actual start 2016-03-21, lead sponsor Savara Inc.) enrolled autoimmune PAP patients with raised GM-CSF autoantibodies. That fits the database disease, pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (MONDO:0001437).

(3) Claim: true. Germline loss-of-function variants in CSF2RA cause hereditary PAP (SMDP4, OMIM 300770). This was first shown in 2008 in two J Exp Med papers: Suzuki et al. found compound heterozygous changes (a 1.6-Mb deletion plus G174R) in two sisters, and Martinez-Moczygemba et al. found a PAR1 deletion. Biallelic CSF2RB variants cause SMDP5: Tanaka 2011 (epub Nov 2010; homozygous c.631del) and Suzuki 2011. Dirksen 1997 reported low beta-c expression and one P602T variant, but Tanaka 2011 says no earlier report had clearly identified a function-associated CSF2RB defect, so 1997 is only suggestive. ClinVar confirms both genes: VCV000010355 (CSF2RA c.586G>A p.Gly196Arg, i.e. G174R in mature-protein numbering) is Pathogenic for SMDP4, and VCV000029744 (CSF2RB c.631del) is Pathogenic for SMDP5. PanelApp panels 111 and 398 rate both genes green (level 3) for PAP and cite these papers.

Dating error in our rows: the 1990 year on the CSF2RA rows does not mark disease evidence. It matches PanelApp's citation of PMID 1972780 (Gough et al., Nature 1990, which maps the GM-CSF receptor gene to the X-Y pseudoautosomal region) and also HGNC's symbol date of 1990-07-03. The real disease link dates to 2008. The 1997 year on the CSF2RB rows matches Dirksen 1997.

Biology caveat: the genetic evidence is receptor loss-of-function in hereditary PAP. The trial treats autoimmune PAP, where the ligand is neutralised by antibodies and the receptor is intact. The direction fits (losing GM-CSF signalling causes PAP, and an agonist restores it), but extra ligand would not be expected to rescue patients whose receptor is broken.

(4) Every source above is dated 1997-2011, all before Phase 2 entry on 2016-03-21.

(5) The key papers come from Cincinnati Children's (Trapnell lab), Texas A&M/Baylor, Nagasaki and Düsseldorf. None has a Savara or Serendex affiliation. Trapnell later led the Savara-sponsored IMPALA paper (NEJM 2020), but the 2008 genetics paper was not sponsor-authored.

Limits: WebSearch budget was used up, so no Savara press releases or SEC filings were checked. Every fact here comes from ClinicalTrials.gov, PubMed, ClinVar, PanelApp and ChEMBL.

outcome.advance_event: Under the literal registry rule, the program advanced: IMPALA-X (NCT03482752), registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as a Phase 3 open-label safety extension of inhaled molgramostim in aPAP, started on 2018-04-16. That is about 2.1 years after the 2016-03-21 entry. Savara also described the entry trial, IMPALA (NCT02702180), as its "pivotal Phase 3" study, although the registry lists it as Phase 2. The caveat is that IMPALA-X was a rollover extension, and it was terminated after IMPALA's results and regulator advice. The randomized pivotal Phase 3, IMPALA-2 (NCT04544293), started on 2021-05-19, about 5.2 years after entry, which is outside the 4-year window. If the benchmark counts only pivotal or efficacy Phase 3 trials, this answer becomes "no".

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Geisterfer-Lowrance AA, Kass S, Tanigawa G, Vosberg HP, McKenna W, Seidman CE, Seidman JG. "A molecular basis for familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: a beta cardiac myosin heavy chain gene missense mutation." Cell 1990 Sep 7;62(5):999-1006 (PMID 1975517). It reports MYH7 Arg403Gln (R403Q) in every affected member of a large familial HCM kindred. This is the variant in ClinVar RCV000015143 / VCV000014087.
outcome_summary: The Phase 2 entry is confirmed. MyoKardia's open-label Phase 2 PIONEER-HCM (NCT02842242) tested MYK-461 in symptomatic obstructive HCM. It started in August 2016, finished in November 2017, and its primary endpoint was the change in post-exercise LVOT gradient at week 12. The drug advanced within four years: the pivotal Phase 3 EXPLORER-HCM (NCT03470545) started on 2018-05-29 and met its primary composite clinical-response endpoint (37% on mavacamten vs 17% on placebo, difference +19.4%, p=0.0005; Olivotto et al., Lancet 2020, PMID 32871100). The FDA approved Camzyos (mavacamten, NDA 214998, new molecular entity, orphan) on 2022-04-28 for adults with symptomatic NYHA class II-III obstructive HCM. Status: approved for the disease. The approval covers the obstructive subtype only. A separate Phase 3 in non-obstructive HCM, ODYSSEY-HCM (NCT05582395), is listed on ClinicalTrials.gov as TERMINATED; this answer does not say why, because no reason was verified. That trial does not change the outcome for this program. Not a failure.

evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: Green et al., Science, Feb 2016 (PMID 26912705) found that MYK-461 "reduces contractility by decreasing the adenosine triphosphatase activity of the cardiac myosin heavy chain". The CAMZYOS label (DailyMed, section 12.1) calls mavacamten "an allosteric and reversible inhibitor selective for cardiac myosin". MYH7 as an inhibitor target is consistent with both. Neither source says the drug acts only on the beta (MYH7) isoform rather than cardiac myosin in general, so I have not claimed that.

(2) Entry trial: NCT02842242 (PIONEER-HCM, MYK-461-004) is a Phase 2 trial sponsored by MyoKardia. It started in 2016-08 (actual) and its listed conditions are "Cardiomyopathy, Hypertrophic Obstructive" and "Left Ventricular Outflow Tract Obstruction". Obstructive HCM is a subtype of HCM (MONDO:0005045), so the disease mapping holds.

(3) Claim: ClinVar RCV000015143 is NM_000257.4(MYH7):c.1208G>A (p.Arg403Gln) for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy 1. It is classified Pathogenic, germline, with multiple submitters and no conflicts. The companion RCV000199447, for HCM in general, was reviewed by an expert panel and classified Pathogenic, last evaluated 2016-12-15. The 1961 year on our rows comes from Pare et al., Am J Med 1961 (PMID 13732753). That paper describes the French-Canadian family clinically but names no gene. The OMIM submission SCV000035400 confirms that Geisterfer-Lowrance 1990 later found R403Q in this same kindred. So the earliest date for gene-level evidence is 1990, not 1961. The year should be corrected, but the result does not change: the evidence still comes long before the August 2016 entry. Other groups replicated the finding early: Epstein/Fananapazir (NIH), Circulation 1992 (PMID 1638703), and Perryman/Roberts, JCI 1992 (PMID 1634614).

(4) Timing: the 1990 paper predates Phase 2 entry (2016-08) by about 26 years.

(5) Sponsor: the 1990 paper came from an academic lab at Brigham and Women's Hospital. MyoKardia was incorporated in June 2012 (2015 S-1), so the company did not exist in 1990. The paper's senior authors, CE Seidman and JG Seidman, did later co-found MyoKardia: the Green 2016 Science competing-interests statement says "L.A.L., J.A.S., J.G.S., and C.E.S. are founders and own shares of MyoKardia". The answer "no" is strict, because the sponsor company did not author the paper. Even so, the people who produced the key genetic evidence are the sponsor's scientific founders, so the evidence is not independent of the sponsor at the person level. Groups with no link to the company replicated it independently.

Program: radiprodil (RGH-896), a GluN2B negative allosteric modulator, in drug-resistant infantile spasms. UCB sponsored it; the entry trial was NCT02829827, which started 2017-12-04.

1) The ClinicalTrials.gov record for NCT02829827 has status TERMINATED, actual enrollment of 3, and primary completion on 2018-10-02. Its whyStopped field reads: "After reviewing the feasibility and projected completion date of the study, UCB has made the decision to stop the study". No results were posted.
2) The sponsor's own report of the trial, Auvin et al., Ann Clin Transl Neurol 2020 (PMID 32106360, PMC7085998), says why. The aim was 10 infants before an interim analysis, but the study "was stopped earlier because of the challenge in recruiting patients meeting all inclusion and exclusion criteria". It was "terminated due to insufficient enrollment ... within a reasonable time frame". The authors name three causes:
   - The design required the first two (sentinel) infants to stay as inpatients for about 2 months, which most centres could not support and which burdened families.
   - The syndrome is rare.
   - Infants are now commonly given vigabatrin and steroids together, and about 72% become spasm-free on that combination, so few infants are drug-resistant and eligible.

Exposure matched the PBPK predictions, and a companion paper (Johnson et al., Br J Clin Pharmacol 2021, PMID 32822519) dosed the infants to 20-60% receptor occupancy. No drug-related adverse events occurred and no infant discontinued because of an adverse event. One of the 3 infants became spasm-free and the other two improved. claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Levy GG et al. 'Mutations in a member of the ADAMTS gene family cause thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.' Nature 2001 Oct 4;413:488-94 (PMID 11586351). The paper used linkage in congenital TTP pedigrees and found 12 ADAMTS13 mutations accounting for 14 of 15 disease alleles. It is the cited source for ClinVar RCV000006154 (VCV5798, p.His96Asp, pathogenic) and the other 2001-dated rows.
outcome_summary:
The program entered Phase 2 as described. The first trial was NCT03922308 (SOAR-HI, SHP655-201), sponsored by Shire/Takeda. It was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of rADAMTS13 added to plasma exchange in acquired TTP. It started on 2019-10-09, enrolled 28 patients and was completed on 2021-08-05.

SOAR-HI's primary endpoints were descriptive pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic measures (ADAMTS13 activity, platelet count and LDH), with no formal hypothesis test. The posted results show target engagement: on day 1, ADAMTS13 activity measured by FRETS shortly after infusion was about 1.35–2.0 IU/mL in the rADAMTS13 arms, against 0.46 with placebo. Platelet counts and LDH at end of study were similar across arms.

Takeda then ran a Phase 2b instead of a Phase 3. That trial, NCT05714969 (TAK-755-2001), tested rADAMTS13 with minimal or no plasma exchange in immune TTP. It started on 2023-07-21, enrolled 29 patients and was completed on 2026-04-16. Its primary endpoint was safety (incidence of adverse events), and no results have been posted.

ClinicalTrials.gov searches under every code name found no Phase 3 trial in immune or acquired TTP. The only Phase 3 trials (NCT03393975, NCT04683003) are in congenital TTP. The FDA approval of ADZYNMA (2023-11-09) also covers congenital TTP only. So the program did not advance within four years of entering Phase 2.

Takeda's pipeline table for Q4 FY2025, dated 2026-05-12, lists TAK-755 for immune TTP at P-II(b) under 'Projects removed from pipeline', with the reason 'TAK-755 development in iTTP was discontinued due to strategic reasons'. The FY2026 Q1 pipeline (July 2026) no longer mentions immune TTP. It lists TAK-755 only for congenital TTP (approved in China, June 2026) and for acute ischemic stroke (Phase 2).

No efficacy or safety failure has been disclosed: target engagement was shown, and the Phase 2b results are unpublished. The best-supported failure code is therefore F8, commercial or strategic. Takeda has not said what the strategy was, for example competition from caplacizumab, and I have not verified it.

- 1984 (PanelApp panel 175): a plasma-infusion case report, Miura 1984 (PMID 6433703).
- 1998 (PanelApp panel 139): Furlan 1998, a protease-deficiency paper (PMID 9828245).
No ADAMTS13 genetic link existed before Levy 2001, so the earliest true germline source is 2001. That is still about 18 years before Phase 2 entry.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Amselem S et al., 'Spectrum of growth hormone receptor mutations and associated haplotypes in Laron syndrome', Hum Mol Genet 1993;2(4):355-9 (PMID 8504296). It is the paper behind the earliest database row, UniProt VAR_002714 R179C ('in LARS and GHIP'). The source that defines the specific evidence disease (partial GHR deficiency, GHIP) is Goddard AD et al., NEJM 1995;333:1093-8 (PMID 7565946), the paper behind ClinVar RCV000009168 and RCV000009169.
outcome_summary: Somapacitan (NNC0195-0092) is Novo Nordisk's once-weekly growth hormone derivative that binds albumin. Its first industry Phase 2 trial in children with GH deficiency was REAL 3 (NCT02616562), which started on 2016-03-31. That trial was randomized against daily Norditropin, and its primary endpoint was height velocity at week 26. At 3 years it showed sustained height-velocity efficacy comparable to daily GH, with similar safety (Savendahl et al., JCEM 2022, PMID 34964458). Novo then started the Phase 3 REAL 4 trial (NCT03811535) on 2019-05-20, within 4 years of Phase 2 entry. REAL 4 randomized 200 treatment-naive children 2:1 to somapacitan or daily GH. Its primary endpoint was annualized height velocity at week 52: 11.2 cm/y on somapacitan versus 11.7 cm/y on daily GH, and noninferiority was confirmed, so the endpoint was met (Miller et al., JCEM 2022, PMID 36062966). The FDA approved the pediatric GHD indication on 2023-04-28 (sBLA 761156/S-005). The current FDA label (revised 2/2026) lists pediatric growth failure due to inadequate endogenous GH secretion, alongside newer pediatric indications (small for gestational age, Noonan syndrome and idiopathic short stature) and adult GHD. The program advanced and was approved, so it is not a failure.

evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action are confirmed. The FDA Sogroya label (BLA 761156, 2020), section 12.1, says 'Somapacitan-beco binds to a dimeric GH receptor in the cell membrane of target cells resulting in intracellular signal transduction', so the drug is a GHR agonist. A paper from before Phase 2 entry, Rasmussen 2014 JCEM (PMID 25013997, Novo Nordisk), describes NNC0195-0092 as an albumin-binding hGH derivative that raises IGF-1 in a dose-dependent way.

(2) The entry trial NCT02616562 (Novo Nordisk, Phase 2, start 2016-03-31, matching the recorded entry date) enrolled GH-treatment-naive prepubertal children with GH deficiency confirmed by GH stimulation tests (peak at or below 7 ng/ml). That fits MONDO:0006909 'pituitary dwarfism' (defined as the pituitary failing to produce enough GH), so the disease mapping is fine. The trial explicitly EXCLUDED 'Laron syndrome ... or absence of GH receptors'.

(3) The claim is only partially supported. The ClinVar records are real OMIM submissions: they are germline, Pathogenic, and say 'no assertion criteria provided'.
- RCV000009168: E62K, evaluated 1995-10-26, PMID 7565946.
- RCV000009169: R179C, 1995, PMID 7565946.
- RCV000009178: c.876-1G>C, 1997, Ayling, Nat Genet 16:13, PMID 9140387.
- RCV000009184: V162I, 1998, Sanchez, JCEM, PMID 9814495. UniProt calls V162I 'uncertain significance', and ClinVar's aggregate classification for V162I is now 'conflicting'.
All four map to MONDO:0011420 'short stature due to partial GHR deficiency'. MONDO does list that term as a child of 'pituitary dwarfism', so the ontology link exists. Biologically, though, the evidence disease is GH INSENSITIVITY, not GH deficiency. Goddard 1995 selected children with 'normal GH secretion' who were 'not deficient in growth hormone'. GHR loss-of-function does show that GHR signalling drives growth, which fits an agonist direction. But GHR is not a causal gene for pituitary GH deficiency (the trial's population), and the trial excluded receptor-defect patients. So the 'subtype or very similar disease' link holds by ontology, not by mechanism.
The gene-disease link goes back further: Amselem 1989 NEJM (PMID 2779634) tied GHR mutations to Laron dwarfism. MONDO gives Laron syndrome the synonym 'pituitary dwarfism II', but does not place it under MONDO:0006909.

(4) Every source predates 2016-03-31: 1989, 1993, 1995, 1997 and 1998. The OMIM submissions to ClinVar were created 2013-04-04.

(5) None of the key papers is sponsor-authored. Goddard 1995 comes from Genentech and the GHI Study Group; Amselem 1989 and 1993 from INSERM Créteil; Ayling 1997 and Sanchez 1998 from academic groups. None is from Novo Nordisk.

Not checked: the Genomics England PanelApp rows for panels 478 and 483 (the API call failed). Web search was unavailable (budget exhausted), so all facts come from direct API and PDF fetches.

outcome_summary: Aficamten (CK-3773274) is a cardiac myosin inhibitor. Its first industry Phase 2 in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was REDWOOD-HCM (NCT04219826, Cytokinetics), a dose-finding study whose primary endpoints were safety and the rate of LVEF below 50%. It started 2020-01-10 and finished 2023-02-28. The Phase 3 SEQUOIA-HCM trial (NCT05186818) started 2022-02-01, inside the 4-year window. SEQUOIA met its primary endpoint, change in peak VO2 at week 24. Results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov give +1.76 mL/kg/min on aficamten versus +0.02 on placebo: a difference of 1.74 (95% CI 1.04 to 2.44), ANCOVA p<0.0001. The FDA approved MYQORZO (aficamten, NDA219083, Cytokinetics, new molecular entity with orphan designation) on 2025-12-19, per Drugs@FDA/openFDA. The label indication is adults with symptomatic obstructive HCM, to improve functional capacity and symptoms. A REMS supplement was approved 2026-02-05. The program advanced and is approved, so it is not a failure. The approval covers obstructive HCM only, which is a subset of the disease as recorded.

evidence.earliest_source: Geisterfer-Lowrance AA, Kass S, Tanigawa G, Vosberg HP, McKenna W, Seidman CE, Seidman JG. "A molecular basis for familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: a beta cardiac myosin heavy chain gene missense mutation." Cell 1990 Sep 7;62(5):999-1006 (PMID 1975517). It reports MYH7 Arg403Gln, which is ClinVar RCV000015143 / VCV000014087, 14_23429278_C_T.
evidence.notes: (1) Target and action: the sponsor's Dec 5, 2018 press release (SEC 8-K Ex. 99.1) describes CK-3773274 (CK-274) as a "novel, oral, small molecule cardiac myosin inhibitor" that binds "directly to cardiac myosin at a distinct and selective allosteric binding site," preventing myosin from entering a force-producing state. Later Cytokinetics papers say the same: the J Med Chem 2021 discovery paper, and Hartman et al., Nat Cardiovasc Res 2024, which has a crystal structure of aficamten bound to the cardiac myosin catalytic domain and shows it is selective over smooth and fast-skeletal myosin. MYH7 encodes beta-cardiac myosin heavy chain, the main ventricular isoform, so "MYH7 inhibitor" is correct. One caveat: the sources say "cardiac myosin" rather than naming MYH7 alone (alpha-cardiac MYH6 is also cardiac myosin). (2) Disease: NCT04219826 (REDWOOD-HCM, sponsor Cytokinetics, actual start 2020-01-10, which matches the entry date) lists "Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM)" and enrolled obstructive and non-obstructive HCM cohorts. ClinVar maps the RCV000015143 trait to MONDO:0005045, so the mapping is exact. (3) Claim: ClinVar VCV000014087, MYH7 c.1208G>A p.Arg403Gln, is Pathogenic for HCM with review status "reviewed by expert panel". The ClinGen Cardiomyopathy VCEP submission SCV000564413 is dated 2019-02-25, and many labs agree. The primary paper behind it is Geisterfer-Lowrance 1990 (Seidman lab, Brigham and Women's Hospital). It found the R403Q missense in every affected member of a large FHC kindred and concluded that "defects in the cardiac MHC genes can cause this disease." The claim is true and predates the 2020-01-10 entry by about 30 years. (4) Problems with the dates in our database: the 1961 date on RCV000015143 comes from Pare et al., Am J Med 1961 (PMID 13732753). That is a clinical description of the kindred ("hereditary cardiovascular dysplasia") from before molecular work, and it does not link MYH7. The gene link dates to 1990. The 1971 date on RCV000015182 (MYH7 L1793P) comes from Cancilla et al., Neurology 1971 (PMID 4104682), a skeletal myopathy paper. That variant's MYH7 link came in 2006 (Dye et al., myosin storage myopathy), so the 1971 year is wrong for an HCM link. Neither error changes the verdict, because the 1990 R403Q paper is well before entry. (5) Sponsor: the key paper is by the Seidman group, with no Cytokinetics authors, so it is not sponsor-authored. I did not research the trial outcome, as instructed.

outcome.advance_event: Phase 3 SEQUOIA-HCM (NCT05186818, Cytokinetics) started 2022-02-01 (actual), about 2 years after REDWOOD-HCM Phase 2 entry on 2020-01-10. The FDA then approved aficamten (MYQORZO, NDA219083) on 2025-12-19 for symptomatic obstructive HCM. That approval came within 4 years of a later date, not of 2020-01-10, so the Phase 3 start is the event that meets the 4-year test.
outcome.summary: Aficamten (CK-3773274) is a cardiac myosin inhibitor. Its first industry Phase 2 in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy was REDWOOD-HCM (NCT04219826, Cytokinetics), a dose-finding study whose primary endpoints were safety and the rate of LVEF below 50%. It started 2020-01-10 and finished 2023-02-28. The Phase 3 SEQUOIA-HCM trial (NCT05186818) started 2022-02-01, inside the 4-year window. SEQUOIA met its primary endpoint, change in peak VO2 at week 24. Results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov give +1.76 mL/kg/min on aficamten versus +0.02 on placebo: a difference of 1.74 (95% CI 1.04 to 2.44), ANCOVA p<0.0001. The FDA approved MYQORZO (aficamten, NDA219083, Cytokinetics, new molecular entity with orphan designation) on 2025-12-19, per Drugs@FDA/openFDA. The label indication is adults with symptomatic obstructive HCM, to improve functional capacity and symptoms. A REMS supplement was approved 2026-02-05. The program advanced and is approved, so it is not a failure. The approval covers obstructive HCM only, which is a subset of the disease as recorded.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Jeunemaitre X, Soubrier F, ... Lifton RP, ... Lalouel JM. "Molecular basis of human hypertension: role of angiotensinogen." Cell 1992 Oct 2;71(1):169-80 (PMID 1394429). This is the UniProt P01019 evidence for "Essential hypertension (EHT), MIM 145500", alongside Ward et al. Nat Genet 1993 on preeclampsia (PMID 8513325).
outcome_summary:
Evazarsen (IONIS-AGT-LRx, ISIS 757456) is Ionis's GalNAc-conjugated antisense drug that lowers hepatic angiotensinogen (AGT). Its first industry-sponsored Phase 2 trial in hypertension was NCT03714776 (n=25, controlled hypertension), which started on 2019-01-03. That trial met its primary endpoint, AGT reduction: -54% vs +13% on placebo, p<0.001. In-clinic systolic blood pressure (SBP) did not differ from placebo at any visit. A second Phase 2, NCT04083222 (n=26, uncontrolled hypertension, started Nov 2019), reduced AGT by 67%, again with no consistent SBP separation. The Ionis paper on these trials (JACC BTS 2021, PMID 34222719) says they were not powered for blood pressure and showed only "trends".

The trial that decided the program was the Phase 2b NCT04714320 (n=160, uncontrolled or treatment-resistant hypertension, 80 or 120 mg weekly for 12 weeks; started 2021-04-28, primary completion 2022-06-29). Its primary endpoint, change in seated automated office SBP at Day 85, failed. The least-squares mean changes were -13 mmHg (80 mg) and -9 mmHg (120 mg) vs -9 mmHg on placebo, with p=0.135 and p=0.867. Plasma AGT fell by about 60% at both doses. Twenty-four-hour ambulatory SBP was also not significant (p=0.094 and 0.842). Safety did not limit the drug: serious adverse events were 2/54 on 80 mg and 1/53 on 120 mg vs 1/53 on placebo.

Ionis listed a Phase 2b readout for H2 2022 (Q2/Q3 2022 8-Ks), but its 10-K filed Feb 2023 described the trial without giving any results. The 10-K filed Feb 2024 no longer lists IONIS-AGT-LRx as a program. It mentions the drug only as the reference for the follow-on AGT drug ION904, which is designed for less frequent dosing. Results for NCT04714320 were not posted on ClinicalTrials.gov until Feb 2025. No later trials or Phase 3 exist.

Ionis never published a reason for stopping. Efficacy is my inference: the program was dropped after a failed SBP primary endpoint and replaced by a next-generation molecule. That is primarily an efficacy failure with a portfolio substitution (F8 element). I chose F2 because the drug clearly engaged its target (about 60% AGT knockdown) but this partial knockdown did not lower blood pressure. F4 is a reasonable alternative, since the AGT biomarker moved while the clinical BP endpoint did not.

evidence.notes:
(1) Target and direction: confirmed. IONIS-AGT-LRx (ISIS 757456) is an antisense inhibitor of angiotensinogen (AGT) that lowers AGT levels. Sources are the NCT03714776 title ("an Antisense Inhibitor") with its AGT/angiotensinogen keywords, and the Ionis-authored Morgan et al., JACC BTS 2021 (PMID 34222719). That paper was used only for mechanism.

(2) Entry trial: confirmed. NCT03714776 is a Phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled study sponsored by Ionis. Its condition is "Mild Hypertension" in hypertensive participants whose blood pressure is controlled. Actual start 2019-01-03, which matches the Phase 2 entry date. Mapping it to MONDO:0005044 "hypertensive disorder" is appropriate, and the evidence disease, essential hypertension, is a subtype.

(3) Claim: partly supported. A curated germline gene-disease link did exist before Phase 2:
- UniProt P01019 lists "Essential hypertension" with the note "Disease susceptibility is associated with variants affecting the gene", citing PMID 1394429 (1992) and PMID 8513325 (1993, preeclampsia).
- Jeunemaitre 1992 reported sib-pair linkage, an association of M235T/T174M with hypertension, and higher plasma AGT by genotype.

But this is complex-trait susceptibility evidence, not Mendelian or ClinVar-pathogenic:
- ClinVar VCV000018068 (rs699, M235T) for "Hypertension, essential, susceptibility to" (RCV000019691) was "risk factor" in 2016 and "Benign, risk factor" from 2018-05-29. So at entry in Jan 2019 it was never classified pathogenic.
- OMIM has since reclassified M235T as a polymorphism (Hamosh 2024, using gnomAD allele frequency of about 0.47).
- ClinVar's pathogenic/likely pathogenic AGT variants are tied to renal tubular dysgenesis, a loss-of-function disease, not hypertension.

So "curated" is true, but "Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic" overstates it.

(4) Timing: the 1992 source predates the 2019-01-03 entry by about 26 years.

(5) Sponsor authorship: no. The authors were academic groups (HHMI/University of Utah and INSERM Paris), and Ionis had no part in the paper.

outcome.advance_event: None. By 2023-01-03 (four years after the 2019-01-03 Phase 2 start of NCT03714776) no Phase 3 of evazarsen (IONIS-AGT-LRx / ISIS 757456) in hypertension had started and there was no FDA approval. ClinicalTrials.gov lists only five trials of the drug: one Phase 1 (NCT03101878) and four Phase 2 (NCT03714776, NCT04083222, NCT04714320, NCT04836182 in HFrEF). ChEMBL records its max phase as 2.

failure_second.reasoning:
I coded this F2. The drug clearly hit its target: plasma angiotensinogen (AGT) fell by 55-67%. But that did not lower blood pressure in the one adequately sized trial. Ionis never published a reason for stopping, so the code rests on the trial results plus the program's quiet removal from Ionis's filings.

Program: evazarsen (IONIS-AGT-LRx, ISIS 757456), an Ionis liver-targeted antisense drug that cuts AGT production, for hypertension. Phase 2 began 2019-01-03 with NCT03714776. No Phase 3 has been registered: a ClinicalTrials.gov search on all code names returns one Phase 1 and four Phase 2 trials.

1) The target was engaged in every trial (ClinicalTrials.gov results):
- NCT03714776 (n=25, mild hypertension): AGT fell 54.2% by Day 43, versus a 12.6% rise on placebo (p<0.001). Office systolic pressure did not differ from placebo (e.g. Day 8 p=0.909, Day 15 p=0.132).
- NCT04083222 (n=26, uncontrolled hypertension): AGT fell 67.4% versus 3.4% on placebo (p<0.001). Systolic pressure did not differ (p=0.21-0.40 at early visits).
- Ionis's own paper (Morgan et al., JACC Basic Transl Sci 2021, PMID 34222719) says the drug "significantly reduced AGT" but the trials were "not powered" for blood pressure, with only "trends" seen.

2) The decisive Phase 2b trial missed its primary endpoint. NCT04714320 enrolled 160 patients with treatment-resistant hypertension on 3 or more drugs, and ran from April 2021 to October 2022.
- AGT fell 54-64% by Days 29-43 (p<0.001).
- The primary endpoint was the change in seated office systolic pressure at Day 85: placebo -9, 80 mg -13 (p=0.135), 120 mg -9 (p=0.867) mmHg. The higher dose did no better than the lower one.
- 24-hour ambulatory systolic pressure was also not significant (80 mg p=0.094, 120 mg p=0.842).
- No safety signal stood out: serious adverse events were 1/53 on placebo, 2/54 at 80 mg and 1/53 at 120 mg.

3) What Ionis's filings show:
- The FY2021 10-K still described the earlier "trends" in blood pressure.
- The Q3 2022 8-K listed the Phase 2b readout for 2022.
- The FY2022 10-K (filed February 2023) described the Phase 2b design but reported no blood-pressure result. It only said the drug lowered AGT and was well tolerated.
- The FY2023 10-K (filed February 2024) drops IONIS-AGT-LRx entirely. Only ION904 remains: "a follow-on medicine targeting AGT, designed to enable less frequent dosing compared to IONIS-AGT-LRx."
- The heart-failure Phase 2 (NCT04836182) completed in January 2023 but has posted no results.

Why F2 and not the alternatives:
- F2 fits because plasma AGT is a direct measure of target engagement, and partial liver AGT knockdown (about 55-65%) did not produce clinical blood-pressure lowering.
- F4 (biomarker moved, outcome didn't) fits less well. AGT is the drug's own target, not a disease surrogate, and the blood-pressure endpoint itself failed.
- F8 (replaced by ION904) is a plausible secondary code, since ION904's Phase 2 started in April 2022, before this readout. Ionis gave no strategic reason, though, and the failed efficacy trial is the documented event that came before the program was dropped.

Caveats: Ionis made no explicit discontinuation statement, so the causal link is inferred from the timing. "Partial inhibition" as the mechanism is my interpretation, not a stated finding.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Goate A et al., 'Segregation of a missense mutation in the amyloid precursor protein gene with familial Alzheimer's disease', Nature 1991 Feb 21;349:704-6 (PMID 1671712). It describes APP V717I (London mutation), which is ClinVar VCV000018088 / RCV000019714: Pathogenic, multiple submitters with no conflicts, Alzheimer disease type 1.
outcome_summary: Eli Lilly's anti-amyloid antibody donanemab (LY3002813) entered Phase 2 in Alzheimer's disease with TRAILBLAZER-ALZ (NCT03367403). That trial started on 2017-12-18 and completed. It met its primary endpoint, change from baseline in iADRS, with a difference of 3.20 and p=0.042 (ClinicalTrials.gov results; Mintun et al., NEJM 2021). The Phase 3 trial TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 (NCT04437511) started on 2020-06-19, well inside the 4-year window. It met its primary iADRS endpoint at week 76 in the overall population (2.92, p<0.0001, per FDA; Sims et al., JAMA 2023). The FDA approved Kisunla (donanemab-azbt) for Alzheimer's disease under BLA 761248 on 2024-07-02, for patients with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia. Drugs@FDA also lists an efficacy supplement approved on 2025-07-01. The program advanced and is approved, so it is not a failure.

evidence.earliest_source: Goate A et al., 'Segregation of a missense mutation in the amyloid precursor protein gene with familial Alzheimer's disease', Nature 1991 Feb 21;349:704-6 (PMID 1671712). It describes APP V717I (London mutation), which is ClinVar VCV000018088 / RCV000019714: Pathogenic, multiple submitters with no conflicts, Alzheimer disease type 1.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and direction: donanemab (LY3002813) is a humanized IgG1 that binds insoluble N-truncated pyroglutamate amyloid beta (Abeta p3-42) and reduces amyloid plaques (Kisunla FDA label, sections 11 and 12.1). Abeta is a cleavage product of APP, so mapping the target to the APP gene is the usual convention. Calling it a depleter fits, because the drug clears Abeta plaque. Before Phase 2 entry, Lilly's own preclinical paper (DeMattos 2012, Neuron, PMID 23217740, Lilly authors) showed that the parent plaque-specific antibody against Abeta(p3-42), mE8, cleared existing plaque. Alzforum records donanemab as a humanized antibody derived from mE8, with Phase 1 running from May 2013 (NCT01837641, start date 2013-05-03). The label postdates entry; it is cited only to confirm the mechanism.
(2) Entry trial: NCT03367403 is TRAILBLAZER-ALZ, Phase 2, sponsored by Eli Lilly, condition 'Alzheimer Disease', in early symptomatic AD with amyloid and tau PET entry criteria. Its actual start date, 2017-12-18, matches the recorded Phase 2 entry date. The evidence disease, Alzheimer disease type 1 (familial early-onset AD caused by APP), is a subtype of the trial disease.
(3) Claim: ClinVar confirms germline Pathogenic APP variants for Alzheimer disease type 1:
- VCV18088, V717I: criteria provided, multiple submitters, no conflicts.
- VCV18089, V717F: multiple submitters, no conflicts.
- VCV18090, V717G: single submitter. Its aggregate trait now reads 'not provided', but the RCV in our row is AD type 1.
- VCV18091, A692G (Flemish): no assertion criteria.
- VCV18098, E693G (Arctic): no assertion criteria.
Primary papers:
- Goate 1991, Nature (V717I). This is the earliest.
- Murrell 1991, Science 254:97 (V717F, PMID 1925564).
- Chartier-Harlin 1991, Nature 353:844 (codon 717, PMID 1944558).
- Naruse 1991 and van Duijn 1991, both Lancet (V717I replication).
The genomics_england row dated 1990 most likely reflects Levy 1990, Science (PMID 2111584). That paper concerns an APP mutation in hereditary cerebral hemorrhage, Dutch type (cerebral amyloid angiopathy), not AD itself, so the earliest AD-specific evidence is 1991.
The genetics points the same way as the drug: the pathogenic APP mutations sit in or near the Abeta region and cause early-onset AD, and Jonsson 2012, Nature 488:96 (PMID 22801501) found a protective APP variant (A673T). Together these support lowering Abeta.
(4) All of the key sources (1991, 1992, 2012) are more than 25 years older than the 2017-12-18 entry date.
(5) Goate 1991 comes from St Mary's Hospital Medical School, London, and the other genetics papers are academic. None were written by Lilly. Only the preclinical antibody paper (DeMattos 2012) is sponsor-authored, and it is not the genetic evidence.
Clinical outcome was not researched.
