claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: O'Rahilly S et al., "Detection of mutations in insulin-receptor gene in NIDDM patients by analysis of single-stranded conformation polymorphisms", Diabetes 1991;40(6):777-82 (PMID 2040394). This is the UniProt-curated INSR variant K1095E (VAR_015924), found in one NIDDM subject. The ClinVar-pathogenic record RCV000015815 (INSR p.Arg1191Gln, historically Arg1152Gln; OMIM 147670.0021) rests on Cocozza S et al., "NIDDM associated with mutation in tyrosine kinase domain of insulin receptor gene", Diabetes 1992;41(4):521-6 (PMID 1607076).
outcome_summary:
PE0139 ("Insumera") is PhaseBio's once-weekly basal insulin: native human insulin fused to an elastin-like polypeptide (ELP). Phase 2 entry is confirmed. NCT02581657 is a PhaseBio-sponsored Phase 2a multiple-ascending-dose trial against placebo in 37 adults with type 2 diabetes. It started in Oct 2015 and completed in Nov 2016. Its primary endpoint was safety and tolerability, but no results were ever posted on ClinicalTrials.gov or published.

In Mar 2015 PhaseBio raised a $40M Series C led by AstraZeneca. The press release said the money would take PE0139 into Phase 2a. In Feb 2017 the company website still described PE0139, saying the Phase 2a had started in 4Q2015, but the page no longer appeared in the "Development Pipeline" menu. By Aug 2017 the homepage described the company as focused on rare diseases, starting with cardiopulmonary ones. By Oct 2018 the pipeline listed only PB2452 and PB1046. PhaseBio's Sept 2018 IPO S-1 does not mention insulin or diabetes at all. It does say that additional Series C-2 and C-3 shares tied to milestones would not be issued because "we discontinued development of the program related to these milestones." That program is not named, though the Series C was raised to fund PE0139 and PB1046, and PB1046 continued. Reviews from 2020 and 2024 say the Phase 2a results were never disclosed and it is unknown whether development continues. PhaseBio filed for Chapter 11 in Oct 2022.

So the program was dropped quietly around 2017, during the company's documented strategic shift to rare cardiopulmonary diseases. No primary source gives a reason for stopping PE0139 specifically, and the Phase 2a data are unpublished. An efficacy, PK or immunogenicity cause therefore cannot be ruled out, so stop_reason and failure_code are recorded as unknown. If one has to be inferred, F8 (strategic) is the most likely, but it is not verified.

evidence.earliest_source: O'Rahilly S et al., "Detection of mutations in insulin-receptor gene in NIDDM patients by analysis of single-stranded conformation polymorphisms", Diabetes 1991;40(6):777-82 (PMID 2040394). This is the UniProt-curated INSR variant K1095E (VAR_015924), found in one NIDDM subject. The ClinVar-pathogenic record RCV000015815 (INSR p.Arg1191Gln, historically Arg1152Gln; OMIM 147670.0021) rests on Cocozza S et al., "NIDDM associated with mutation in tyrosine kinase domain of insulin receptor gene", Diabetes 1992;41(4):521-6 (PMID 1607076).
evidence.notes: (1) Target and action: PhaseBio's archived PE0139 pipeline page (snapshot dated Jan 2016, page copyright 2015) describes PE0139 as "a fully mature, native insulin molecule (B and A chains) genetically fused to our ELP biopolymer". It calls it a once-weekly, super-long-acting basal insulin. An insulin molecule acts as an agonist at the insulin receptor (INSR), so "INSR (agonist)" is correct. The AntriaBio SEC 8-K of Jan 2017 independently lists PE0139 as PhaseBio's weekly basal insulin. (2) Disease: NCT02581657 is the PhaseBio "Phase 2a" multiple ascending dose study (37 patients, started 2015-10, condition "Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus"), so the mapping to T2D matches. (3) Claim: the evidence the claim needs does exist, but it is weak. ClinVar RCV000015815 is an OMIM submission (SCV000036082, created 2013-04-04) that marks INSR c.3572G>A p.Arg1191Gln as Pathogenic for T2D. Its review status is "no assertion criteria provided". It rests on one heterozygous NIDDM patient whose receptor showed no kinase activity (Cocozza 1992). OMIM also cites Esposito 1995 (PMID 7814014), which did not find this variant in Italian NIDDM patients or controls. Today the variant has conflicting classifications in ClinVar: Likely benign (Blueprint Genetics) and uncertain (PreventionGenetics, which notes the variant was inherited from an unaffected father). The other UniProt T2D variants are each one-patient or one-family reports: K1095E (O'Rahilly 1991), R1158Q (Kasuga 1992, PMID 1470163) and T858A, which is 19_7141787_T_C / rs182552223 (Kan 1995, PMID 7657032). None of these shows Mendelian causation of common T2D. Strong Mendelian evidence ties INSR loss of function to rare monogenic insulin-resistant diabetes: type A insulin resistance (Yoshimasa 1988 Science, PMID 3283938), Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome and leprechaunism. That would support the claim only if type A insulin resistance counts as a "very similar disease". The genetic direction is consistent with the drug: loss of receptor function causes insulin resistance and diabetes, and the drug is an agonist. One caution is that kinase-defective receptors argue against simply adding more ligand. (4) Timing: all the cited papers (1988 to 1995) and the ClinVar record (2013) came before Phase 2 entry on 2015-10-01. (5) Authors: academic groups (Naples CNR, Beth Israel/Oxford, Kobe, Tokushima, U Chicago). None is affiliated with PhaseBio. I did not research the clinical outcome.

outcome.advance_event: None. PE0139 has only two trials on ClinicalTrials.gov, both sponsored by PhaseBio: the Phase 1 single-ascending-dose trial NCT01835730 (2013-2014) and the Phase 2a multiple-ascending-dose trial NCT02581657 (Oct 2015 to Nov 2016). No Phase 3 trial by any sponsor and no FDA approval for type 2 diabetes appeared by Oct 2019 or since.

An efficacy, PK or immunogenicity cause therefore cannot be ruled out, so stop_reason and failure_code are recorded as unknown. If one has to be inferred, F8 (strategic) is the most likely, but it is not verified.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: PE0139 (also called "Insumera"), from PhaseBio Pharmaceuticals. It is a once-weekly basal insulin made of native human insulin fused to PhaseBio's elastin-like polypeptide (ELP), tested in type 2 diabetes.

What the primary sources establish:
1. Entry trial NCT02581657 was a Phase 2a, randomized, placebo-controlled multiple-ascending-dose study (6 weekly doses, 37 enrolled). It started 2015-10 and completed 2016-11 (status COMPLETED). It has no posted results and no whyStopped field. A Phase 1 single-ascending-dose study (NCT01835730) ran 2013-04 to 2014-05.
2. March 2015: PhaseBio's Series C press release (AstraZeneca-led, $40M) said the money would move PE0139 into Phase 2a. The 2018 IPO prospectus shows only the first $20M tranche (C-1) was issued. The milestone-linked C-2/C-3 tranches were never issued because "We discontinued development of the program related to these milestones."
3. The same prospectus attributes lower 2017 R&D spending to "the discontinuation of a prior clinical program at the end of 2016." That timing matches the PE0139 Phase 2a completing in Nov 2016, but the prospectus never names the program.
4. Feb 2017: PhaseBio's website listed PE0139 under "Internal Pipeline", separate from the "Development Pipeline" of PB1046 and PB1120. The page reported no Phase 2a results; it only said the study "was initiated in 4Q2015".
5. Jan 18, 2017: a press release announced $14.7M in convertible notes to fund PB1046 in orphan cardiopulmonary disorders. It described the company as focused on orphan diseases. By May 2017 the homepage gave the focus as "serious rare diseases, with an initial focus on cardiopulmonary indications." By Oct 2018 the pipeline page listed only PB2452 and PB1046.
6. The words "insulin" and "diabetes" do not appear in the 2018 IPO prospectus or the FY2018 10-K. On EDGAR, a full-text search for "PE0139" finds only a competitor's Jan 2017 shareholder letter (AntriaBio), which calls PE0139 an active rival program.
7. No peer-reviewed report of the Phase 2a results was found, in PubMed or in a Crossref search for conference abstracts. A 2024 review (Biomedicines, PMC11048618) says the results "have not been published, and it is unknown whether Insumera is still in active development." A 2021 review (PMC8601199) says only that the ELP diabetes constructs "have not been developed for clinical use."

Why the code is unknown and not F8: the timeline strongly suggests PE0139 was dropped around the end of 2016 as PhaseBio pivoted from metabolic disease to orphan cardiopulmonary disease. That makes a strategic or portfolio reason (F8) the leading hypothesis. However, no primary source names PE0139 as the discontinued program or says why it was stopped. The Phase 2a safety, PK, glucose-lowering and immunogenicity data were never disclosed. So a data-driven failure cannot be ruled out: inadequate glucose control or weekly profile (F1/F2), hypoglycemia (F5), or immunogenicity or injection-site problems (F6). The pivot may have been a result of those data rather than the cause.

Limitations: the WebSearch budget for this session was used up, so news and trade-press coverage (e.g., BioCentury, Fierce) could not be searched. Primary sources were reached directly through the CT.gov API, SEC EDGAR full-text search and filings, PubMed/Europe PMC/Crossref, and Wayback Machine captures of phasebio.com.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Cocozza S et al., "NIDDM associated with mutation in tyrosine kinase domain of insulin receptor gene", Diabetes 1992 Apr;41(4):521-6 (PMID 1607076). This is the paper behind ClinVar RCV000015815 (OMIM 147670.0021, INSR c.3572G>A p.Arg1191Gln, rs121913150, GRCh38 19:7120707 C>T; OMIM submission SCV000036082, "Pathogenic", no assertion criteria, literature only, last evaluated 1995-01-01, created in ClinVar 2013-04-04), and behind UniProt P06213's T2D variant annotation.
outcome_summary: Insulin 338 (I338, OI338GT, NN1953) is Novo Nordisk's once-daily oral tablet form of a long-acting basal insulin analogue. It uses the absorption enhancer sodium caprate. The Phase 2 entry trial, NCT02470039 (NN1953-4163), was industry-sponsored and started on 1 June 2015. It ran for 8 weeks, was randomised, double-blind and double-dummy, and enrolled 50 insulin-naive people with type 2 diabetes, comparing I338 with subcutaneous insulin glargine. The primary endpoint was the treatment difference in fasting plasma glucose (FPG) at week 8. FPG was 7.1 mmol/L with I338 and 6.8 mmol/L with glargine, a difference of 0.3 mmol/L (95% CI -0.5 to 1.1, p=0.46). Both arms lowered FPG by about 2.5 mmol/L and I338 was well tolerated, so the drug showed glycaemic efficacy comparable to glargine. The 'met' rating is a judgement call: the abstract reports no formal non-inferiority margin, but both the authors and Novo Nordisk described the results as encouraging, with no evidence of a difference from glargine. In its H1 2016 report (August 2016) Novo Nordisk said it was assessing the therapeutic use and investment needs of the oral insulin programme. Its Q3 2016 report (6-K filed with the SEC, dated 28 October 2016) states that in October 2016 it decided to stop developing OI338GT 'as the emergent product profile and required overall investments have been assessed not to be commercially viable in the increasingly challenging payer environment'. The same report says that under its updated R&D strategy it would not progress any oral insulin projects. The 2019 Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology paper on the trial adds that I338 doses were high: the starting dose was 2700 nmol and the maximum 16200 nmol, so producing enough drug for wide use was judged not commercially viable. Low oral bioavailability lay behind the high doses, but the company framed the decision as commercial and strategic, not as an efficacy or safety failure. No Phase 3 trial was ever registered, so the program counts as stopped (F8).

evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: insulin 338 (I338/OI338, NNC0123-0000-0338) is a long-acting basal insulin analogue (Halberg et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2019, PMID 30679095). In Novo Nordisk's own engineering paper (Hubálek et al., Nat Commun 2020, PMID 32719315), the OI338 analogue has insulin-receptor affinity lowered on purpose (about 500-fold) but still drives glucose disposal with maximal efficacy similar to human insulin, which makes it an INSR agonist. ChEMBL and Open Targets have no entry for it under any of its code names, so the mechanism comes from those papers.

(2) Disease: NCT02470039 (NN1953-4163, Novo Nordisk) is a Phase 2 trial that started 2015-06-01 (actual). It lists the conditions "Diabetes" and "Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2" and enrolled people with type 2 diabetes on oral antidiabetic therapy.

(3) Claim: the literal claim holds. ClinVar RCV000015815 classes INSR p.Arg1191Gln (formerly R1152Q/R1164Q) as germline Pathogenic for type 2 diabetes mellitus. UniProt P06213 lists "Type 2 diabetes mellitus" with these citations:
- PMID 1607076 (Cocozza 1992)
- PMID 1470163 (Kasuga 1992)
- PMID 7657032 (Kan 1995). This paper is the source of the T858A/rs182552223 row, GRCh38 19:7141787 T>C, which I confirmed through dbSNP.

The evidence behind it is weak, however:
- It is a "no assertion criteria" OMIM, literature-only submission based on one heterozygous NIDDM patient. That patient had normal insulin binding and normal autophosphorylation, and only lost kinase activity toward an exogenous substrate.
- Esposito et al. 1995 (PMID 7814014, cited in the same OMIM record) found the variant in none of 68 Italian NIDDM patients or 65 controls.
- UniProt words the T2D link as "may be involved in disease pathogenesis", not "caused by".
- The ClinVar variant is now "Conflicting classifications" (Likely benign 2018 and VUS 2025 from other submitters), though that came later.
- This is not Mendelian segregation evidence. INSR's strong Mendelian links are to severe insulin-resistance syndromes that are related to T2D but distinct from it: type A insulin-resistant diabetes (Yoshimasa 1988 Science, PMID 3283938; Odawara 1989 Science, PMID 2544998), Donohue syndrome and Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome.

(4) Date check: the DB's 1991 uniprot_literature date seems to come from Kusari et al. 1991 JCI (PMID 1918382), which found NO INSR coding changes in NIDDM patients. That date rests on negative evidence, so the earliest supporting source is really 1992. Either way, every supporting source, and the ClinVar SCV created 2013-04-04, comes before the 2015-06-01 Phase 2 entry.

(5) Sponsor: the key evidence paper comes from an academic group in Naples (CNR/University), not Novo Nordisk. The mechanism papers (Halberg 2019, Hubálek 2020) are by Novo Nordisk, but they are not the genetic evidence.

The trial's outcome was not researched or used.

outcome.advance_event: None. No Phase 3 trial or FDA approval followed. failure_second.reasoning:
Program: Novo Nordisk's oral basal insulin I338 (OI338GT, NN1953, NNC0123-0000-0338), a long-acting insulin analogue in a tablet with the absorption enhancer sodium caprate, for type 2 diabetes. The Phase 2 entry trial was NCT02470039 (NN1953-4163). It was an 8-week, randomised, double-blind, double-dummy trial against subcutaneous insulin glargine in 50 insulin-naive patients. It started in June 2015 and was completed in December 2015. No later trial reached Phase 3.

Why it did not advance (primary sources):
(1) Novo Nordisk's Q3 2016 financial report, filed with the SEC as a 6-K on 2016-11-01, says: "In October 2016, Novo Nordisk decided to discontinue the further development of the oral insulin project OI338GT, as the emergent product profile and required overall investments have been assessed not to be commercially viable in the increasingly challenging payer environment."
(2) The H1 2016 6-K (2016-08-08) says the Phase 2a results were "generally encouraging": fasting plasma glucose fell by about 2.5 mmol/L in both arms, and OI338GT "generally appeared safe and well-tolerated". It adds that Novo was "assessing the therapeutic use and investment needs".
(3) The sponsor's peer-reviewed Phase 2 paper (Halberg et al., Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol 2019, PMID 30679095) found no significant difference in 8-week fasting glucose versus glargine: 7.1 vs 6.8 mmol/L, difference 0.3 [-0.5 to 1.1], p=0.46. Tolerability was similar, with no severe hypoglycaemia. The paper says: "Further development of this particular oral insulin project was discontinued because I338 doses were high and, therefore, production of the required quantities of I338 for wide public use was deemed not commercially viable."

Coding: exposure and target engagement were shown, because fasting glucose fell as much as with glargine, so the code is not F1. Efficacy and safety did not fail, so it is not F2 to F7. The sponsor's stated reason is commercial. Low oral bioavailability meant very high doses (2,700 to 16,200 nmol a day), which made the cost of making the drug and the investment needed not viable in the payer environment. The root cause is a formulation and bioavailability limit, but the decision is explicitly commercial or strategic, so the code is F8.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Goate A et al., 'Segregation of a missense mutation in the amyloid precursor protein gene with familial Alzheimer's disease', Nature 1991 Feb 21;349(6311):704-6 (PMID 1671712). It reports APP V717I (London mutation), which is ClinVar RCV000019714 / VCV 18088, NM_000484.4(APP):c.2149G>A, Pathogenic for Alzheimer disease type 1.
outcome_summary:
The industry-sponsored Phase 2 entry is confirmed. NCT04693520 is an open-label biomarker study by Alzheon of ALZ-801 in APOE4 carriers with early Alzheimer's disease. It started on 2020-09-30 (actual), and ClinicalTrials.gov lists it as COMPLETED.

The program advanced within four years. Alzheon's Phase 3 APOLLOE4 trial (NCT04770220; 325 APOE4/4 patients with early Alzheimer's disease; 265 mg twice daily vs placebo for 78 weeks) started on 2021-05-19 and completed in 2024.

APOLLOE4 missed its primary endpoint, ADAS-Cog13 (the cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale). The posted results give a least-squares mean difference of -0.51 with p=0.6058. Alzheon's topline release of 2025-04-10 says the primary endpoint was 'not met' (11% slowing, p=0.607). The key secondary clinical outcomes also showed no effect in the overall population. Hippocampal atrophy slowed significantly (18%, p=0.017). In the prespecified MCI subgroup (MMSE above 26, N=125) results were only nominally significant: ADAS-Cog13 p=0.041, DAD p=0.016, CDR-SB p=0.053. The full results were published in Drugs in 2025. The common adverse events were gastrointestinal, and there was no increase in ARIA (the brain swelling and bleeding seen with amyloid antibodies). Plasma p-tau217 fell significantly in the overall population (Drugs, 2026).

The Phase 3 long-term extension (NCT06304883) was TERMINATED in March 2026, with the reason given as 'Sponsor business decision'.

Current status: the drug is not approved and no marketing application has been filed. As of October 2026, ClinicalTrials.gov lists no new Phase 3 trial. Alzheon's press releases still describe the drug as 'currently in Phase 3 development' (April 2026). In February and September 2026 the company said it is 'moving forward with plans for the next Phase 3 study', which appears to focus on APOE4/4 patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). The program has not been formally stopped.

On the coding: because the program advanced to Phase 3 within the window, the failure code is not_a_failure. However, the advancing Phase 3 itself failed its primary endpoint. If that trial were coded as a failure, the best code would be F3 (wrong disease stage, with benefit limited to MCI). status_now is a judgment call: the program is in Phase 3 by the company's own description, but no Phase 3 trial is active and nothing has been filed.

evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: valiltramiprosate (ALZ-801) is an oral valine prodrug of tramiprosate. This is not inhibition or activation of APP itself, so the recorded 'APP (other)' fits. Both mechanism papers are from Alzheon. Neurochem's independent Gervais 2007 Neurobiol Aging paper describes tramiprosate keeping soluble Abeta non-fibrillar.

(2) Entry trial: NCT04693520 (Alzheon, Phase 2, single arm, ALZ-801 265 mg BID) studied 'Early Alzheimer's Disease' in APOE4/4 and APOE3/4 carriers. Its actual start date is 2020-09-30, which matches phase2_entry. Mapping to MONDO:0004975 is correct.

(3) Claim: true. The ClinVar records in the evidence rows check out. RCV000019714 = V717I (London), RCV000019715 = V717F (Indiana), RCV000019716 = V717G, RCV000019718 = A692G (Flemish), RCV000019725 = E693G (Arctic). All are germline Pathogenic in ClinVar. The earliest primary paper is Goate et al., Nature, February 1991, which describes V717I segregating with familial AD. Other 1991 papers confirm it: Naruse and van Duijn in Lancet (April 1991), Yoshioka in BBRC, and Murrell in Science (October 1991, V717F). All of these are about 29 years before the September 2020 Phase 2 entry.

This does not affect the conclusion. The 1990 genomics_england row has no traceable paper and was not used.

(4) Sponsor: the Goate paper comes from St Mary's Hospital Medical School, London, and has no connection to Alzheon. Only the mechanism papers are sponsor-authored, not the genetic evidence.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Genovese G, Friedman DJ, ... Pollak MR. "Association of trypanolytic ApoL1 variants with kidney disease in African Americans." Science 2010;329:841 (published online 15 Jul 2010; PMID 20647424; doi:10.1126/science.1193032). It is the paper behind OMIM allelic variant 603743.0002 and ClinVar SCV000026637 (OMIM, submitted 2010-10-25), which sits under RCV000006454 (APOL1 G2 deletion rs71785313, "Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis 4, susceptibility to").
outcome_summary: Inaxaplin (VX-147) is Vertex's oral small-molecule APOL1 channel inhibitor. Its first industry Phase 2 trial for this disease was NCT04340362, an open-label, single-arm Phase 2a in 16 adults with two APOL1 variants and biopsy-proven FSGS. It started 2020-06-08 and completed in December 2021. It met its primary endpoint: among the 13 adherent participants, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (UPCR) fell by a mean of 47.6% from baseline at week 13 (95% CI -60.0 to -31.3). Adverse events were mild or moderate and none led to discontinuation (NEJM 2023, PMID 36920755). On these results Vertex started pivotal development in 2022 with a single Phase 2/3 adaptive trial in APOL1-mediated kidney disease (AMKD), called AMPLITUDE (NCT05312879), which began 2022-03-30. The FDA gave inaxaplin Breakthrough Therapy designation for APOL1-mediated FSGS, and the EMA gave it Orphan Drug and PRIME designations for AMKD. Vertex finished enrolling the Phase 2b dose-ranging part in 2023. After the independent data monitoring committee reviewed the unblinded data, the trial moved into its Phase 3 portion by Q1 2024 (10-Q filed 2024-05-07) and was expanded to adolescents aged 10 to 17. The program therefore advanced within four years whether the 2022 Phase 2/3 start or the 2024 move into the Phase 3 portion is counted. Today AMPLITUDE is listed as active, not recruiting, with 522 participants actually enrolled (ClinicalTrials.gov, record verified 2026-10). Its primary endpoints are UPCR change at week 48 and eGFR slope at the interim and final analyses, with estimated primary completion 2028-06-02. Vertex's Q2 2026 10-Q (filed 2026-08-04) expects full enrollment in the second half of 2026, data from a 48-week interim analysis in early 2027, and that interim as a possible basis for US accelerated approval. No FDA approval exists yet; no source found here reports one or a filing. A separate Phase 2 trial in APOL1-mediated kidney disease with or without comorbidities (NCT06794996, started 2025-02-04) is completed. The program has not stopped.

evidence.earliest_source: Genovese G, Friedman DJ, ... Pollak MR. "Association of trypanolytic ApoL1 variants with kidney disease in African Americans." Science 2010;329:841 (published online 15 Jul 2010; PMID 20647424; doi:10.1126/science.1193032). It is the paper behind OMIM allelic variant 603743.0002 and ClinVar SCV000026637 (OMIM, submitted 2010-10-25), which sits under RCV000006454 (APOL1 G2 deletion rs71785313, "Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis 4, susceptibility to").
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: Vertex's 2019 10-K, filed 2020-02-13 (before entry), says "a Phase 1 clinical trial evaluating VX-147 as a small molecule inhibitor of APOL1 function". Egbuna et al., NEJM 2023 (PMID 36920755) says inaxaplin "selectively inhibited APOL1 channel function in vitro". So APOL1 inhibitor is confirmed.

(2) Entry trial: NCT04340362 (VX19-147-101) is sponsored by Vertex. It is a Phase 2a, open-label, single-arm study of VX-147 (IXP) in adults with APOL1-mediated FSGS. The condition is "Glomerulosclerosis, Focal Segmental"; patients needed an APOL1 G1/G1, G2/G2 or G1/G2 genotype and biopsy-proven FSGS. Actual start was 2020-06-08, which matches the recorded entry date. FSGS is a subtype of kidney disorder (MONDO:0005240), so the disease mapping holds. The supporting evidence diseases (FSGS, steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome) are the same disease or close subtypes.

(3) The claim is true. Genovese 2010 found that two APOL1 variants, G1 (S342G/I384M) and G2 (6-bp deletion N388_Y389del, rs71785313), were associated with FSGS in African Americans (OR 10.5, 95% CI 6.0-18.4) and with hypertension-attributed ESKD. Tzur et al., Hum Genet 2010 (PMID 20635188, online 16 Jul 2010) independently found the same link. UniProt O14791 cites both papers for FSGS4. ClinVar VCV000006081 / RCV000006454 currently reads "Pathogenic/Likely risk allele; risk factor" (criteria provided, multiple submitters, no conflicts).

Caveats:
- Strictly, this is a germline susceptibility (risk) allele with a recessive two-allele model and incomplete penetrance, not a classic fully penetrant Mendelian cause. It is curated as a disease-susceptibility variant (OMIM FSGS4 612551, UniProt DI-02864).
- Before 2020-06-08, the ClinVar submissions were OMIM "risk factor" (2010), Nemours "risk factor" (created 2019), LMM "risk factor", and NIHR BioResource "Pathogenic" (created 2020-02-27, for FSGS/nephrotic-range proteinuria findings). The explicit "Pathogenic" classification against the FSGS4 RCV came later (e.g., Variantyx 2026), but the underlying variant-disease evidence clearly predates entry.

(4) Date: 2010 is about 10 years before the 2020-06-08 entry.

(5) Sponsor authorship: all Genovese 2010 authors are academic (BIDMC/Harvard, Wake Forest, NCI/Frederick, Université Libre de Bruxelles). Vertex had no role. Two of the authors, Pollak and Friedman (BIDMC), later co-authored the Vertex-sponsored inaxaplin NEJM 2023 paper, but the 2010 genetics paper was not sponsor work.

PanelApp panel 106 could not be checked because the API returned 404 or HTML. OMIM was blocked by Cloudflare, so the OMIM text was read through ClinVar's copy of the OMIM submission.

Vertex's Q1 2024 10-Q (filed 2024-05-07) says the trial had moved into its Phase 3 portion. Both dates fall before the four-year cutoff of 2024-06-08.

evidence.notes:
(1) Target/action. TOL-3021 (formerly BHT-3021) is a bacterial plasmid that encodes human proinsulin (hINS), according to the intervention description on CT.gov NCT03895437. It is an antigen-specific tolerising DNA vaccine meant to reduce proinsulin-specific CD8+ T cells (Roep et al., Sci Transl Med 2013, PMID 23803704, authored by Bayhill/Tolerion). INS is the encoded antigen and is not inhibited or activated, so the action "other" is correct.
(2) Disease. NCT03895437 (sponsor Tolerion; Phase 2; start 2019-06-17, matching the entry date) enrolled new-onset or established type 1 diabetes, condition "Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1". The mapping is correct.
(3) Claim. The DB row is Genomics England PanelApp panel 293, "Neonatal diabetes". There INS is Green (level 3), with phenotype "Diabetes mellitus, insulin-dependent, 2, 125852" (OMIM IDDM2), which Open Targets maps to MONDO_0005147. The panel cites PMIDs 17855560 (Stoy 2007, PNDM) and 26101329 (Carmody 2015, intronic INS mutation causing neonatal-onset diabetes). INS was already Green with the IDDM2 and T1D phenotype strings in panel v1.0 (version_created 2017-11-05).
ClinVar also has OMIM-submitted Pathogenic assertions under "TYPE 1 DIABETES MELLITUS 2". One is INS c.163C>T p.Arg55Cys (VCV000013392), citing Molven 2008: a girl and her mother with ketoacidosis-onset, GAD/IA-2 antibody-negative "type 1" diabetes. The other is p.Gly32Ser (VCV000021122), a PNDM allele from Stoy 2007, which a University of Chicago lab submitted as IDDM2 in 2014.
So curated Mendelian and ClinVar-pathogenic evidence linking INS to a label that MONDO and OMIM treat as a T1D subtype exists, and it predates 2019. I rate it "partial" because every Mendelian INS diabetes is monogenic, autoantibody-negative, insulin-deficient diabetes (PNDM, MODY10, antibody-negative T1D), caused by proinsulin misfolding and beta-cell ER stress. It is not the autoimmune T1D the trial treats. The only genetic link to autoimmune T1D is the common IDDM2 INS-VNTR susceptibility locus (Bell 1984; Bennett et al., Nat Genet 1995, PMID 7773291). That is association evidence, not Mendelian, although it is mechanistically relevant to proinsulin tolerance.
(4) All of these sources (1984, 1995, 2007, 2008, 2015; PanelApp 2017) predate 2019-06-17.
(5) None of the genetics papers were authored by Bayhill Therapeutics or Tolerion; their authors are at the University of Chicago, Exeter, Bergen and Oxford. Only the Phase 1 trial paper (Roep 2013) is sponsor-authored, and it is not the genetic evidence.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: TOL-3021 (formerly BHT-3021), a bacterial plasmid that encodes human proinsulin. It was given as a weekly intramuscular injection to tolerize proinsulin-reactive T cells in type 1 diabetes. Sponsor: Tolerion, Inc.

Why it did not advance (primary sources):
1) The Phase 2 entry trial, SUNRISE (NCT03895437), started 2019-06-17. It randomized 78 patients aged 12 to <41 within 5 years of diagnosis 2:1 to drug or placebo for 52 weeks. It is TERMINATED. ClinicalTrials.gov gives the reason as "The DSMB concluded that there was a low probability the study would meet it is primary endpoint as designed." The results population note says the interim analysis came after at least 30 TOL-3021 subjects reached Week 24, and "The DSMB determined that the investigational drug showed no efficacy relative to placebo and recommended termination." Limitations field: "Early termination following interim analysis showing lack of efficacy." All 78 participants are listed as not completed, with "Lack of Efficacy" as the reason.
2) Primary endpoint numbers (change in log MMTT C-peptide AUC, MMRM, p=0.368): Week 12, -0.04 vs -0.03; Week 24, -0.06 vs -0.05, drug vs placebo. Secondary endpoints also showed no benefit: HbA1c p=0.109 (numerically worse on drug), insulin dose p=0.146, hypoglycemia p=0.976.
3) Safety was not the cause. There were no SAEs or deaths, no severe related AEs, and only 3 related TEAEs (injection-site pain or hypoaesthesia, headache).
4) The two follow-on Phase 2b trials, DAY (NCT03794960) and DAWN (NCT03794973), were WITHDRAWN with 0 enrolled. Their stated reason is "Modification to Clinical Development Plan", last updated 2020-12-08, which is when SUNRISE ended (2020-12-21). No other TOL-3021 trial appears on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Why F2 rather than another code: engagement of the intended mechanism had been shown before Phase 2. In the Phase 1/2a trial (Roep et al., Sci Transl Med 2013, PMID 23803704; NCT00453375), BHT-3021 lowered proinsulin-reactive CD8+ T cells but not T cells against other islet or viral antigens (P<0.006). The same trial reported a C-peptide gain at the 1 mg dose at Week 15 (+19.5% vs -8.8%, P<0.026). The SUNRISE protocol (v1.07) cites this antigen-specific CD8 reduction as its rationale, keeps the 1 mg weekly dose and lengthens dosing to 52 weeks. In the adequately controlled Phase 2, this antigen-specific immune modulation did not turn into preserved beta-cell function: C-peptide was the same as placebo. That fits F2: engagement shown, biology did not translate.

Why not the alternatives:
- F5 and F6 are ruled out by the clean safety data.
- F8 is ruled out because the DSMB futility finding came first; the withdrawal of DAY and DAWN followed from it and was not a separate portfolio decision.
- F7 is not supported. The trial used the best Phase 1 dose for longer, with a pre-specified O'Brien-Fleming interim analysis, and no source blames design or power.
- F3 is not supported. The population matched the Phase 1 trial (diagnosed within 5 years, autoantibody-positive) with adolescents added, and no source blames population.
- F4 is not chosen because SUNRISE reported no biomarker that moved. C-peptide, the accepted efficacy endpoint, did not move.

Caveats (marked unclear):
- Whether TOL-3021 engaged its target within SUNRISE is unclear. The protocol planned Q-dot multimer CD8+ T-cell assays (section 13.3.5), but no immunology results were posted or published.
- No source explains mechanistically why the effect did not translate. The small, multi-dose Phase 1 C-peptide signal may simply have been a false positive, which would point more toward F1/F2 ambiguity.
- No Tolerion press release or paper on SUNRISE was found. tolerion.com now redirects to an unrelated sign-in page, and the Wayback Machine has only a 2018 homepage. The WebSearch budget for this session was exhausted, so the press-release search was limited to direct fetches.
- Confidence in F2 over F1 is moderate.

claim: Curated Mendelian / ClinVar-pathogenic germline evidence links the target gene to this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease), and it was published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Weber S et al., "Muscarinic Acetylcholine Receptor M3 Mutation Causes Urinary Bladder Disease and a Prune-Belly-like Syndrome", Am J Hum Genet 2011 Nov 11;89(5):668-74 (PMID 22077972). The OMIM-submitted ClinVar record VCV000029626 (CHRM3 c.1173_1184delinsT, p.Pro392fs, Pathogenic, Prune belly syndrome, OMIM 118494.0001) cites it and was created 2013-04-04.
outcome_summary:
ASP8302 is an oral positive allosteric modulator of the muscarinic M3 receptor from Astellas. Its first Phase 2 was NCT03702777 (8302-CL-0201), a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2a proof-of-concept study in underactive bladder (UAB). It started on 2018-11-20, enrolled 135 patients, gave 100 mg once daily or placebo for 4 weeks, and completed on 2020-04-28.

The primary endpoint, change in post-void residual volume after standardized bladder filling (PVRc2) at week 4, was missed. The median change was -40 mL on drug versus -35 mL on placebo, a difference of -5 mL (p=0.960). Adverse events were similar between arms (33.3% vs 31.4%).

Target engagement was shown:
- In Phase 1, salivary secretion rose with dose from 100 mg upward, the dose then used in Phase 2.
- In male patients, maximum urine flow rate (Qmax) rose by 3.8 mL/s (p=0.031) and detrusor pressure at Qmax by 12.7 cmH2O (p=0.034). Incontinence episodes also fell in males.

The authors concluded the drug did not work in UAB patients selected by non-urodynamic clinical criteria (PVR above 100 mL). They noted that both baseline flow and voiding pressure were low, and that bladder voiding efficiency measured by ultrasound would have been a better endpoint than PVR.

Astellas's pipeline update of 30 Oct 2020 (Q2 FY2020) states: "ASP8302: Discontinued the development for underactive bladder after Phase 2 study did not meet its primary endpoint." No Phase 3 or approval followed, and the compound is no longer on Astellas's pipeline page. A 2024 ICI-RS review lists ASP8302 among agents that have shown no unequivocal clinical benefit in detrusor underactivity.

Code F3 was chosen because pharmacology was shown but the benefit appeared only in the male subgroup. The authors attribute the miss to a heterogeneous population chosen without urodynamic testing. F7 is the runner-up, since the authors also faulted PVR as a noisy primary endpoint with a large placebo response.

evidence.earliest_source: Weber S et al., "Muscarinic Acetylcholine Receptor M3 Mutation Causes Urinary Bladder Disease and a Prune-Belly-like Syndrome", Am J Hum Genet 2011 Nov 11;89(5):668-74 (PMID 22077972). The OMIM-submitted ClinVar record VCV000029626 (CHRM3 c.1173_1184delinsT, p.Pro392fs, Pathogenic, Prune belly syndrome, OMIM 118494.0001) cites it and was created 2013-04-04.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: ASP8302 is an Astellas small-molecule positive allosteric modulator of the muscarinic M3 receptor (CHRM3). In cells it shifts the carbachol concentration-response curve leftward at M3 and M5, with no significant effect at other subtypes. It does the same in human bladder strips (Okimoto et al., JPET 2021, PMID 34244231; Takusagawa et al. 2024, PMID 39120583). These papers came out after Phase 2 entry, but they confirm the target and direction recorded in our database.

(2) Entry trial: NCT03702777 (8302-CL-0201; EudraCT 2017-003693-13; lead sponsor Astellas Pharma Europe B.V.) is a Phase 2a proof-of-concept study of ASP8302 100 mg against placebo in Underactive Bladder. Inclusion required chronic incomplete emptying with PVR >= 75 mL. Actual start was 2018-11-20, matching the recorded entry date. Mapping it to MONDO:0006026 "urinary bladder disorder" is broad but correct.

(3) Claim: true. Weber 2011 (AJHG) reported a homozygous CHRM3 frameshift in a family with a congenital prune-belly-like syndrome. Cystometry in four affected boys showed "detrusor hyporeflexia with high residual volumes after micturition". Urethral patency was normal, and the boys also had impaired pupil constriction and dry mouth. This is a congenital form of an underactive detrusor with incomplete emptying, so it is a very similar phenotype to UAB. The direction also fits: M3 loss-of-function stops the bladder emptying, and the drug potentiates M3.
- PanelApp lists CHRM3 as Green (confidence 3, biallelic) on panels 156 (Unexplained kidney failure in young people), 234 (CAKUT) and 1537 (Unexplained young onset ESRD - additional genes). The phenotypes are Prune belly syndrome (OMIM 100100), Megacystis and Urinary Bladder Disease. The cited PMIDs are 10944224, 22077972 and 31441039.

CAVEAT on dating: our database dates this evidence to 2000. That year comes from PMID 10944224 (Matsui et al., PNAS 2000, Univ. Tokyo), which describes M3-knockout mice with urinary retention. It is not human germline evidence. The earliest human Mendelian or ClinVar evidence is Weber 2011. The second human family (Beaman et al., Clin Genet 2019, PMID 31441039, homozygous p.Gly118Arg with bladders that fail to empty fully) and its ClinVar record VCV974798 (2020) both came after the 2018-11-20 entry. So before entry, the evidence was a single consanguineous family with a rare congenital disease. The claim still holds, because 2011 and 2013 are both before 2018.

(4) The 2011 paper and the 2013 ClinVar/OMIM record both predate Phase 2 entry. I did not verify when the PanelApp Green ratings were assigned.

(5) Weber 2011 authors are from academic centres only (Essen, Cologne, Bonn, Izmir, Manchester, Aurora, Munster, Mainz, Heidelberg, Munich). Funding was the Wellcome Trust and NIGMS, and Astellas is not mentioned. Matsui 2000 is from the University of Tokyo. Neither is sponsor-authored.

I did not research or report the clinical outcome.

outcome.advance_event: None. No Phase 3 started and there was no FDA approval in the window from 2018-11-20 to 2022-11-20. ClinicalTrials.gov lists only two ASP8302 trials: Phase 1 NCT03361540 and Phase 2a NCT03702777. ChEMBL gives max_phase 2 for CHEMBL6068539. Astellas discontinued the program in October 2020.

failure_second.reasoning:
I coded this F2 with moderate confidence. F3 is the main alternative.

Program: ASP8302 (Astellas) is an oral small molecule that boosts the muscarinic M3 receptor (a positive allosteric modulator). It was tested for underactive bladder in NCT03702777, a double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2a proof-of-concept trial. The trial started 2018-11-20, completed 2020-04-28 with 135 patients enrolled, and gave 100 mg once daily or placebo for 4 weeks. No results are posted on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Why it stopped: Astellas's Q2 FY2020 supplementary results document (published around October 2020) says: "ASP8302: Discontinued the development for underactive bladder after Phase 2 study did not meet its primary endpoint." The FY2019 Q4 and FY2020 Q1 pipeline tables still list the program as Phase 2, in-house. The Q2 FY2020 presentation moves it to the "Discontinuation" list. No commercial or safety reason is given.

What the trial showed (van Till et al., Neurourol Urodyn 2022, PMID 35419807, abstract only; the full text is behind a paywall):
- Primary endpoint missed. The primary endpoint was the change in urine left in the bladder after voiding (post-void residual, PVR), measured by catheter after standardized filling. The median change was -40 ml on ASP8302 versus -35 ml on placebo, a difference of -5 ml (p=0.960). Voiding efficiency (BVE) was also not different between groups.
- Safety was not the problem. Adverse events were similar in both groups (33.3% vs 31.4%).
- Men responded on secondary measures. Peak urine flow rose by 3.8 ml/s (p=0.031) and bladder-muscle pressure at peak flow rose by 12.7 cmH2O (p=0.034). Incontinence episodes fell.
- The authors' conclusion: patients were selected by "nonurodynamic clinical criteria", there was no efficacy on the primary endpoint, men improved, and BVE is a better outcome measure than PVR.

Was the target engaged? Yes. The Phase 1 studies (PMID 39120583) showed a dose-dependent effect on saliva production "from 100 mg onward", which is an M3-driven effect. That is the dose used in Phase 2a. The rise in bladder-muscle pressure in men shows the drug also acted on the bladder.

Why F2: the drug reached its target at the trial dose and changed bladder physiology, at least in men. Potentiating M3 still did not improve bladder emptying in the overall underactive-bladder population. That is engagement without clinical translation. The failure was not exposure (F1) or toxicity (F5/F6), and the company gave no commercial reason (F8).

Why F3 is close: the abstract stresses that patients were chosen without urodynamic testing, that men responded, and that baseline flow and bladder pressure were low. That could point to the wrong population or disease stage. However, the men-only signal comes from secondary subgroup analyses, and I could not read the full discussion to confirm the authors blame the population.

Endpoint choice (F7) is a lesser contributor. The authors say BVE is a better measure than PVR, but BVE also showed no difference between groups.

adjudication.reasoning:
Outcome: ASP8302 did not advance within 4 years.
- The entry trial NCT03702777 (8302-CL-0201; Astellas Pharma Europe) is a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 2a proof-of-concept study in underactive bladder. Actual start was 2018-11-20, completion 2020-04-28, with 135 patients enrolled. No results are posted on ClinicalTrials.gov.
- A ClinicalTrials.gov search for ASP8302 returns only this trial and the Phase 1 NCT03361540. No Phase 3 exists.
- Astellas's Q2 FY2020 supplementary document, which I downloaded and searched, says: "ASP8302: Discontinued the development for underactive bladder after Phase 2 study did not meet its primary endpoint."

The pipeline's record is right: s4=0 and the reason is "efficacy: primary endpoint not met". Two labels are slightly off but do not change the outcome:
- The event is coded "suspended" when the program was in fact discontinued.
- years_to_event = 1.44 matches the trial completion date (2020-04-28), not the Oct 2020 announcement.

Trial result (van Till et al., Neurourol Urodyn 2022, PMID 35419807, abstract):
- The primary endpoint, change in post-void residual volume (PVRc2), was missed: -40 mL on drug vs -35 mL on placebo, a difference of -5 mL (p=0.960).
- Adverse events were similar between arms (33.3% vs 31.4%).
- Men improved on secondary measures: peak flow rate (Qmax) +3.8 mL/s (p=0.031), detrusor pressure at Qmax +12.7 cmH2O (p=0.034), and fewer incontinence episodes.
- The authors conclude the drug "did not show efficacy" in patients "identified by nonurodynamic clinical criteria". They note that baseline flow and voiding pressure were low, and that bladder voiding efficiency (BVE) measured by ultrasound is a better endpoint than PVR.

The drug did reach its target:
- In Phase 1 (PMID 39120583), saliva production rose with dose from 100 mg onward, which is the Phase 2 dose.
- In men, detrusor pressure rose in the pressure-flow subgroup.
That rules out F1. Safety was clean, which rules out F5 and F6. Astellas gave efficacy, not strategy, as the reason, which rules out F8.

Failure code: I chose F3 over F2 and F7.
- The primary source explains the miss through the population: a heterogeneous group selected without urodynamics, with low baseline voiding pressure. A positive allosteric modulator can only amplify the cholinergic drive that remains, and the benefit appeared only in men. That is a wrong population or disease subtype.
- F2 is a close second. The genetic evidence is congenital CHRM3 loss of function causing a developmental bladder disease, while the drug potentiates M3 in acquired adult detrusor underactivity, so the biology may not carry over. However, no source makes that argument.
- F7, the noisy PVR endpoint with a large placebo response, contributes but is secondary.

Claim: holds, and the evidence predates entry.
- Weber et al., AJHG 2011 (PMID 22077972) reports a homozygous CHRM3 frameshift in a family with a congenital bladder malformation and prune-belly-like syndrome. I confirmed the PMC full text says cystometry "revealed detrusor hyporeflexia with high residual volumes after micturition", with normal urethral patency. That is a very similar phenotype to underactive bladder, and its direction (M3 loss means failed emptying) fits a drug that potentiates M3.
- The ClinVar record for this variant, VCV000029626 (p.Pro392fs), is Pathogenic for prune belly syndrome (OMIM 100100), last evaluated 2011-11-11.
- Both the paper and the ClinVar record are well before the 2018-11-20 entry.
- Mapping the disease to MONDO:0006026 "urinary bladder disorder" is broad but acceptable.

Roche's own Phase 2 abstract (Finch et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2019;78 Suppl 2:189) describes the study drug, RG6125, as "a novel humanized monoclonal antibody directed against Cadherin-11". That abstract matches NCT03001219 point for point: sponsor Roche; adjunct therapy in anti-TNF-inadequate-responder RA; 4 IV doses up to Week 12 (Days 1, 14, 28 and 56 in the registry); 109 randomized, matching the registry's 109 enrolled. Senolt 2019 (PMC6719675) also describes anti-cadherin-11 RG6125 given on top of anti-TNF therapy. No single source I found states RO7123520 = RG6125 outright; the identity rests on that design match. What happened: RO7123520 is Roche's RG6125. NCT03001219 (BP39261, EudraCT 2016-002126-36) was a Phase 2 trial in RA patients who had responded inadequately to anti-TNF. The drug was given IV on top of the patients' existing anti-TNF plus methotrexate, and the trial ran from 22 Dec 2016 to 6 Nov 2018.

- **Why it stopped:** ClinicalTrials.gov says the trial "was prematurely terminated due to a lack of efficacy of the investigational drug" and that "there were no serious safety issues or adverse events contributing to the decision." Part 3, the planned dose-ranging part, was never run.
- **Results:** At week 12, ACR50 was 11.1% on 810 mg versus 16.2% on placebo. ACR20 was 27.8% versus 43.2%. DAS28 fell by 1.15 versus 1.62 and CDAI by 14.4 versus 17.4. Anti-drug antibodies were 0%.
- **Same drug, two names:** The EULAR 2019 abstract OP0224 (Finch et al., Roche) describes the identical trial: 109 patients randomized 2:1 (72 drug, 37 placebo), 810 mg IV, 4 doses to week 12, primary endpoint ACR50. That is how RG6125 is identified as RO7123520. The abstract concludes the drug "did not show a discernible treatment effect", with only mild-to-moderate adverse events.
- **Later reviews:** Senolt 2019 (PMC6719675), Németh et al. 2022 (PMC9279838) and a 2024 review (PMC11112866) all record the reason as lack of efficacy. The last says the trial was discontinued in 2018.

Why F1 rather than F2:
- Blood levels of the drug were shown: the abstract reports that RG6125 pharmacokinetics "appears linear", with "no significant relationship" between exposure group and efficacy at week 12.
- No marker showing cadherin-11 was actually blocked was reported, and the drug was never shown to reach or act in the joint. Drug concentration in synovial fluid was a planned secondary endpoint. ClinicalTrials.gov and the EU register say neither serum nor synovial-fluid concentrations were analyzed "due to an insufficient number of available participant samples." That contradicts the abstract's PK statement and is unresolved.
- F2 requires engagement to have been shown, and no source shows it. The flat exposure-response at a high dose is ambiguous: the target may have been saturated, or the drug may never have engaged it in the joint.
- F3 is possible but no source states it: the population was anti-TNF-refractory with a median disease duration of 12.4 years. F5/F6 are ruled out by the sponsor's statement on safety. F8 is not suggested by any source.

Data correction for our records: the abstract describes RG6125 as "a novel humanized monoclonal antibody directed against Cadherin-11". The record's "multispecific_antibody" modality and its TNF target are probably wrong. The TNF inhibitor was background therapy that patients were already taking, not part of the drug.

Unclear: when Roche formally removed the drug from its pipeline. I found no Roche press release or pipeline document.

Program: vimnerixin (RIST4721, formerly AZD4721), an oral CXCR2 antagonist from Aristea Therapeutics, tested in palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP). It entered Phase 2 on 2019-02-13 with NCT03988335.

Why it did not advance: the sponsor stopped development for safety reasons.
- On 10 Feb 2023, inside the 4-year window, Aristea announced it had "discontinued the RIST4721 development program in order to protect patient safety" "due to safety findings in the ongoing Phase 2 clinical trials". It also said it would dissolve the company. Source: the archived Aristea press release.
- ClinicalTrials.gov gives the same reason for every later Phase 2 trial:
  - NCT05194839, the Phase 2b dose-ranging study in PPP: terminated "Due to safety findings in ongoing Phase 2 trials".
  - NCT05348681, the Phase 2a study in hidradenitis suppurativa: terminated for the same reason.
  - NCT05448391, the familial Mediterranean fever study: withdrawn "due to safety findings in other ongoing Phase 2 trials".
- Closing the company was a result of the safety stop, not its cause, so F8 does not apply.

Why F6 rather than F5:
- The sponsor never named the safety finding, so this split is an inference.
- Target engagement was shown. In the Phase 2a paper (Bissonnette 2021, PMID 34716902), mean absolute neutrophil count (ANC) fell from 4.04 to 2.50 ×10^9/L on drug and recovered off drug. The authors call this the "on-target effect". The two neutropenia events were mild, and the 300 mg dose was picked from modelling to avoid moderate or severe neutropenia.
- The safety signal in the posted results is in the liver, which is not a known CXCR2 on-target effect:
  - NCT05194839, 200 mg arm: one participant had serious adverse events (SAEs) of "hepatic lesion" and "blood bilirubin increased". The same arm had ALT increased (2), AST increased (1) and hepatic enzyme increased (2). Placebo had none of these.
  - NCT05348681: "liver function test increased" in 2 of 17 on drug versus 0 of 8 on placebo.
  - The on-target effect, neutropenia, appeared in only 1 of 27 participants (400 mg arm) in the Phase 2b, and infections were balanced against placebo.
- Neutropenia, which would have been on-target (F5), shows no comparable signal, so the posted data point to a molecule-specific liver toxicity. F6 is therefore the best single code, with moderate confidence. If the undisclosed finding were neutropenia or infection, the code would be F5.

Context: efficacy was also weak, but it was not the stated reason.
- The Phase 2a missed both primary endpoints: fresh pustule ratio p=0.24 and total pustule ratio p=0.804. Only a post hoc subgroup with progressing disease showed a benefit.
- In the truncated Phase 2b, PPPASI-50 at week 12 was 6/12 (400 mg), 3/13 (200 mg) and 5/12 (placebo). Only completers were analysed: 37 of the 79 randomised.

Note: the record's code_names list includes AZD5069. That is a separate AstraZeneca CXCR2 antagonist (Gardiner 2019, PMID 31113795), not vimnerixin.

EVIDENCE CLAIM. The Open Targets credible set 55deadc8f08e4758c279111b8833a07d checks out mechanically: lead SNP rs11676348, PICS fine-mapping, p=2e-11, CXCR2 locus-to-gene (L2G) score 0.939. Its source is study GCST005537 (Ellinghaus 2016, PMID 26974007, published 2016-03-14). That study is a pleiotropy meta-analysis of five diseases, and the psoriasis tag comes from mapping the whole study to all five. The paper's own table shows locus 35 (rs11676348, CXCR2) with OR(PS)=0.980, against 1.055 to 1.136 for the other four diseases. The best-fitting disease model is AS_CD_UC_PSC, which leaves psoriasis out (MeanProb 0.638). The only other GWAS Catalog association for this SNP is from a ulcerative colitis GWAS (GCST000964). In MONDO, psoriasis is an ancestor of PPP, not a subtype. So there is no psoriasis or PPP genetic signal at CXCR2, and the claim is not supported in substance, even though the study predates Phase 2 entry and the L2G score is correct.

ALIAS. The case lists AZD5069 as a code name. That is a separate AstraZeneca CXCR2 antagonist, which was tested together with AZD4721 in NCT01962935. This does not change the target.

outcome_summary: Bristol-Myers Squibb ran the Phase 2 trial of deucravacitinib (BMS-986165, an oral allosteric TYK2 inhibitor) in active psoriatic arthritis (NCT03881059), which started 2019-04-01 and finished 2021-01-27. (3) Evidence rows. All three supplied rows check out against the Open Targets API:
- fc63b7c0...: Eyre 2012, GCST005568, RA (ACPA+), rs34536443, TYK2 L2G 0.991.

outcome_summary: Palazestrant (OP-1250; Olema) is an oral complete ER antagonist and SERD. Its first industry Phase 2 for breast cancer was the Phase 1/2 dose escalation/expansion study NCT04505826, which started 2020-08-13 (actual) and was completed 2024-07-30. The program reached Phase 3 within four years: OPERA-01 (NCT06016738) started 2023-11-16 (actual) and is now active, not recruiting. Its primary endpoint is BICR-assessed PFS, analysed separately in ESR1-mutant and no-mutation-detected patients, and its estimated primary completion is 2026-10-31. OPERA-02 (NCT07085767, combination with ribociclib in first line) started 2025-11-03 and is recruiting. Olema's Q2 2026 results release (SEC 8-K exhibit 99.1, filed 2026-08-10) says OPERA-01 enrollment is complete and moves top-line data from fall 2026 to Q1 2027. It also mentions preparations for a possible commercial launch. Olema's 8-K filings through 2026-10-16 contain no top-line announcement. There is no FDA approval. The program is ongoing in Phase 3 and has not failed.

evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: palazestrant (OP-1250) is an oral complete estrogen receptor antagonist (CERAN) and selective ER degrader (SERD). The Olema-authored paper Parisian et al., Mol Cancer Ther 2024 (PMID 38102750) says it 'has no agonist activity on the ER and completely blocks estrogen-induced transcriptional activity'. The ClinicalTrials.gov intervention entry for NCT04505826 also calls OP-1250 a 'Complete Estrogen Receptor ANtagonist (CERAN)'. So ESR1 (antagonist) is correct. ChEMBL (CHEMBL5314475) lists no curated mechanism. The paper confirming the mechanism dates from 2024, but the 2020 trial registration already gave the CERAN description.

(2) Disease: NCT04505826 was sponsored by Olema, first submitted 2020-07-21, and started 2020-08-13, which matches the Phase 2 entry date. It is a Phase 1/Phase 2 study in advanced or metastatic HR+/HER2- breast cancer. That is a subtype of breast cancer (MONDO:0007254), so the mapping is fine.

(3) Claim: I queried the Open Targets Platform GraphQL API. Both studyLocusIds are real.
- 5efd476b0e2040f4762437a318a6a6d9 is study GCST90435601, 'Breast cancer [female] (PheCode 174.1)'.
- aff12a12dd75cbc393edcfc2eb5901af is study GCST90435600, 'Breast cancer (PheCode 174)'.
- Both have lead variant rs910416 (6_152111767_C_T, in the ESR1 region at 6q25). Both assign ESR1 an L2G score of 0.819, the top gene; the next is SYNE1 at 0.442.
- Both studies come from PMID 30104761, Zhou et al., Nat Genet, epub 2018-08-13. The GWAS Catalog v2 API confirms them: about 12.7-12.9k UK Biobank cases, 388,549 controls, pubmed_id 30104761, mapped to MONDO_0007254.
- Other pre-entry ESR1 credible sets with L2G of at least 0.8 also exist: Shu 2020-03-05 (PMID 32139696, breast carcinoma, 0.816) and Zhang 2020-05-18 (PMID 32424353, HER2-positive / luminal B subtypes, 0.837 and 0.807).

outcome_summary: Stapokibart (CM310) is Keymed Biosciences' anti-IL-4Rα antibody. The entry trial NCT04893941 was a Phase Ib/IIa multiple-dose-escalation study in moderate-to-severe AD. It started on 2020-07-21 and was completed on 2021-01-22, with safety as its primary endpoint; no results are posted on ClinicalTrials.gov. The Phase 2b trial NCT04805411 ran from February to November 2021 and met its primary endpoint, EASI-75 at week 16: 70% on 300 mg and 65% on 150 mg versus 20% on placebo, p<0.0001 (Chin Med J 2024, PMID 37482623). The pivotal Phase 3 trial NCT05265923 started on 2022-04-22, within the four-year window. It met both co-primary endpoints at week 16: EASI-75 was 66.9% versus 25.8%, and IGA 0/1 with a reduction of at least 2 points was 44.2% versus 16.1% (Allergy 2025, PMID 39450683). The effect held through 52 weeks. China's NMPA approved stapokibart (Kangyueda) in September 2024 for adults with moderate-to-severe AD that is poorly controlled by, or not suitable for, topical therapy; this was the drug's first approval (Drugs 2025, PMID 40095376). It was later approved in China for CRSwNP and seasonal allergic rhinitis. Trials in adolescent and pediatric AD continue, including the Phase 3 trials NCT06277765 and NCT06495229. I found no FDA approval or US filing. The program advanced, so it is not a failure.

(1) Target and action: stapokibart (CM310) is a humanized anti-IL-4Rα monoclonal antibody that blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signalling (Zhao et al., Chin Med J 2024, PMID 37482623; Zhang et al., Adv Ther 2024, PMID 38833140, Keymed authors). That matches IL4R as a binder/neutralizer. The ClinicalTrials.gov intervention entry also says "IL-4Rα monoclonal antibody".
(2) Entry trial: NCT04893941 (CM310AD001, sponsored by Keymed Biosciences) is a Phase Ib/IIa multiple-dose-escalation study in moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. Its actual start date was 2020-07-21, which matches the recorded Phase 2 entry. Adv Ther 2024 reports it as the MAD study in 39 AD patients.
(3) The claim holds. Open Targets credible set 93a5f5dd33992eaf9a6c54fe1f9205f1 comes from study GCST007075 (Kichaev 2018, UK Biobank, about 459k Europeans, trait "Eczema", mapped to MONDO_0004980 atopic eczema). The lead variant is rs3024665 (16_27360218_C_T), p=8e-9, fine-mapped with PICS. L2G gives IL4R 0.923 and IL21R 0.223. The GWAS Catalog maps this association to IL4R. In the GWAS Catalog, it is the earliest eczema-specific association mapped to the IL4R gene. Later ones include Johansson 2019 "Hay fever and/or eczema" (PMID 31361310), whose credible set has an IL4R L2G of only 0.242. Open Targets returns just these two IL4R/atopic-eczema credible-set evidence rows.
Caveats: the "Eczema" trait is a broad UK Biobank phenotype (GWAS Catalog EFO: eczematoid dermatitis), not clinician-diagnosed atopic dermatitis. That counts as a "very similar disease" under the claim. Also, the 0.92 L2G score is a retrospective calculation from the current Open Targets release. The L2G method did not exist in 2018. The GWAS association itself was public in Dec 2018, about 19 months before Phase 2 entry.
(4) It predates entry: epub 2018-12-27, print Jan 2019, versus entry on 2020-07-21.
(5) It was not written by the sponsor. The authors are from UCLA, the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Broad Institute (Price/Pasaniuc labs), with no Keymed affiliation. Per the task instructions, I did not research the clinical outcome.

error_source: other: phase label. The pipeline counted RIVER-AD (NCT05492578), an open-label long-term safety extension registered as PHASE2/PHASE3 and started 2022-08-22, as a Phase 3 start. Program dating, disease mapping and the target label are all correct.
evidence_source: Ferreira MA et al., 'Shared genetic origin of asthma, hay fever and eczema elucidates allergic disease biology', Nat Genet 2017;49:1752-1757 (PMID 29083406, online 2017-10-30; GWAS Catalog GCST005038)
outcome_summary:
Amlitelimab (KY1005/SAR445229) is a non-depleting anti-OX40L monoclonal antibody. Its first Phase 2 trial in atopic dermatitis was NCT03754309, sponsored by Kymab and started 2018-12-13 (89 patients, IV dosing). On the co-primary endpoint, the low dose met it: EASI change -80% vs -49% on placebo, p=0.009. The high dose did not (p=0.07). Safety was unremarkable (Br J Dermatol 2023). Sanofi, by then Kymab's owner, ran the Phase 2b STREAM-AD trial (NCT05131477, started 2021-12-13, 390 patients). It met its primary endpoint of EASI % change at week 16 (p<.001), and responses lasted after treatment stopped (JACI 2025).

Phase 3 started only in November 2023 with COAST 1, about 4.9 years after Phase 2 entry, so the program did not advance within 4 years. The one exception is an open-label Phase 2/3 safety extension, RIVER-AD, which started in August 2022.

Phase 3 results:
- COAST 1 was positive (September 2025).
- SHORE met all primary and key secondary endpoints.
- COAST 2 was mixed: it met the US primary endpoint but missed the EU/Japan co-primaries.
- Two cutaneous Kaposi's sarcoma cases were reported, in January and March 2026, both in patients with known risk factors. The OX40 antibody rocatinlimab was halted over the same signal in March 2026.

In January 2026 Sanofi still planned global filings for H2 2026. On 2026-07-24, after the positive ESTUARY maintenance readout, Sanofi said it would not submit and discontinued development in atopic dermatitis. Its stated reasons were that "the totality of efficacy and safety evidence generated to date does not support further development" and that amlitelimab "would not represent a meaningful improvement to the standard of care."

Classification:
- Stop reason: efficacy. The drug beat placebo, but by too little to stand out against existing treatments.
- Failure code: F8 (competition). The biology did carry through to patients, since the drug beat placebo; the program failed to beat the bar set by existing AD drugs. The Kaposi's sarcoma signal may have contributed through the "safety evidence" wording, but Sanofi did not name it.
- Key trial: ESTUARY, the readout that came just before the decision. Sanofi called it positive but did not publish numbers for its primary endpoint.

evidence.earliest_source: Ferreira MA et al., 'Shared genetic origin of asthma, hay fever and eczema elucidates allergic disease biology', Nat Genet 2017;49:1752-1757 (PMID 29083406, online 2017-10-30; GWAS Catalog GCST005038)
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: KY1005/amlitelimab is an OX40L (TNFSF4)-blocking antibody. A Kymab-co-authored primate GVHD paper from before entry (Tkachev 2017 Sci Transl Med, PMID 28931653) describes it as 'the OX40L-blocking antibody KY1005'. The Phase 1 paper (Saghari 2022, PMID 35092305) says 'anti-OX40L monoclonal antibody (KY1005, currently amlitelimab)', and the Phase 2a paper (PMID 37463508) calls it a nondepleting anti-OX40L mAb, also named SAR445229. The CT.gov intervention reads 'A human anti-OX40 ligand monoclonal antibody'. So binder/neutralizer of TNFSF4 is correct.

(2) Disease: NCT03754309 (Kymab, KY1005-CT02) is a Phase 2a trial in moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, with condition 'Dermatitis, Atopic'. It started 2018-12-13 (actual), which matches the entry date.

(3) Claim: only partly supported. The Open Targets credible set a960ba9b55088dfe18ae2347f1ac0282 (SuSiE-inf, lead rs11811788, p=5.4e-11) belongs to GCST005038 (Ferreira 2017). It gives TNFSF4 an L2G score of 0.833; next is TNFSF18 at 0.26. But that study's trait is a composite 'Allergic disease (asthma, hay fever or eczema)', mapped to MONDO_0005271 'allergic disease'. That is a broader parent category, not a subtype of atopic eczema. Two points in its favour come from the paper itself. Supplementary Table 3 names TNFSF4 as the likely target gene for locus 10 (sentinel rs4090390, P=1.3e-15, via expression-associated variants). Supplementary Table 9 shows no eczema-specific heterogeneity: asthma vs eczema P=0.57, hay fever vs eczema P=0.31.

Before entry the TNFSF4 locus had also been reported for asthma (Pickrell 2016, PMID 27182965, rs6691738, P=3e-8), but not for eczema alone. Using Open Targets indirect evidence for atopic eczema (MONDO_0004980), the earliest eczema-specific credible set with TNFSF4 L2G >=0.8 is Kichaev et al., GCST007075 (eczema, L2G 0.828). outcome.advance_event: None within the 4-year window, which closed 2022-12-13. The first dedicated Phase 3 efficacy trial, COAST 1 (NCT06130566, Sanofi), started 2023-11-08, about 4.9 years after Phase 2 entry. Other pivotal trials started later: COAST 2 (NCT06181435) on 2023-12-21, SHORE (NCT06224348) on 2024-01-18, AQUA (NCT06241118) on 2024-02-29 and ESTUARY (NCT06407934) on 2024-05-08. Caveat: an open-label long-term safety extension, RIVER-AD (NCT05492578), is registered as Phase 2/Phase 3 and started 2022-08-22, inside the window. Its primary endpoint is TEAE incidence, and it enrolls patients from earlier amlitelimab trials. I did not count it as a Phase 3 start. A rule that counts any PHASE2/PHASE3 label as Phase 3 would answer yes. No FDA approval.
outcome.summary:
Amlitelimab (KY1005/SAR445229) is a non-depleting anti-OX40L monoclonal antibody. Its first Phase 2 trial in atopic dermatitis was NCT03754309, sponsored by Kymab and started 2018-12-13 (89 patients, IV dosing). On the co-primary endpoint, the low dose met it: EASI change -80% vs -49% on placebo, p=0.009. The high dose did not (p=0.07). Safety was unremarkable (Br J Dermatol 2023). Sanofi, by then Kymab's owner, ran the Phase 2b STREAM-AD trial (NCT05131477, started 2021-12-13, 390 patients). It met its primary endpoint of EASI % change at week 16 (p<.001), and responses lasted after treatment stopped (JACI 2025).

Phase 3 started only in November 2023 with COAST 1, about 4.9 years after Phase 2 entry, so the program did not advance within 4 years. The one exception is an open-label Phase 2/3 safety extension, RIVER-AD, which started in August 2022.

Phase 3 results:
- COAST 1 was positive (September 2025).
- SHORE met all primary and key secondary endpoints.
- COAST 2 was mixed: it met the US primary endpoint but missed the EU/Japan co-primaries.
- Two cutaneous Kaposi's sarcoma cases were reported, in January and March 2026, both in patients with known risk factors. The OX40 antibody rocatinlimab was halted over the same signal in March 2026.

In January 2026 Sanofi still planned global filings for H2 2026. On 2026-07-24, after the positive ESTUARY maintenance readout, Sanofi said it would not submit and discontinued development in atopic dermatitis. Its stated reasons were that "the totality of efficacy and safety evidence generated to date does not support further development" and that amlitelimab "would not represent a meaningful improvement to the standard of care."

Classification:
- Stop reason: efficacy. The drug beat placebo, but by too little to stand out against existing treatments.
- Failure code: F8 (competition). The biology did carry through to patients, since the drug beat placebo; the program failed to beat the bar set by existing AD drugs. The Kaposi's sarcoma signal may have contributed through the "safety evidence" wording, but Sanofi did not name it.
- Key trial: ESTUARY, the readout that came just before the decision. Sanofi called it positive but did not publish numbers for its primary endpoint.

failure_second.reasoning:
Our record is wrong on the substance. Amlitelimab (KY1005/SAR445229) did reach Phase 3 in atopic dermatitis, about 11 months after the four-year window closed. It did not fail between Phase 2 and Phase 3.

Timeline, from primary sources:
(1) Phase 2a NCT03754309 (Kymab) started 2018-12-13 and finished 2020-10-08 (ClinicalTrials.gov). The published results met the primary endpoint at the 200 mg low dose: EASI -80.1% vs -49.4% for placebo, p=0.009. The high dose gave -70.0%, p=0.07. Safety was unremarkable (Weidinger, Br J Dermatol 2023, PMID 37463508).
(2) Sanofi agreed to buy Kymab on 2021-01-11 for about $1.1B upfront plus up to $350M in milestones, to get KY1005, citing the positive Phase 2a (Sanofi 6-K Ex-99.1).
(3) Under Sanofi, the Phase 2b dose-ranging study STREAM-AD (NCT05131477) ran from 2021-12-13 to primary completion on 2023-04-26. It was positive: EASI fell significantly for every dose vs placebo, p<0.001 (JACI 2025, PMID 39522654).
(4) The first Phase 3, COAST 1 (NCT06130566), started 2023-11-08. About 4.9 years after Phase 2 entry, that is past the four-year cutoff (2022-12-13). COAST 2, SHORE, AQUA and ESTUARY (NCT06181435, NCT06224348, NCT06241118, NCT06407934) followed between Dec 2023 and May 2024. Separately, the long-term extension RIVER-AD (NCT05492578) is listed as Phase 2/3 and started 2022-08-22, inside the window.

So the program did not miss the cutoff for lack of efficacy. The gap came from the change of sponsor in 2021 and the extra Phase 2b dose-ranging study. That makes it not_a_failure under the codebook rule that a program which advanced is not a failure.

Later history, for context only, since it is outside the Phase 2 to Phase 3 question: COAST 1 was positive (Sept 2025). SHORE was positive, and COAST 2 was mixed: positive on the US endpoints, but the EU co-primary endpoints were not significant (Sanofi press release, 2026-01-23). In the same release Sanofi planned global submissions for H2 2026 and reported a cutaneous Kaposi's sarcoma case in a patient with known risk factors. A 2026 Front Immunol perspective counts two Kaposi cases among about 3,778 exposed patients. On 2026-07-24 Sanofi stopped development in atopic dermatitis and decided not to file. It said the "totality of efficacy and safety evidence ... does not support further development" and that amlitelimab "would not represent a meaningful improvement to the standard of care" (Sanofi 6-K Ex-99.2 and Q2 2026 results release). If a later stage needs coding, that post-Phase 3 discontinuation reads as F8 (competitive/strategic: not differentiated enough against standard of care), with efficacy and safety contributing. The Phase 2 transition itself was not a failure.

adjudication.reasoning:
OUTCOME. Phase 2 entry is confirmed. NCT03754309 is a Kymab Phase 2a in atopic dermatitis that started 2018-12-13 (actual), with an anti-OX40L intervention, so the 4-year window closed on 2022-12-13. The pipeline's years_to_event of 3.69 works out to 2022-08-22. That is the start date of NCT05492578 (RIVER-AD, LTS17367), the only amlitelimab trial with a Phase 3 label that started inside the window.

RIVER-AD should not count as a Phase 3 start:
- It is an open-label, non-randomised extension, and its primary endpoint is the rate of treatment-emergent adverse events.
- It enrolls people who finished earlier amlitelimab trials. When it started in August 2022, the only feeder trial running was the Phase 2b DRI17366 (STREAM-AD, NCT05131477, started 2021-12-13). The Phase 3 feeders EFC17599 and EFC17600 (COAST 1 and 2) did not begin until late 2023.
- Sanofi's Q3 2022 results release (2022-10-28) mentions amlitelimab only under Phase 2, for the asthma dose-ranging study.
- Sanofi's Q4 2023 release says COAST 1 (NCT06130566) and COAST 2 (NCT06181435) "had their first participants treated" and "were initiated following positive results from the STREAM-AD Phase 2b study", which were presented at EADV 2023.

The first real Phase 3, COAST 1, started 2023-11-08, about 4.9 years after entry. There is no FDA approval. So the program did not advance within 4 years, and the pipeline's s4=1 is wrong because it treated the PHASE2/PHASE3 label on a safety extension as a Phase 3 start.

FAILURE CODE. At the 4-year mark the program was still active and positive:
- The Phase 2a met its primary endpoint at the low dose: EASI -80% vs -49% on placebo, p=0.009 (Br J Dermatol 2023, PMID 37463508).
- Sanofi agreed to buy Kymab on 2021-01-11, citing that Phase 2a result.
- Sanofi then ran the Phase 2b STREAM-AD, which was also positive (JACI 2025, PMID 39522654).
- Phase 3 followed in Nov 2023.

The delay came from the change of sponsor and an extra dose-ranging Phase 2b, not from a failed transition. Under the codebook ("advanced or is still progressing"), that makes it not_a_failure. Sanofi stopped development in AD on 2026-07-24, saying it was not a meaningful improvement over standard of care, which reads as F8. That decision came after Phase 3 and is outside the Phase 2 to Phase 3 question, so the outcome agent's F8 applies to the wrong stage.

EVIDENCE CLAIM (M4). I checked Open Targets directly:
- Credible set a960ba9b55088dfe18ae2347f1ac0282 (SuSiE-inf, lead rs11811788, p=5.4e-11) comes from GCST005038, Ferreira MA, Nat Genet, published online 2017-10-30 (PMID 29083406), which is before entry. It gives TNFSF4 an L2G of 0.833; the next gene, TNFSF18, scores 0.26.

evidence_source: Franke A et al., 'Genome-wide meta-analysis increases to 71 the number of confirmed Crohn's disease susceptibility loci', Nat Genet 2010;42(12):1118-25 (published online 2010-11-21), PMID 21102463, GWAS Catalog GCST000879: rs12720356 at TYK2 (19p13), combined P = 1.4e-12. outcome_summary:
Pfizer started PIZZICATO (NCT03395184, B7981007), a Phase 2a trial of ritlecitinib and brepocitinib against placebo in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease, on 2018-02-02. Brepocitinib 60 mg once daily met the primary endpoint, SES-CD50 at week 12: 33.8% versus 12.8% on placebo, a difference of 21.4% (90% CI 10.0 to 32.9), p=0.0012, according to the ClinicalTrials.gov posted results and Vermeire et al., EClinicalMedicine 2026. Safety was described as acceptable.

Even so, the paper says that after protocol amendment 5 (27 July 2021) 'a strategic business decision was taken by the study sponsor to discontinue the brepocitinib arm.' No new patients were randomised to brepocitinib, and the drug was not given in the open-label extension. In September 2021 Pfizer granted Roivant's subsidiary Priovant an exclusive worldwide license to brepocitinib for all human uses (Roivant 10-K, FY ending 2026-03-31).

Priovant has developed it in dermatomyositis (NDA accepted with Priority Review, PDUFA target in the third quarter of 2026), non-infectious uveitis (Phase 3), cutaneous sarcoidosis and lichen planopilaris. Its pipeline has no Crohn's program. Roivant lists the Crohn's study only as a positive Pfizer-run Phase 2. No Phase 3 in Crohn's ever started.

The program stopped after a positive Phase 2 because of a portfolio decision and the out-licensing that followed, not because of efficacy or safety, so the code is F8. One limit on the evidence: the sources do not say why Priovant chose not to take up Crohn's.
