failure_second.reasoning:
Code: F8 (commercial or strategic). Brepocitinib (PF-06700841, a TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor) was tested in Crohn disease in the Pfizer Phase 2a umbrella trial PIZZICATO (NCT03395184). The trial started 2018-02-02 and finished 2023-10-19. ClinicalTrials.gov lists no later brepocitinib trial in Crohn disease, at any phase.

1. The trial met its primary endpoint. On ClinicalTrials.gov, SES-CD50 at week 12 was 33.8% with brepocitinib 60 mg once daily versus 12.8% with placebo (difference 21.4%, 90% CI 10.0-32.9, p=0.0012). The endoscopic secondary endpoints also favoured brepocitinib:
   - clinically meaningful endoscopic improvement 57.7% vs 29.5% (p=0.0001)
   - mean SES-CD change -5.0 vs -0.1 (p<0.0001)
   - mucosal healing 16.9% vs 5.1% (p=0.011)
   - endoscopic remission 12.7% vs 5.1% (p=0.045)
   The paper (Vermeire et al., EClinicalMedicine 2026, PMID 41852927) concludes the drug "showed significant improvement in the primary outcome versus placebo ... with acceptable safety profiles". So this is not F1-F4. Induction safety looked like placebo, so it is not F5 or F6 either: serious adverse events 5.6% vs 7.6%, and stopping treatment because of adverse events 5.6% vs 7.6%.

2. The paper's methods section states the reason directly: "Following the protocol amendment 5 (27 July 2021), a strategic business decision was taken by the study sponsor to discontinue the brepocitinib arm. Consequently, no new patients were randomised to receive brepocitinib ... nor was brepocitinib administered in the OLE phase ... Specifically, this decision was not based on safety, efficacy, or quality concerns." This cut enrolment (brepocitinib n=72 vs ritlecitinib n=93) and lowered the power of the brepocitinib comparison. That was a result of the business decision, not the reason the program stopped, so F7 does not apply.

3. Business context from SEC filings: Roivant's 10-K (filed 2023-06-28) says that in September 2021 its subsidiary Priovant Therapeutics took a worldwide license from Pfizer to develop brepocitinib. Pfizer kept commercial rights outside the US and Japan. Priovant's stated focus was dermatomyositis, SLE and other immune diseases; the filing names no IBD program. On ClinicalTrials.gov, Priovant's later brepocitinib trials cover dermatomyositis (Phase 3), non-infectious uveitis (Phase 2 and Phase 3), cutaneous sarcoidosis and lichen planopilaris; none cover Crohn disease. The arm was stopped about two months before this license. That timing fits a portfolio or licensing decision, but no source explicitly links the two, so I treat the licensing as context only. The primary source's own statement is enough to support F8.

Not verified (unclear): any company statement naming the exact portfolio reason for not taking Crohn disease forward, such as competition from upadacitinib or the move into rare autoimmune diseases.

evidence_source: Strange A et al. (Genetic Analysis of Psoriasis Consortium & WTCCC2), "A genome-wide association study identifies new psoriasis susceptibility loci and an interaction between HLA-C and ERAP1", Nat Genet 2010;42(11):985-90, epub 2010-10-17, PMID 20953190 (GWAS Catalog GCST000833; TYK2 lead SNP rs12720356, p=4e-11)
outcome_summary:
Brepocitinib (PF-06700841) is an oral TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor. Pfizer started the industry Phase 2a trial NCT02969018 (n=212) in moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in Dec 2016. The trial met its primary endpoint: on week-12 change from baseline in PASI, 30 mg once daily beat placebo by -10.07 (p<0.0001), with 86% PASI75 versus 13% for placebo. Five of seven arms were significant. There was no herpes zoster and no MACE (CT.gov results; Forman et al., J Invest Dermatol 2020). A Pfizer exposure-response paper modelled 10/30/60 mg doses for a "subsequent Phase 2b", but no oral Phase 2b or Phase 3 in psoriasis was ever registered.

Pfizer's own pipeline shows oral psoriasis at Phase 2 in Jul 2018, Apr 2019 and Jul 2019. It is absent from Jul 2020 onward. In its place Pfizer advanced its TYK2-selective inhibitor PF-06826647 for psoriasis and a topical brepocitinib cream. The Jan 2020 Pfizer 8-K names PF-06826647 as the TYK2 inhibitor for psoriasis and describes brepocitinib as topical for psoriasis/AD and oral for psoriatic arthritis. The topical Phase 2b NCT03850483 (n=344) missed its primary PASI endpoint at every dose (Landis et al., Br J Dermatol 2023). In Sep 2021 Pfizer out-licensed brepocitinib to Roivant's Priovant. Priovant focuses on "orphan and specialty autoimmune diseases" (dermatomyositis Phase 3, non-infectious uveitis Phase 3, cutaneous sarcoidosis and lichen planopilaris Phase 2/3), not psoriasis, even though Roivant's filings call the psoriasis data "statistically significant and clinically meaningful".

The program stopped despite positive efficacy and a clean safety readout. No source gives an explicit reason for dropping oral psoriasis. The pattern (Pfizer reprioritising toward a TYK2-selective oral and a topical, then out-licensing to a licensee with an orphan-disease strategy) points to a portfolio/strategic decision, so the code is F8, though that reason is inferred rather than stated. The topical formulation failed separately on efficacy.

The program stopped despite positive efficacy and a clean safety readout. No source gives an explicit reason for dropping oral psoriasis. The pattern (Pfizer reprioritising toward a TYK2-selective oral and a topical, then out-licensing to a licensee with an orphan-disease strategy) points to a portfolio/strategic decision, so the code is F8, though that reason is inferred rather than stated. The topical formulation failed separately on efficacy.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: oral brepocitinib (PF-06700841; TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor) from Pfizer for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. It entered Phase 2 with NCT02969018 in December 2016.

1. The Phase 2 trial worked, so this is not an efficacy failure. NCT02969018 was a Phase 2a trial (n=212) that completed in March 2018. The posted results show significant PASI reductions at week 12 against placebo. The largest was 30 mg once daily: LS mean -17.28 vs -7.21, difference -10.07, p<0.0001. Five of seven arms were significant. The paper (Forman 2020, J Invest Dermatol, PMID 32311398) reports no herpes zoster, no MACE and no thromboembolic events, and calls the drug "generally effective and well tolerated." An earlier biopsy study (PMID 31972249) showed target engagement in skin: IL-17A, IL-17F and IL-12B mRNA fell, and about 70% of lesional gene expression normalised. That rules out F1, F2 and F4.

2. Pfizer dropped the indication on its own while keeping the molecule. Pfizer's Q3 2018 earnings release (SEC 8-K, Oct 2018) said PF-06700841 "will continue to be evaluated for psoriasis, CD and UC." Pfizer pipeline documents for May 2018, Jul 2018, Apr 2019 and Jul 2019 all list "PF-06700841 TYK2/JAK1 Psoriasis Phase 2." The 29 Oct 2019 pipeline update lists "PF-06700841 TYK2/JAK1 Psoriasis Phase 2" under "Programs Discontinued from Development since July 29, 2019." It gives no reason. Oral psoriasis is missing from the Jul 2020, Oct 2020 and Feb 2021 pipelines.

3. The context points to portfolio prioritisation:
   - **Pfizer's own selective TYK2 inhibitor took the indication.** PF-06826647 (ropsacitinib) started a Phase 2 trial in moderate-to-severe psoriasis in June 2019 (NCT03895372). It appears as "TYK2 Inhibitor, Psoriasis, Phase 2" in the same Jul 2019 pipeline.
   - **Brepocitinib's psoriasis work moved to a topical cream** for mild-to-moderate disease (NCT03850483). That cream later failed against vehicle (Landis 2023, Br J Dermatol, PMID 36972293), but it was a separate formulation and population.
   - **Oral brepocitinib carried on in other indications.** These were psoriatic arthritis (NCT03963401), lupus, hidradenitis suppurativa and alopecia areata.
   - **A 2023 review describes the same split.** It says that for psoriasis the drug had "oral, phase 2 completed; further development pursued only as a topical formulation" (Martin 2023, Dermatol Ther, PMC9884727).
   - **The molecule was later out-licensed.** In September 2021 Pfizer licensed brepocitinib and ropsacitinib exclusively to Roivant's new company Priovant, keeping a 25% stake (Pfizer Q2 2022 8-K). Priovant chose orphan and specialty diseases: dermatomyositis, lupus and uveitis. Its filings still cite the positive psoriasis Phase 2 (Roivant FY2022 10-K and June 2022 8-K).

Why not the other codes:
- No source reports a safety signal that stopped the psoriasis program, and Pfizer kept developing the oral drug elsewhere. That argues against F5 and F6.
- No trial design or population problem was cited, so F3 and F7 do not fit.

Caveat: no primary source states Pfizer's reason in words. The discontinuation date is documented. F8 (portfolio prioritisation in favour of PF-06826647 and other brepocitinib indications) is an inference from the evidence above, not a stated reason. If a stated reason is required, the fallback code would be "unknown."

evidence_source: Bentham J et al., "Genetic association analyses implicate aberrant regulation of innate and adaptive immunity genes in the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythematosus", Nat Genet 2015 (PMID 26502338, doi:10.1038/ng.3434, published online 2015-10-26). outcome_summary:
The Phase 2 entry is confirmed. Pfizer started NCT03845517 (B7931028) on 2019-04-18. It was a Phase 2b, randomized, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial in active SLE (n=350), with 15, 30 or 45 mg once daily for 52 weeks. Primary completion was 2023-10-05.

The primary endpoint, SRI-4 at Week 52, was not met. Results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov:
- SRI-4 response was 64.6% on placebo, versus 57.4% at 15 mg, 69.7% at 30 mg and 66.3% at 45 mg.
- Risk differences versus placebo were -7.5, +5.2 and +1.7 percentage points.
- One-sided CMH p-values were 0.81, 0.22 and 0.40.

On 2023-11-27, Roivant and Priovant (an 8-K exhibit filed with the SEC) said the trial failed its primary endpoint. They blamed "the highest placebo response rate observed in any significant SLE study", which made it "not possible to truly assess the impact of the drug, or to establish sufficient differentiation from other therapies". They also said "we do not plan to progress the program in SLE."

No SLE Phase 3 was started within 4 years of Phase 2 entry, and none has started since. Development of brepocitinib continued in other diseases: a Phase 3 in dermatomyositis, a Phase 3 in uveitis, and Phase 2/3 trials in sarcoidosis and lichen planopilaris. Roivant's FY2025 10-K (May 2026) lists no SLE program for brepocitinib.

The stop reason is efficacy, since the primary endpoint failed. The failure code is F7 (trial design or power) because the sponsor's own explanation is an unusually high placebo response that kept the trial from showing a separation from placebo. This call is a judgement. The data can also be read as no meaningful drug effect, with active arms only about 2 to 5 points above placebo at the higher doses. A secondary strategic factor was weak differentiation from other lupus therapies.

(1) Target and action: Pfizer's discovery paper (Fensome et al., J Med Chem 2018, PMID 30113844) describes PF-06700841 (brepocitinib) as a dual TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor. (3) Claim: I queried each of the 7 studyLocusIds through the Open Targets Platform GraphQL API. Each returns TYK2 as the top L2G gene with a score of 0.91 to 0.99, matching our rows. The loci are rs12720356, rs2304256 and rs34536443 in GCST003155/GCST003156 (Bentham 2015, Nat Genet, published 2015-10-26); rs2304256 in GCST003622 (Morris 2016, Nat Genet); rs34725611 and rs34536443 in GCST007400/GCST005752 (Langefeld 2017, Nat Commun); and rs11085725 in GCST007278 (Acosta-Herrera 2018, Ann Rheum Dis). It has no Open Targets credible set, so it is not the earliest source for this specific claim.
(4) Bentham 2015 (October 2015) and every supporting study (2015 to 2018) came out before 2019-04-18.
(5) Sponsor authorship: Bentham 2015 is an academic consortium paper led from King's College London (Vyse lab). No author is a Pfizer employee. Two authors are from Genentech. One author, Alarcón-Riquelme, is affiliated with GENYO, a joint public research centre of Pfizer, the University of Granada and the Junta de Andalucía. I do not count that as authorship by the sponsor. Funding listed is Wellcome Trust, NIH, Arthritis Research UK/Versus Arthritis, HHMI and CIHR.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: brepocitinib (PF-06700841, a TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor) in systemic lupus erythematosus. It entered Phase 2 with NCT03845517, a Pfizer-sponsored Phase 2b study: dose-ranging, placebo-controlled, 52 weeks, n=350, start 2019-04-18, completed 2023-10-05.

What happened (from the ClinicalTrials.gov posted results):
- The primary endpoint, SRI-4 at week 52, was missed. Response rates were 64.6% on placebo, 57.4% on 15 mg, 69.7% on 30 mg and 66.3% on 45 mg. One-sided p-values were 0.81, 0.22 and 0.40.
- Secondary endpoints moved in the drug's favour at 30 and 45 mg but none reached significance:
  - BICLA: 43.8% placebo vs 52.5% and 53.3% (p=0.11 and 0.09)
  - LLDAS: 22.6% vs 35.1% and 34.1%
  - steroid taper: 26.4% vs 37.0% and 41.9%
- Safety did not drive the decision. Serious adverse events were 8, 4, 8 and 9 across the arms, and discontinuations for adverse events were 6, 2, 1 and 3.

Why it did not advance (from the Roivant/Priovant press release of 27 Nov 2023, SEC 8-K Ex. 99.1):
- The trial "did not meet its primary endpoint." The sponsor blamed "the highest placebo response rate observed in any significant SLE study, and as such it was not possible to truly assess the impact of the drug, or to establish sufficient differentiation from other therapies in lupus patients."
- The sponsor said "we do not plan to progress the program in SLE" and turned to non-infectious uveitis and dermatomyositis.
- Lupus is gone from Roivant's FY2024 10-K (filed 2024-05-30); a full-text search found no mention.

Coding: The trial did not separate drug from placebo because the placebo response was very high (SRI-4 64.6%). It was not powered for that, so it could not tell whether the drug worked. That fits F7 (trial design, comparator or power) best. Two limits:
- Exposure and target engagement were not measured in SLE. The trial reported no biomarker or pharmacodynamic outcomes, so true lack of efficacy (F2) cannot be ruled out.
- The placebo-response explanation is the sponsor's own reading.
The stated reason for dropping lupus ("not possible ... to establish sufficient differentiation from other therapies") also has a strategic side (F8). F7 is primary because the trigger was a failed primary endpoint driven by placebo response.

Note: no peer-reviewed full publication of the SLE Phase 2b results was found in PubMed or Europe PMC.

outcome_summary: Sibeprenlimab (VIS649) is a humanized IgG2 antibody that binds and neutralizes APRIL (TNFSF13), developed by Visterra/Otsuka. The first industry-sponsored Phase 2 in IgA nephropathy was ENVISION (NCT04287985, sponsor Otsuka), which started 2020-07-20 (actual) and completed 2023-06-18. It met its primary endpoint, the change in log 24-hour uPCR at month 12: proteinuria fell 47.2%, 58.8% and 62.0% at 2, 4 and 8 mg/kg, against 20.0% on placebo. The eGFR decline was also smaller on drug (NEJM 2024;390:20-31, PMID 37916620). The Phase 3 VISIONARY trial (NCT05248646) started 2022-03-15 (actual), well inside the 4-year window. Its primary endpoint is the change in uPCR-24h at month 9. In a prespecified interim analysis of 320 patients, drug versus placebo reduced proteinuria by 51% (96.5% CI 43-58%, p<0.0001): -50% on drug, +2% on placebo. On that basis the FDA granted accelerated approval on 2025-11-25 (BLA 761434, Voyxact, 400 mg SC every 4 weeks) to reduce proteinuria in adults with primary IgAN at risk of progression. Keeping the approval depends on a confirmatory trial showing benefit on kidney function. VISIONARY is active, not recruiting: primary completion 2026-05-13, estimated full completion 2027-01. Otsuka has also listed a pediatric Phase 3 (NCT07770815, not yet recruiting) and a Phase 2 kidney-tissue study (NCT06740526). The program advanced and was approved, so it is not a failure. Web search was unavailable in this session, so I took every fact from ClinicalTrials.gov, openFDA/Drugs@FDA (the approval letter and the label) and PubMed. I did not separately confirm whether the full eGFR-based confirmatory readout of VISIONARY has been reported.

evidence.earliest_source: Yu XQ et al., "A genome-wide association study in Han Chinese identifies multiple susceptibility loci for IgA nephropathy", Nat Genet 2011 Dec 25 (epub; print 2012;44(2):178-82), doi:10.1038/ng.1047, PMID 22197929 (GWAS Catalog GCST001364)
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: Myette et al., Kidney Int 2019 (PMID 31027890), written by Visterra authors, describes VIS649 as a humanized IgG2k antibody "targeting and neutralizing human APRIL". Mathur et al., Kidney Int Rep 2022 (PMID 35570983) calls VIS649 (sibeprenlimab) an "APRIL-Neutralizing IgG2 Monoclonal Antibody". UniProt O75888 confirms that APRIL is the product of the TNFSF13 gene. So "TNFSF13 (binder_neutralizer)" is correct.
(2) Disease: NCT04287985 (VIS649-201) is a Phase 2 randomized, placebo-controlled study of VIS649 in IgA nephropathy. Its actual start date is 2020-07-20, which matches the recorded Phase 2 entry. The lead sponsor is Otsuka Pharmaceutical Development & Commercialization; Otsuka owns Visterra, the developer. IgA nephropathy maps to MONDO:0005342 (IgA glomerulonephritis).
(3) Claim: Open Targets returns this for credible set 37dec5e472e9788e0079745efe8757f0:
- lead variant rs3803800 (17_7559652_A_G)
- study GCST001364, "IgA nephropathy", mapped to MONDO_0005342
- Yu XQ, publication date 2011-12-25, PMID 22197929
- top locus-to-gene (L2G) prediction TNFSF13, score 0.9286, above the 0.8 threshold
The PubMed abstract reports the 17p13 association (rs3803800, P=9.40e-11, OR 1.21; rs4227, P=4.31e-10). It names TNFSF13 as a susceptibility gene. The GWAS Catalog record for GCST001364 confirms the trait mapping and the sample sizes: 1,434 cases and 4,270 controls in discovery, 2,703 cases and 3,464 controls in replication.
Caveat: the L2G score itself is a recent Open Targets calculation. It did not exist in 2011. The GWAS association that implicates TNFSF13 was published long before Phase 2 entry, though.
(4) The source was published online 2011-12-25 (print February 2012), about 8.5 years before 2020-07-20.
(5) The GWAS authors are from Sun Yat-sen University, other Chinese academic centres and the Genome Institute of Singapore. None is from Visterra or Otsuka. The sponsor's own preclinical paper (Myette 2019) cites the APRIL biology but is not the genetic evidence.

evidence_source: Zhou W et al., "Efficiently controlling for case-control imbalance and sample relatedness in large-scale genetic association studies" (SAIGE; UK Biobank PheCode GWAS), Nat Genet 2018;50:1335-1341, epub 2018-08-13, PMID 30104761 (GWAS Catalog GCST90435600 / GCST90435601)
outcome_summary: Camizestrant (AZD9833) is AstraZeneca's oral SERD that degrades ESR1. Its Phase 2 entry is confirmed: SERENA-2 (NCT04214288, sponsored by AstraZeneca) is registered as Phase 2 with an actual start date of 2020-04-22. SERENA-2 met its primary endpoint of investigator-assessed PFS against fulvestrant 500 mg. Median PFS was 7.2 months at 75 mg and 7.7 months at 150 mg, versus 3.7 months with fulvestrant (HR 0.59, p=0.017 and HR 0.64, p=0.0090; Lancet Oncol 2024). The program reached Phase 3 within 4 years. SERENA-4 (NCT04711252) started 2021-01-28 and SERENA-6 (NCT04964934) started 2021-06-30. SERENA-6 met its primary endpoint of investigator-assessed PFS. In patients whose ESR1 mutation emerged during first-line AI plus CDK4/6i therapy, switching to camizestrant gave 16.0 months versus 9.2 months (HR 0.44, P<0.0001; NEJM 2025). The FDA granted accelerated approval on 2026-09-04 (NDA 220359, brand name Etcamah). The approved use is camizestrant plus a CDK4/6 inhibitor in adults with HR+/HER2- locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer when an ESR1 mutation is detected during AI plus CDK4/6i therapy. Continued approval depends on a confirmatory trial. The label carries a boxed warning about QTc and arrhythmia risk when combined with QTc-prolonging drugs such as ribociclib. The program was never stopped, so it is not a failure.
key_trial: NCT04964934 (SERENA-6, Phase 3, the basis for approval). The entry Phase 2 was NCT04214288 (SERENA-2).

evidence.earliest_source: Zhou W et al., "Efficiently controlling for case-control imbalance and sample relatedness in large-scale genetic association studies" (SAIGE; UK Biobank PheCode GWAS), Nat Genet 2018;50:1335-1341, epub 2018-08-13, PMID 30104761 (GWAS Catalog GCST90435600 / GCST90435601)
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: AstraZeneca's discovery paper (Scott JS et al., J Med Chem 2020, PMID 32910656) describes AZD9833 (camizestrant) as a potent oral selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) and antagonist. It degrades ERα, the product of ESR1, in MCF-7 and CAMA-1 cells, with a profile comparable to fulvestrant. So "ESR1 (degrader)" is correct. The paper came out in Sep 2020, after Phase 2 entry, but question 1 is only about mechanism.

(2) Disease: NCT04214288 is SERENA-2, a Phase 2 trial run by AstraZeneca comparing oral AZD9833 with fulvestrant in advanced ER+/HER2- breast cancer. ClinicalTrials.gov gives an actual start date of 2020-04-22, matching phase2_entry. Mapping it to MONDO:0007254 (breast cancer) is fine.

(3) Claim: Open Targets GraphQL returns both studyLocusIds (5efd476b... and aff12a12...). Each has lead variant rs910416 (GRCh38 6:152111767 C>T), which falls inside the ESR1 gene span (6:151,651,284-152,129,619 per Ensembl). Each gives ESR1 an L2G score of 0.819, with SYNE1 next at 0.442. The two studies are GCST90435600 "Breast cancer (PheCode 174)" (12,898 cases / 388,549 controls) and GCST90435601 "Breast cancer [female] (PheCode 174.1)". Both are linked to PMID 30104761, Zhou et al., Nat Genet, epub 2018-08-13.

The variant is genome-wide significant in the SAIGE UKB PheWeb: p=1.7e-13 for PheCode 174 and 8.8e-14 for 174.1.

(4) Timing: the paper's data statement says summary statistics for all 1,403 binary PheCode phenotypes were released for public download (leelabsg.org/resources) and shown on Michigan PheWeb, so the GWAS data existed in Aug 2018, before the 2020-04-22 entry. Two things came later:
- The GWAS Catalog deposit is dated Jan-Feb 2025 on the FTP server.
- The credible set and L2G score are later Open Targets computations, not something available in 2018.

On the earliest source, three points:
- The ESR1/6q25.1 breast-cancer GWAS signal goes back to Zheng W et al., Nat Genet 2009 (PMID 19219042, rs2046210). In Open Targets that credible set gives ESR1 an L2G of only 0.08.
- Michailidou 2017 (PMID 29059683) reaches 0.786, just under the threshold.
- Of the 69 Open Targets ESR1/breast-cancer credible sets, Zhou 2018 is therefore the earliest to reach L2G ≥ 0.8.

Zhou 2018 is a SAIGE methods paper, so the ESR1 result is in its released summary statistics rather than discussed in its text.

(5) Sponsor: the Zhou 2018 authors are from the University of Michigan, Vanderbilt and NTNU, and the paper declares no competing financial interests. It was not authored by AstraZeneca.

failure_second.reasoning:
The program did fail. Galegenimab (FHTR2163/RG6147) is Genentech's intravitreal Fab that inhibits HtrA1. Its Phase 2 trial, GALLEGO (NCT03972709), started on 2019-06-03 and was TERMINATED on 2022-10-27. The ClinicalTrials.gov reason for stopping is: "The benefit to risk balance did not support further treatment with galegenimab (FHTR2163)." The open-label extension (NCT04607148) was terminated for the same stated reason on 2022-11-14. No other galegenimab trial is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, and no Phase 3 exists.

Why it did not advance:
(1) Efficacy was null. The primary endpoint was change in GA area on FAF at Week 72. Posted results show 2.60 mm2 for Q4W, 2.43 for Q8W and 2.31 for sham. The difference versus sham was +0.29 mm2 for Q4W (95% CI -0.08 to 0.66, p=0.12) and +0.12 mm2 for Q8W (p=0.61), so lesions grew numerically faster on drug. BCVA showed no benefit either. The peer-reviewed Phase 2 paper (Eichenbaum et al., Am J Ophthalmol 2025, PMID 40089174) concludes: "Inhibition of HtrA1 with a Fab did not slow down GA progression."
(2) Safety added to the decision. The same paper reports intraocular inflammation in 7.1% of treated patients (16/224) and says "The DMC recommended early termination of the study based on an early benefit/risk analysis." The posted adverse-event data agree: study-eye ocular AEs were about 49% on drug vs 32% on sham, and AESIs (which include sight-threatening grade 4+ intraocular inflammation) were 6.7% vs 2.0%.

Why F2 and not F1: target engagement had been shown. The Phase 1 study (Khanani et al., AJO 2021, PMID 34214452) reported "a sustained pharmacodynamic effect of anti-HtrA1 ... in the aqueous humor, as measured by levels of cleaved DKK3" at 20 mg given every 4 weeks. That is the same dose Phase 2 used. Genentech's PNAS 2020 paper (PMID 32345717) validated DKK3 as the readout of HtrA1 inhibition in patients. So exposure and engagement were established, and the biology did not translate into slower GA growth.

The genetics support F2. The rationale for the program was the ARMS2/HTRA1 10q26 risk locus. Williams et al. (PNAS 2021, PMID 34301870) found that 10q26 risk carriers have lower HTRA1 mRNA and protein in the RPE, and suggest "HtrA1 augmentation, not inhibition" as the therapy. If so, inhibiting HtrA1 pushes the target the wrong way relative to the genetic risk.

Secondary factors, not chosen as the primary code:
- F3: Keenan's comment on the trial (AJO 2025, PMID 40348352) argues that ARMS2/HTRA1 risk variants drive GA growth only at very early GA, while GALLEGO enrolled lesions of at least 2.5 mm2.
- F6: the intraocular inflammation is specific to this molecule and contributed to the DMC's benefit/risk call.
Efficacy was null even at the final analysis, so I coded the main reason as F2.

Unclear: I could not read the full Phase 2 paper (paywalled, HTTP 403), so I do not know whether Phase 2 measured DKK3 engagement or ran a genotype subgroup analysis. I found no Roche press release or filing on the discontinuation; my web-search budget was used up, so I did not look further.

claim: A GWAS credible set for this disease (or a subtype or very similar disease) assigns the target gene a locus-to-gene score of at least 0.8, from a study published before the program entered Phase 2.
evidence_source: Kichaev G et al., 'Leveraging Polygenic Functional Enrichment to Improve GWAS Power', Am J Hum Genet 2019;104(1):65-75, epub 2018-12-27 (PMID 30595370). This is GWAS Catalog GCST007075, trait 'Eczema' in about 459,000 UK Biobank Europeans. Lead variant rs59185885 (chr2:102327786), p=4e-79, mapped genes IL18R1/IL1RL1. In the Open Targets credible set c491b434b422c2864a395997af3dc118 (PICS), the locus-to-gene score for IL1RL1 (now IL33R, ENSG00000115602) is 0.899. Earlier qualifying studies of broader allergy phenotypes: Ferreira 2017 Nat Genet (PMID 29083406, epub 2017-10-30, 'asthma, hay fever or eczema', L2G 0.926) and Pickrell 2016 Nat Genet (PMID 27182965, epub 2016-05-16, self-reported 'Allergy', L2G 0.85).
outcome_summary: Astegolimab is an anti-ST2 (IL1RL1) IgG2 antibody that blocks IL-33 signalling. Genentech's Phase 2 trial in moderate to severe atopic dermatitis (NCT03747575, GS40965) started on 2019-02-06 and finished with 65 patients randomized, against 90 planned. The primary endpoint, percent change in EASI from baseline to week 16, was -51.47% on astegolimab and -58.24% on placebo. Placebo did numerically better, and the difference of 6.77% was not significant (95% CI -16.57 to 30.11; P=.5624). Secondary efficacy outcomes showed no difference, and neither did the exploratory biomarkers (blood eosinophils, serum IL-5, CCL13). The paper reports that the loading dose gave sufficient drug exposure from week 1. The accompanying JACI editorial adds that trough levels were similar to those in the asthma trial where the drug worked, and that the trial still had about 80% power. The drug was well tolerated, so safety did not stop the program. The editorial concludes the trial most likely failed for biological reasons. One possibility it raises is that IL-33, as an alarmin, matters for starting the disease rather than keeping chronic AD going; another is the varied immune picture in adults with chronic AD. That points to F2: exposure was shown but blocking the pathway did not translate into clinical benefit, with F3 (chronic adult population) as the alternative reading. No AD Phase 3 was ever registered. Roche's current pipeline (HY 2026) lists astegolimab only for COPD, now in registration, and not for atopic dermatitis. This shows the AD program has been dropped, but I found no company statement giving the reason, so the efficacy attribution comes from the trial results.

evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action. Astegolimab (AMG 282 / MSTT1041A / RG6149) is a fully human IgG2 mAb. It binds ST2, the IL-33 receptor encoded by IL1RL1 (HGNC now calls it IL33R; it is the same Ensembl gene, ENSG00000115602), and blocks IL-33 binding. That makes it an antagonist, consistent with binder_neutralizer (PMID 41036707; PMID 33872652).

(2) Entry trial. NCT03747575 (Genentech, GS40965) is a Phase II randomized placebo-controlled trial of MSTT1041A/astegolimab in moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis. Its actual start date, 2019-02-06, matches the recorded entry date, so the disease mapping is correct.

(3) Claim. All three DB rows check out against the live Open Targets credibleSet API:
- f28f7dd1… = GCST003990, Pickrell 2016, rs950881, L2G 0.850
- b40cd20e… = GCST005038, Ferreira 2017, rs10865050, SuSiE-inf, L2G 0.926
- c491b434… = GCST007075, Kichaev 2018, rs59185885, L2G 0.899

IL1RL1 is the top L2G gene in each; IL18R1 and IL18RAP score at most 0.2. The GWAS Catalog v2 API confirms the IL1RL1/IL18R1 associations in each study:
- GCST007075: p=4e-79
- GCST005038: rs10865050, p=7e-61
- GCST003990: rs950881, p=6e-27

(4) Timing. Only the 2018 row is mapped to atopic eczema itself. The 2016 and 2017 rows are the broader 'allergic disease' term. Ferreira's phenotype includes eczema; Pickrell's is self-reported allergy from 23andMe and is the loosest match. Taking the strict eczema-specific source, Kichaev went online 2018-12-27, only about 6 weeks before Phase 2 entry; the broader 2016 and 2017 studies predate entry comfortably.

Caveats:
- The L2G scores are Open Targets' current retrospective computations. They did not exist at entry; the underlying GWAS publications did.
- Kichaev is a methods paper that reanalysed UK Biobank, and the GWAS Catalog maps its trait to 'Eczematoid dermatitis' (HP_0000964).
- Earlier dedicated atopic dermatitis GWAS have credible sets at this locus but with low IL1RL1 L2G: Hirota 2012 (PMID 23042114, L2G 0.42) and Paternoster 2015 (PMID 26482879, L2G 0.11). So eczema-specific support at 0.8 or higher dates only to Kichaev 2018.

(5) Sponsor. The PubMed affiliations for Kichaev 2018 (UCLA, Harvard T.H. Chan, Broad) and Ferreira 2017 (QIMR and academic consortia, plus 23andMe) list no Genentech, Roche or Amgen authors. PubMed has no affiliations for Pickrell 2016; its listed authors include 23andMe researchers and none are from the sponsor, but this is not verified from affiliations. Web search was unavailable (budget exhausted), so verification used the ClinicalTrials.gov, PubMed E-utilities, Open Targets GraphQL and GWAS Catalog v2 APIs.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: astegolimab (MSTT1041A/AMG 282/RG6149), an anti-ST2 (IL1RL1) IgG2 mAb, tested in moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis in the Genentech Phase 2 trial NCT03747575 (GS40965/ZARNIE). The trial started 2019-02-06, reached primary completion 2020-03-11 and is marked completed. ClinicalTrials.gov lists no other astegolimab AD trial. Later development is COPD only: Phase 3 trials NCT05595642 and NCT05878769.

Why it did not advance: the drug had no efficacy in AD.
- Primary endpoint missed. EASI % change at week 16 was -51.47% on astegolimab vs -58.24% on placebo. The difference of 6.77% (95% CI -16.57 to 30.11; P=.5624) numerically favoured placebo (CT.gov posted results; Maurer et al., JACI 2022, PMID 36041655).
- All secondary efficacy outcomes showed no difference.
- Safety was not the problem. Astegolimab was well tolerated, with AEs at 41% vs 58% on placebo (Kelsen et al., Respir Res 2025, PMID 41163220).

Exposure was shown. The paper says "pharmacokinetic exposure was sufficient from week 1." The JACI editorial (Schuler & Gudjonsson, PMID 36270492, PMC10087095) adds that trough levels were "similar ... compared to a successful astegolimab asthma trial."

The editorial also rules out power as the explanation, though the trial was under-enrolled (65 randomized vs 90 planned). The smaller sample "still provided approximately 80% power to detect a difference of 34%," and the point estimate favoured placebo. Its explanation for the failure is the biology: "IL-33 could be critical for initiation of skin-based inflammation but have a more limited or superfluous role in ongoing skin inflammatory responses." It adds that chronic AD gains mixed Th1/Th17 features. It notes the same pattern for etokimab, an anti-IL-33 antibody: a positive Phase 2a followed by a negative Phase 2b. This fits F2: exposure shown, but blocking the pathway in adults did not translate in established disease (wrong timing).

Caveats:
- The exploratory downstream biomarkers (blood eosinophils, serum IL-5, CCL13) did not differ between arms. So engagement in AD skin was never shown directly; the evidence is adequate exposure. F1 is a secondary alternative.
- F3 (wrong disease stage: chronic rather than early AD) is also arguable.
- The placebo response was unusually high (-58% EASI).
- No sponsor press release or filing explaining the AD discontinuation was found. The web-search budget was used up during this task, so press-release and SEC coverage is incomplete. The code rests on the trial results, the primary paper and the editorial.

Sources: the full text of the primary paper was blocked (HTTP 403), so its findings come from the PubMed abstract. The editorial and the safety review were read in full via PMC.

evidence_source: Yu XQ, Li M, Zhang H, ... Liu JJ. "A genome-wide association study in Han Chinese identifies multiple susceptibility loci for IgA nephropathy." Nat Genet 2012;44:178-82, published online 2011-12-25 (PMID 22197929, doi:10.1038/ng.1047; GWAS Catalog GCST001364)
outcome_summary:
Zigakibart (BION-1301) is an anti-APRIL (TNFSF13) monoclonal antibody. It was developed by Chinook Therapeutics, and Novartis now sponsors it. It entered the Phase 1/2 trial NCT03945318 on 2019-04-08. That trial had healthy-volunteer SAD/MAD parts and open-label IgAN cohorts, and its primary endpoints were safety/tolerability, blood pressure and eGFR change. No results have been posted on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Interim data reported by Chinook in February 2023 showed lasting reductions in IgA and Gd-IgA1 and roughly 30% falls in 24-hour UPCR. There were no serious adverse events and no anti-drug antibodies. Chinook guided to a Phase 3 start in mid-2023. The Phase 3 BEYOND trial (NCT05852938) began on 2023-07-06, about 3 months after the 4-year window closed on 2023-04-08, so the strict answer to "advanced within 4 years" is no. The program was not stopped, though. It moved to Phase 3 on its planned timeline.

Novartis reported 100-week Phase 1/2 data in its Q2 2025 report: a 60.4% proteinuria reduction and stable eGFR. Its Q2 2026 report (July 2026) says BEYOND is ongoing, with readout expected in H1 2027. BEYOND is active and no longer recruiting; estimated primary completion is 2027-08.

Other activity:
- An open-label extension study listed as Phase 3 (NCT06858319) started on 2025-07-28.
- A Phase 3 study of zigakibart plus atrasentan (NCT07850752) is not yet recruiting.
- A new Phase 2 (NCT07146906) started in 2026.

No FDA approval yet. Because the program is still progressing, there is no failure code and no stop reason. The key trial is the Phase 1/2 trial that supported the move to Phase 3. Its primary endpoint is marked not_applicable because the primary outcome is safety and no formal results have been posted.

evidence.notes: (1) Target and direction: zigakibart is BION-1301 (ChEMBL CHEMBL5095316 lists BION-1301 as a synonym; the CT.gov record lists Zigakibart as another name). Aduro's 8-K press release of 2019-05-07 (SEC EDGAR) describes BION-1301 as "a first-in-class humanized IgG4 monoclonal antibody that fully blocks APRIL binding to both the BCMA and TACI receptors". HGNC confirms that APRIL is an alias of TNFSF13. So the binder/neutralizer of TNFSF13 is correct. ChEMBL has no mechanism record for this molecule. Tai et al. 2016 (Blood, PMID 27127303), with Aduro/BioNovion co-authors, describes the parent antagonist antibody hAPRIL01A, which blocks APRIL-BCMA binding. (2) Disease: NCT03945318 is a Phase 1/2 study titled "...BION-1301 in Healthy Volunteers and Adults With IgA Nephropathy". Its condition is IgA Nephropathy, it started 2019-04-08 (actual, matching the recorded entry date), and Part 3 doses IgAN patients. The lead sponsor is now listed as Novartis; it was originally Aduro, and the record keeps the Chinook code ADU-CL-19. The Aduro Q1-2019 8-K says "Phase 1 clinical trial of BION-1301 initiated for the treatment of IgA nephropathy". (3) Claim: Open Targets credible set 37dec5e472e9788e0079745efe8757f0 is study GCST001364 (Yu XQ, Nat Genet, pub date 2011-12-25, PMID 22197929), lead variant rs3803800 (17_7559652_A_G, p=9e-11), with a TNFSF13 L2G score of 0.9286, which is at least 0.8. The PubMed abstract reports the 17p13 association (rs3803800 P=9.40e-11, OR 1.21; rs4227) and names TNFSF13 as a susceptibility gene. Ensembl VEP calls rs3803800 a missense variant in TNFSF13. The GWAS Catalog v2 maps GCST001364 to MONDO_0005342 (IgA glomerulonephritis), the same disease as the case. One caveat: the L2G score is a recent Open Targets computation, but the underlying GWAS finding and its explicit naming of TNFSF13 were published in 2011. (4) Online publication on 2011-12-25 (print Feb 2012) is about 7 years before Phase 2 entry on 2019-04-08. (5) The authors are from Sun Yat-sen University and other Chinese academic institutions (corresponding author yuxq@mail.sysu.edu.cn). None are from Aduro/BioNovion, so the paper is not sponsor-authored. I did not research or consider the clinical outcome.

outcome.advance_event: The Phase 3 BEYOND trial (NCT05852938, zigakibart vs placebo in adults with IgAN, primary endpoint eGFR change to week 104) started on 2023-07-06 (actual). That is about 4 years and 3 months after the Phase 2 entry on 2019-04-08, so it falls about 3 months outside the 4-year window, which closed on 2023-04-08. Chinook had guided to a "mid-2023" Phase 3 start in February and May 2023, and its Q2 2023 10-Q describes zigakibart as in Phase 3. There has been no FDA approval.
outcome.summary:
Zigakibart (BION-1301) is an anti-APRIL (TNFSF13) monoclonal antibody. It was developed by Chinook Therapeutics, and Novartis now sponsors it. It entered the Phase 1/2 trial NCT03945318 on 2019-04-08. That trial had healthy-volunteer SAD/MAD parts and open-label IgAN cohorts, and its primary endpoints were safety/tolerability, blood pressure and eGFR change. No results have been posted on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Interim data reported by Chinook in February 2023 showed lasting reductions in IgA and Gd-IgA1 and roughly 30% falls in 24-hour UPCR. There were no serious adverse events and no anti-drug antibodies. Chinook guided to a Phase 3 start in mid-2023. The Phase 3 BEYOND trial (NCT05852938) began on 2023-07-06, about 3 months after the 4-year window closed on 2023-04-08, so the strict answer to "advanced within 4 years" is no. The program was not stopped, though. It moved to Phase 3 on its planned timeline.

Novartis reported 100-week Phase 1/2 data in its Q2 2025 report: a 60.4% proteinuria reduction and stable eGFR. Its Q2 2026 report (July 2026) says BEYOND is ongoing, with readout expected in H1 2027. BEYOND is active and no longer recruiting; estimated primary completion is 2027-08.

Other activity:
- An open-label extension study listed as Phase 3 (NCT06858319) started on 2025-07-28.
- A Phase 3 study of zigakibart plus atrasentan (NCT07850752) is not yet recruiting.
- A new Phase 2 (NCT07146906) started in 2026.

No FDA approval yet. Because the program is still progressing, there is no failure code and no stop reason. The key trial is the Phase 1/2 trial that supported the move to Phase 3. Its primary endpoint is marked not_applicable because the primary outcome is safety and no formal results have been posted.

failure_second.reasoning:
This program did not fail. It reached Phase 3 about three months after the four-year cutoff, and it is still running.

1. The entry trial, NCT03945318, is a Phase 1/2 study that started on 2019-04-08. That date is when the healthy-volunteer dosing parts began (Parts 1 and 2). The IgA nephropathy patients were enrolled later, in Part 3. So the date in our records sets the clock early, before any patient was treated.

2. Through early 2023 the company described the drug as in Phase 2 and said Phase 3 would start in mid-2023:
   - The FY2022 results release (2023-02-27) said Chinook had "finalized trial design" and was "completing global regulatory interactions to enable initiation of a phase 3 trial of BION-1301 in mid-2023".
   - The Q1 2023 release (2023-05-09) said the company was "on track to initiate the phase 3 BION-1301 IgAN clinical trial mid-year".

3. The Phase 3 BEYOND trial, NCT05852938, started on 2023-07-06. It is randomized, double-blind and placebo-controlled, with 383 patients enrolled and Novartis as sponsor. Four years from 2019-04-08 is 2023-04-08, so the start missed the window by about three months. On 2023-07-28 Chinook announced that the first patient had been enrolled in BEYOND.

4. Novartis agreed to acquire Chinook on 2023-06-12. The announcement said Novartis would use its resources to pursue broader development of zigakibart. The acquisition supported the program rather than ending it.

5. The program is still moving forward as of 2026:
   - BEYOND is active and not recruiting. Its primary completion is estimated for 2027-08.
   - A Phase 3 open-label extension, NCT06858319, started on 2025-07-28 and is recruiting.
   - A new Phase IIIb trial, NCT07850752, was registered on 2026-09-30 and is not yet recruiting. It tests zigakibart plus atrasentan against zigakibart plus placebo.

No source reports a safety, efficacy or strategic setback before Phase 3. The company's interim Phase 1/2 results to May 2023 reported the drug as well tolerated, with no treatment discontinuations due to adverse events. They also reported lower IgA and Gd-IgA1 levels and lower proteinuria (UPCR). The "did not reach Phase 3 within four years" flag reflects how the entry date was set and a normal gap before the pivotal trial, not a failure.

Pipeline error (trial linking): The pipeline recorded s4=1, event=advanced, years_to_event=1.68. Counting 1.68 years from 2019-04-08 lands on about 2020-12-12. That matches the actual start date (2020-12-11) of NCT04573478, which is ALIGN, Chinook/Novartis's Phase 3 trial of atrasentan in IgAN, not of zigakibart. The current CT.gov record for ALIGN lists "Drug: Zigakibart (FUB523, BION-1301)" as an intervention. It was added for a later co-administration substudy, given "after completion of OL extension period", which comes after 132 weeks double-blind plus 48 weeks open-label. So the ALIGN start date marks atrasentan's Phase 3 start, not zigakibart's. The pipeline linked that trial to zigakibart through the intervention name.

Zigakibart's first Phase 3 for IgAN was BEYOND (NCT05852938, actual start 2023-07-06). Chinook's 8-K of 2023-07-28 announced the first patient enrolled. Four years from the recorded entry (2019-04-08, the actual start of Phase 1/2 trial NCT03945318) ends on 2023-04-08, so BEYOND missed the window by about 89 days (4.24 years). There is no FDA approval. Under the pipeline's own entry date, the correct label is s4=0.

- BEYOND: active, not recruiting
- Phase 3 OLE NCT06858319: started 2025-07-28
- Phase 3 zigakibart + atrasentan trial NCT07850752: registered 2026-09

outcome_summary:
Taiho Oncology's FOENIX-MBC2 (NCT04024436, TAS-120-201) was the Phase 2 entry trial. It started on 2020-01-28 and treated 64 patients with metastatic breast cancer carrying FGFR1 or FGFR2 amplification. Taiho terminated it and recorded the reason as 'The Sponsor decided to discontinue the study due to strategic considerations and not due to any safety-related concerns.' The primary completion date was 2023-05-31.

The results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov in 2025-11 show the main cohorts failed the protocol's own futility test. The protocol used a Simon two-stage design for the ORR cohorts, comparing a poor response of 15% or less against a promising response of 30% or more. Stage 1 needed at least 4 responses in 19 patients.
- Cohort 1 (HR+/HER2- with FGFR2 amplification): ORR 0% (0 of 17; 95% CI 0-19.5).
- Cohort 2 (TNBC with FGFR2 amplification): ORR 9.5% (2 of 21; 95% CI 1.2-30.4).
- Cohort 3 (non-measurable disease): only 4 of the planned 9 enrolled; clinical benefit rate 50% (95% CI 6.8-93.2), which cannot be interpreted at that size.
- Cohort 4 (HR+/HER2- with FGFR1 amplification, futibatinib plus fulvestrant): 6-month PFS 45.5% in 22 patients (95% CI 24.4-67.8). The null rate was 25%, so the interval does not exclude it, and the cohort fell short of the planned 28 patients and the rejection rule of at least 14 of 28 progression-free.
No cohort met its primary endpoint.

The drug clearly reached its target: hyperphosphataemia, the usual sign of FGFR inhibition, occurred in 55 of 64 patients. At the same 20 mg dose futibatinib is effective and FDA-approved in FGFR2-fusion cholangiocarcinoma. In FGFR2-amplified breast cancer, though, inhibiting the target produced almost no tumour responses.

Taiho's statement says strategic, but the efficacy data are the substantive reason, so I set stop_reason to efficacy and the failure code to F2. A grader who goes by the sponsor's wording would score this F8. F3 (wrong biomarker subtype, amplification rather than fusion or mutation) is also arguable, but no source tested it.

No Phase 3 trial or breast cancer approval followed. Taiho's current pipeline page does not list breast cancer for futibatinib. I found no peer-reviewed publication of the FOENIX-MBC2 results; the figures above come from the ClinicalTrials.gov record and the attached protocol and statistical analysis plan.

evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: futibatinib (TAS-120) is a covalent, irreversible small-molecule inhibitor of FGFR1, 2, 3 and 4. The FDA label for LYTGOBI (NDA214801), section 12.1, gives IC50 values below 4 nM for FGFR1-4. Before Phase 2 entry, a 2019 ChemMedChem paper (PMID 30600916) reported TAS-120 bound irreversibly to FGFR1, and a 2019 Cancer Discov paper (PMID 31109923) described it as an FGFR inhibitor. The full FGFR1-4 profile (IC50 1.4-3.7 nM) was published in Sootome et al., Cancer Res 2020 (PMID 32973082, online Sep 2020). Taiho authored that paper; it is mechanism support only, not the key evidence.

(2) Entry trial: NCT04024436 (FOENIX-MBC2, TAS-120-201) is a Phase 2 study of futibatinib in metastatic breast cancer with FGFR1 or FGFR2 amplification. Its cohorts are HR+/HER2- and TNBC, and Cohort 4 adds fulvestrant. Actual start date is 2020-01-28, which matches the recorded entry date. Sponsor is Taiho Oncology. The breast cancer (MONDO:0007254) mapping is correct. The evidence disease is breast carcinoma (MONDO_0004989), essentially the same disease.

(3) Claim: I queried all 10 studyLocusIds in the Open Targets Platform GraphQL API (credibleSet endpoint). Each one is an FGFR2 intronic lead variant (rs2981582, rs1219648, rs2981579, rs2981575, rs2981578, rs2420946) from a breast cancer GWAS. FGFR2 is the top L2G gene in every one, scoring 0.858-0.946. The two earliest are:
- cb7188a1…, Easton 2007 Nature, GCST000035, rs2981582: L2G 0.946
- 42271021…, Hunter 2007 Nat Genet, GCST000036, rs1219648: L2G 0.894

Later sets come from Thomas 2009, Turnbull 2010, Li 2010, Gaudet 2010 and 2013 (BRCA2 carriers), Fletcher 2011, Michailidou 2013 and Low 2013. All are at or above 0.8. The GWAS Catalog v2 API confirms GCST000035 and GCST000036 map to breast carcinoma (MONDO_0004989). Caveat: the L2G score comes from the current Open Targets model, which postdates 2020. What existed before entry is the GWAS association itself, and both 2007 abstracts named FGFR2 as the implicated gene.

(4) Both 2007 papers came out roughly 12.5 years before the 2020-01-28 entry.

(5) Sponsor authorship: Easton's paper is from the Cambridge CR-UK Genetic Epidemiology Unit and international consortia, with Perlegen genotyping. Hunter's is from Harvard/Channing Lab with NCI CGEMS. Neither includes Taiho authors.

Context, not a defect: the GWAS signal is germline common-variant risk for breast cancer, mainly ER+. The trial enrolled tumours with somatic FGFR1/2 amplification, which is a different biological rationale from the germline signal.

outcome.advance_event: None. From 2020-01-28 to 2024-01-28, no Phase 3 trial of futibatinib in breast cancer started under any sponsor, and the FDA gave no breast-cancer approval. A ClinicalTrials.gov search of every futibatinib trial (all sponsors) finds Phase 3 trials only in biliary tract cancer or cholangiocarcinoma. The one Phase 2/3 study, NCT06506955, is a rollover for patients from earlier futibatinib trials, not a breast cancer trial, and it started in 2024-10, after the window. The only FDA approval of futibatinib (LYTGOBI, NDA 214801, approved 2022-09-30) is for previously treated intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma with FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements.

failure_second.reasoning:
The program is futibatinib (TAS-120), a covalent FGFR1-4 inhibitor, tested in breast cancer in one Phase 2 trial: FOENIX-MBC2 (NCT04024436), sponsored by Taiho Oncology. It started on 2020-01-28 and has four cohorts:
- C1: HR+/HER2- disease with FGFR2 amplification
- C2: TNBC with FGFR2 amplification
- C3: non-measurable disease with FGFR2 amplification
- C4: HR+/HER2- disease with high-level FGFR1 amplification, given futibatinib plus fulvestrant

**Why it stopped (the only stated reason).** The ClinicalTrials.gov record shows status TERMINATED, with primary completion on 2023-05-31 and study completion on 2023-09-06. Its whyStopped field reads: "The Sponsor decided to discontinue the study due to strategic considerations and not due to any safety-related concerns." The EU register (EudraCT 2019-001164-30) gives the same reason: "Completed (prematurely ended)". The participant flow shows 23 patients withdrawn because the sponsor ended the study (4 in C1, 6 in C2, 2 in C3, 11 in C4), so patients were still on study when it was stopped.

**Enrollment fell short of plan.** The trial-in-progress abstract (SABCS 2019) planned about 168 patients: up to 55, 55, 24 and 34 in C1 to C4, with Simon two-stage designs for C1 to C3. The trial enrolled 64 (17, 21, 4 and 22).

**Target engagement was shown.** Hyperphosphatemia is the on-target pharmacodynamic sign of FGFR inhibition. It occurred in 13/17, 18/21, 3/4 and 21/22 patients in the posted adverse-event data. The SABCS 2023 abstracts report it as a treatment-related event in 85.7% of the TNBC cohort and 95.5% of C4.

**Efficacy (ClinicalTrials.gov posted results and SABCS 2023 abstracts):**

| Cohort | n | Objective response rate | Median PFS | 6-month PFS rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C1 | 17 | 0% (95% CI 0 to 19.5) | 3.7 mo | — |
| C2 | 21 | 9.5% | 1.9 mo | — |
| C3 | 4 | Clinical benefit rate 50% | — | — |
| C4 | 22 | 18.2% | 7.2 mo | 45.5% (primary endpoint) |

The authors called the TNBC result "modest anticancer activity." They described C4 as showing antitumor activity, with "doubling in PFS relative to historical fulvestrant results." Both abstracts say biomarker work is ongoing.

**Nothing later reached Phase 3.** The only later futibatinib study that lists breast cancer is NCT06506955. It is labelled Phase 2/3 but is a continued-access rollover for patients from earlier Taiho futibatinib trials, with about 15 patients, not a breast efficacy trial. Taiho's pipeline page ("As of Jun. 30, 2026") still lists TAS-120 for breast cancer at Phase II in the US and Europe. That page appears out of date: it also lists TAS0728, whose only trial (NCT03410927) was terminated in 2022 for toxicity.

**Coding.** F8 is the only reason a primary source states for stopping, and the sponsor explicitly rules out safety. Stopping despite C4 being described as active also fits a portfolio or market decision.

**Caveat.** Weak single-agent activity in the FGFR2-amplified cohorts (0% and 9.5% response rates despite clear engagement) probably contributed. That would argue for F2, or for F3 if FGFR amplification is treated as the wrong way to select patients. However, no primary source says efficacy drove the decision, so F8 stays as the coded answer and F2/F3 is the alternative.

adjudication.reasoning:
ADVANCEMENT: The program did not advance. NCT04024436 (FOENIX-MBC2, Taiho) is a Phase 2 trial with an actual start date of 2020-01-28, which matches the recorded entry. Its status is TERMINATED, with primary completion on 2023-05-31 and study completion on 2023-09-06. The pipeline's 3.61 years to event matches that completion date. A ClinicalTrials.gov search of every futibatinib trial found Phase 3 trials only in biliary tract cancer, cholangiocarcinoma or sarcoma profiling. NCT06506955, labelled Phase 2/3, is a rollover for patients from earlier futibatinib trials (advanced/metastatic cancer). It started in 2024-10, after the window. The only approval in Drugs@FDA is NDA214801 (LYTGOBI, approved 2022-09-30) for FGFR2-fusion intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. So s4=0 is correct. One small point: the pipeline's event label "suspended" is imprecise, since the registry status is TERMINATED, but that does not change the outcome.

CLAIM: I re-queried the Open Targets GraphQL API.
- Credible set cb7188a1… is rs2981582 from GCST000035 (Easton DF, Nature, 2007-05-27, PMID 17529967), mapped to breast carcinoma MONDO_0004989. Its top L2G gene is FGFR2 at 0.946.
- Credible set 42271021… is rs1219648 from GCST000036 (Hunter DJ, Nat Genet, 2007-05-27, PMID 17529973). FGFR2 scores 0.894.
Both PubMed abstracts name FGFR2. Both studies came out about 12.5 years before the 2020 entry, so the claim holds and predates entry. One caveat: the L2G score comes from today's Open Targets model, but the claim's criterion is that the study was published before entry, and both were.

FAILURE CODE: I code F2, with F8 and F3 as alternatives.
- The registry's whyStopped field says "strategic considerations and not due to any safety-related concerns." Taiho uses the same boilerplate on other futibatinib trials (NCT04601857, NCT04965818), so it says little about why this trial stopped. The pipeline's "business or strategic (explicit)" accurately transcribes it.
- Target engagement was clear. Hyperphosphataemia, the on-target sign of FGFR inhibition, appears in the posted adverse-event data in nearly all patients, and the SABCS 2023 abstracts report it as treatment-related in 85.7% and 95.5% of two cohorts.
- No cohort met its prespecified efficacy bar. In SAP v1.0 (04 Feb 2020), Cohorts 1 and 2 use a Simon optimal design (15% vs 30%) that continues past stage 1 only with at least 4 responses in 19 patients:
  - Cohort 1 (HR+/HER2-, FGFR2 amplified): posted ORR 0/17, 0%.
  - Cohort 2 (TNBC, FGFR2 amplified): 2/21, 9.5%, which the authors called "modest". Both cohorts fall below their futility boundaries.
  - Cohort 3: only 4 of the 9 planned patients enrolled.
  - Cohort 4 (FGFR1 amplified, with fulvestrant): 6-month PFS 45.5% (95% CI 24.4-67.8). The null rate was 25% and the rejection rule was at least 14 of 28 progression-free; the cohort had 10 of 22, so the null was not rejected.
- The drug reached its target and works in FGFR2-fusion cholangiocarcinoma at the same dose, yet produced almost no responses in FGFR-amplified breast cancer. That is the F2 pattern: engagement shown, biology did not translate.
- This also fits the evidence agent's point that the genetic rationale was germline FGFR2 risk alleles, while the trial tested inhibition in established tumours with somatic amplification.
- F8 is the sponsor's stated wording but not the substantive cause. F3 (amplification as the wrong selection biomarker) is arguable, but no source tested another subtype.

Because the pipeline outcome is correct, error_source is none. The pipeline's stop reason should be read as the sponsor's stated wording, not as the substantive cause.

evidence_source: Ellinghaus D et al., "Analysis of five chronic inflammatory diseases identifies 27 new associations and highlights disease-specific patterns at shared loci", Nat Genet 2016;48(5):510-518, epub 2016-03-14 (PMID 26974007; GWAS Catalog GCST005537; lead SNP rs4129267 at IL6R)
outcome_summary:
I-Mab ran NCT03235752, a Phase 2 trial with 91 patients across East Asia. It started on 2018-02-06, finished in December 2020 and met its primary endpoint for the 600 mg biweekly IV dose. At week 12, 58.6% of patients on 600 mg had a clinical response versus 34.5% on placebo (adjusted difference 26.6%, P=.03). The 300 mg dose did not separate from placebo (P=.52). Safety was acceptable (JAMA 2023, PMID 36881032; I-Mab topline press release of April 2021).

I-Mab said in August 2021 that a Phase 3 was being planned, but none ever started. Its 20-F filings explain the stall as a strategic decision. I-Mab called olamkicept "unessential to our immuno-oncology focus" and moved it into its affiliate I-Mab Hangzhou, later renamed TJBio Hangzhou. In May 2022 it sublicensed rights outside Greater China and Korea to Ferring. The 20-F for fiscal 2024 says "TJBio Hangzhou has ceased the development of olamkicept." By June 30, 2025 I-Mab was no longer party to any olamkicept license with Ferring.

Ferring still holds the global rights and has gone back to dose-finding instead of starting Phase 3. Its two 2024 Phase 1 studies tested doses up to 2400 mg (NCT06298032, NCT06515834; published in Clin Transl Sci in 2026). The paper reporting NCT06298032 says unpublished exposure-response data showed "a trend toward greater efficacy with higher trough concentrations". It says 600 mg every 4 weeks did not keep troughs above 1 ug/mL. It concludes that higher doses should be tested "in future efficacy trials" and "future phase II trials". No such trial is registered yet.

So the drug is effectively still at the Phase 2 stage for IBD. Ferring's papers say IBD, not ulcerative colitis specifically, and no new Phase 2 is open. The China/Korea program, which owned the positive Phase 2, stopped for portfolio reasons and not because of efficacy or safety. Dose re-optimization (PK/exposure) is a secondary reason for the global delay.

evidence.earliest_source: Ellinghaus D et al., "Analysis of five chronic inflammatory diseases identifies 27 new associations and highlights disease-specific patterns at shared loci", Nat Genet 2016;48(5):510-518, epub 2016-03-14 (PMID 26974007; GWAS Catalog GCST005537; lead SNP rs4129267 at IL6R)
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: I-Mab's F-1 (Oct 2019) says "TJ301 (INN: olamkicept)" is a gp130 extracellular-domain/IgG1 Fc fusion. It works as a decoy that binds the IL-6/soluble IL-6R complex (Kd 130 pM) and blocks only IL-6 trans-signaling, not classic signaling. Rose-John 2017 (PMID 28675418) describes sgp130Fc the same way. So "IL6R + IL6, binder/neutralizer" is right in direction (inhibition). One caveat: the drug neutralizes the IL-6:sIL-6R complex. It does not block membrane IL-6R or free IL-6 the way tocilizumab or siltuximab do. Olamkicept has no ChEMBL or Open Targets drug entry.

(2) Trial: NCT03235752 (I-Mab, CTJ301UC201) is a Phase 2 placebo-controlled study of TJ301 (FE 999301) given IV in active ulcerative colitis. Actual start 2018-02-06, which matches the entry date.

(3) Claim: the Open Targets credible set 64c1b40c... exists. Study GCST005537, PICS fine-mapping, lead variant rs4129267, P=9e-18, IL6R L2G 0.987. Open Targets maps the study to UC, CD, PSC, psoriasis and AS. But it is a five-disease cross-phenotype (pleiotropy) subset meta-analysis, not a UC GWAS. Supplementary Table 3a (locus 12) shows what drives the IL6R signal:
- AS: P=3.7e-19, OR 0.848
- CD: P=1.8e-4
- UC: only nominal, P=0.0104, OR 0.962 (0.935-0.991)
- PSC and psoriasis: about P=0.03
The SBM best subset was AS,CD (protective). The locus was already known for AS (KNOWN(AS); Cortes 2013, GCST005529), and KNOWN(UC)=NA. This is the only Open Targets gwas_credible_sets row for IL6R in UC. There is none for IBD, and the only CD row is the same pleiotropy study. So the claim is literally true in Open Targets, but the UC-specific genetic support is weak and inherited from a mostly AS-driven pleiotropic signal. rs4129267 is in perfect LD (r2=1, per the paper's coding table) with IL6R missense rs2228145 (Asp358Ala).

(4) Published 2016-03-14, nearly 2 years before the 2018-02-06 entry.

outcome.summary:
I-Mab ran NCT03235752, a Phase 2 trial with 91 patients across East Asia. It started on 2018-02-06, finished in December 2020 and met its primary endpoint for the 600 mg biweekly IV dose. At week 12, 58.6% of patients on 600 mg had a clinical response versus 34.5% on placebo (adjusted difference 26.6%, P=.03). The 300 mg dose did not separate from placebo (P=.52). Safety was acceptable (JAMA 2023, PMID 36881032; I-Mab topline press release of April 2021).

I-Mab said in August 2021 that a Phase 3 was being planned, but none ever started. Its 20-F filings explain the stall as a strategic decision. I-Mab called olamkicept "unessential to our immuno-oncology focus" and moved it into its affiliate I-Mab Hangzhou, later renamed TJBio Hangzhou. In May 2022 it sublicensed rights outside Greater China and Korea to Ferring. The 20-F for fiscal 2024 says "TJBio Hangzhou has ceased the development of olamkicept." By June 30, 2025 I-Mab was no longer party to any olamkicept license with Ferring.

Ferring still holds the global rights and has gone back to dose-finding instead of starting Phase 3. Its two 2024 Phase 1 studies tested doses up to 2400 mg (NCT06298032, NCT06515834; published in Clin Transl Sci in 2026). The paper reporting NCT06298032 says unpublished exposure-response data showed "a trend toward greater efficacy with higher trough concentrations". It says 600 mg every 4 weeks did not keep troughs above 1 ug/mL. It concludes that higher doses should be tested "in future efficacy trials" and "future phase II trials". No such trial is registered yet.

So the drug is effectively still at the Phase 2 stage for IBD. Ferring's papers say IBD, not ulcerative colitis specifically, and no new Phase 2 is open. The China/Korea program, which owned the positive Phase 2, stopped for portfolio reasons and not because of efficacy or safety. Dose re-optimization (PK/exposure) is a secondary reason for the global delay.

failure_second.reasoning:
I coded this F8 (commercial or strategic). The trial worked at its higher dose, and none of the sources say it stopped because of safety or efficacy. My confidence is moderate, because no source states outright why no Phase 3 was started.

Program: olamkicept (TJ301 / FE 999301), a fusion protein that blocks only one route of IL-6 signalling ("trans-signalling"), tested in active ulcerative colitis. The entry trial was NCT03235752, sponsored by I-Mab Biopharma HongKong under a 2016 licence from Ferring that covered Greater China and South Korea. It started 2018-02-06 and finished 2020-12-21 with 91 patients.

1. **The trial met its primary endpoint at 600 mg.** I-Mab's press release of 2021-04-26 reported positive topline results. Clinical response at week 12 was higher on 600 mg than placebo (p=0.032), and clinical remission and mucosal healing were also better (p<0.001). The company called the drug "well tolerated".
   - The JAMA 2023 paper (PMID 36881032) gives 58.6% response on 600 mg versus 34.5% on placebo (p=.03). The 300 mg dose was not significantly better than placebo (p=.52).
   - Adverse events were 53% on 600 mg versus 50% on placebo. Bilirubin in the urine, high uric acid and raised AST (a liver enzyme) were more common on the drug.
   - An earlier open-label trial in 16 patients (PMID 33667488) showed the drug was hitting its target in the gut: phosphorylated STAT3 fell.
   - So exposure, target engagement and clinical efficacy were all shown, and no source names a safety reason for stopping.

2. **I-Mab moved the drug out of its core business before the results came in.** I-Mab's 20-F for 2021 says that in September 2020 it handed the rights to I-Mab Hangzhou, an affiliate, for the "continued development of selected biologics assets that are unessential to our immuno-oncology focus, i.e., olamkicept…".
   - In May 2022, rights outside Greater China and Korea were consolidated with Ferring under a new licence and cell-line agreement (20-F for 2022).
   - In April 2024 I-Mab closed the sale of its Greater China assets and business operations (20-F for 2023).
   - I-Mab's 20-F for 2024, filed 2025-04-03, says: "To our knowledge, TJBio Hangzhou has ceased the development of olamkicept."
   - Its mid-2025 6-K says I-Mab is no longer party to any olamkicept licence with Ferring.

3. **Ferring still has the drug, but no Phase 3 has started.** In 2024 Ferring ran two Phase 1 studies in healthy volunteers (NCT06298032, and NCT06515834 in Japanese men). They tested doses up to 2400 mg "to support the clinical development program", on the hypothesis that higher doses give greater clinical improvement. Both are completed. Ferring's current pipeline page lists olamkicept for ulcerative colitis at Phase 1, trials completed. ClinicalTrials.gov shows no Phase 2b or Phase 3 registered as of October 2026.

**Why F8:**
- The sponsor of the entry trial dropped the asset as non-core.
- The company that took it over, TJBio Hangzhou, then stopped developing it.
- Global rights changed hands, and Ferring restarted dose-finding at Phase 1.

**Codes I considered and rejected:**
- **F7 (trial design or power):** Ferring's return to Phase 1 at higher doses, after 300 mg failed and 600 mg gave a modest effect, hints the dose was never fully worked out. No source says this is why Phase 3 did not start.
- **not_a_failure:** Ferring still lists the drug, but there has been no trial activity since November 2024.

Websearch was unavailable (session limit reached), so these findings come from ClinicalTrials.gov, PubMed, SEC EDGAR and the Ferring website, fetched directly.

outcome_summary:
Vepdegestrant (ARV-471/PF-07850327) is an oral PROTAC that degrades the estrogen receptor (ESR1). It entered the clinic in the Arvinas Phase 1/2 trial NCT04072952, which started on 2019-09-22 and is now completed. Its Part B primary endpoint was clinical benefit rate. Pfizer started the Phase 3 VERITAC-2 trial (NCT05654623) on 2023-03-03, inside the four-year window, comparing 200 mg once daily against fulvestrant in 624 patients who had already received a CDK4/6 inhibitor.

VERITAC-2 had two primary endpoints, and the result was mixed:
- In the 270 patients with ESR1 mutations, progression-free survival by blinded independent central review was 5.0 vs 2.1 months (HR 0.58, P<0.001), so this endpoint was met.
- In the full randomized population it was 3.8 vs 3.6 months (HR 0.83, P=0.07), so this endpoint was not met (NEJM 2025, PMID 40454645).

The NDA was received on 2025-06-05. FDA approved the drug as VEPPANU (NDA 219835, a Type 1 new molecular entity) on 2026-05-01. The label covers adults with ER+/HER2-, ESR1-mutated advanced or metastatic breast cancer, detected by an FDA-authorized test, whose disease progressed after at least one line of endocrine therapy. openFDA now lists Rigel Pharmaceuticals as the NDA sponsor. The program advanced and was approved for this disease, so it is not a failure. The approval is limited to the ESR1-mutant subgroup because the all-comers endpoint missed.

Its breast cancer PheCodes 174 and 174.1 (GWAS Catalog GCST90435600 and GCST90435601) carry the ESR1 credible set (lead rs910416, p=8.7e-14, SuSiE-inf), where Open Targets gives ESR1 an L2G of 0.819.
evidence.notes: (1) Target and action: vepdegestrant (ARV-471) is an oral PROTAC degrader of estrogen receptor alpha (ESR1). It induces at least 90% degradation of wild-type and mutant ER (Gough et al., Clin Cancer Res 2024, PMID 38819400; Arvinas authors). A pre-entry abstract exists: SABCS 2018, P5-04-18, Cancer Res 79(4 Suppl), titled 'ARV-471, an oral estrogen receptor PROTAC degrader...'. Only the DOI redirect confirmed it; the page itself returned 403. (2) Disease: NCT04072952 (sponsor Arvinas, collaborator Pfizer; Phase 1/2; actual start 2019-09-22, matching the entry date) enrolled ER+/HER2- locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer. That is a subtype of MONDO:0007254 breast cancer, so the mapping holds. (3) Claim: both studyLocusIds in our rows resolve in the Open Targets GraphQL API. They are credible sets from GCST90435600 (PheCode 174) and GCST90435601 (PheCode 174.1), both from PMID 30104761 with publication date 2018-08-13. ESR1 is the top L2G gene in each at 0.819, followed by SYNE1 at 0.44. Two other credible sets from the same paper sit in the 0.70-0.74 range. In Open Targets these are the earliest breast cancer credible sets for ESR1 with L2G of at least 0.8. Earlier GWAS at the 6q25.1/ESR1 locus score lower: Zheng 2009 (PMID 19219042) 0.08, Siddiq 2012 0.73, Michailidou 2015 0.735 and Michailidou 2017 (PMID 29059683) 0.786, which is just under the threshold. So the claim passes only narrowly, at 0.819 against a cutoff of 0.8. Caveats: the L2G score and the SuSiE-inf fine-mapping are computed after the fact by the current Open Targets release and did not exist in 2018. The GWAS Catalog accessions are a later curation of the SAIGE summary statistics. The paper itself is a statistical-methods paper that ran a PheWAS of more than 1,400 UK Biobank phenotypes. The underlying association data were public in August 2018, about 13 months before Phase 2 entry. The ESR1 breast cancer locus had been known from GWAS since 2009. (4) Sponsor authorship: the authors are from the University of Michigan, Vanderbilt and NTNU, with no Arvinas or Pfizer authors. outcome_summary:
Recaticimab (SHR-1209) is Jiangsu Hengrui's long-acting anti-PCSK9 monoclonal antibody.

Phase 2 entry is confirmed. The industry-sponsored Phase 1b/2 trial NCT03944109 (n=110, on a stable statin) started on 2019-06-20 and finished on 2020-12-22. The BMC Medicine 2022 paper reports that it met its primary endpoint: compared with placebo, LDL-C fell by 48–60% across regimens given every 4, 8 or 12 weeks, with no serious adverse events.

The program advanced within four years. Three Hengrui Phase 3 trials started in 2021:
- REMAIN-3, NCT04844125, in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia: started 2021-04-14.
- REMAIN-1, NCT04849000, monotherapy: started 2021-04-23.
- REMAIN-2, NCT04885218, add-on to statins: started 2021-07-30.

REMAIN-1 and REMAIN-2, published in JACC in November 2024, both met their primary LDL-C endpoints (p<0.0001). Against placebo, LDL-C fell by about 45–53% in REMAIN-1 and by about 53–62% in REMAIN-2, with safety similar to placebo.

According to the Adis "First Approval" review (Drugs, 2025), China's drug regulator first approved recaticimab on 8 January 2025. The approval covers primary hypercholesterolemia (heterozygous familial and non-familial) and mixed dyslipidemia, either with statins or, in non-familial disease, as monotherapy. I found no FDA approval or US filing. The "approved" status therefore rests on the Chinese approval, not an FDA one.

This is not a failure. The web-search budget was used up, so I could not check a Hengrui press release directly. The approval date comes from the Adis review.

GWAS Catalog GCST90435754, trait "Hyperlipidemia (PheCode 272.1)", MONDO_0021187.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: the Hengrui phase 1b/2 paper (Xu M et al., BMC Med 2022, PMID 35039035) describes recaticimab (SHR-1209) as "a humanized monoclonal antibody against PCSK9" that lowers LDL-C. Lamb 2025 (Drugs, PMID 40545518) describes it as a humanized IgG1 that targets PCSK9. Both papers postdate phase 2 entry, but they establish the mechanism, which fits a PCSK9 binder/neutralizer.

(2) Entry trial: NCT03944109 (SHR-1209-102), sponsored by Jiangsu HengRui. It is a phase Ib/II randomized, placebo-controlled study in hyperlipidemia patients on stable statin therapy (LDL-C >=2.6 mmol/L). Its listed condition is "Hyperlipidemia", and the actual start date of 2019-06-20 matches phase2_entry. The disease mapping is correct.

(3) Claim: the Open Targets GraphQL API shows both studyLocusIds come from GWAS Catalog study GCST90435754, the SAIGE UK Biobank GWAS of Hyperlipidemia PheCode 272.1 (35,844 cases and 373,034 controls; PMID 30104761). The study maps to MONDO_0021187, the same disease as the case.
- Credible set 1ab08473 has lead variant rs11591147 (1_55039974_G_T), a PCSK9 missense variant at codon 46 per Ensembl VEP. Its p-value is 3.2e-24, fine-mapped with SuSiE-inf, and it gives PCSK9 an L2G of 0.946 (the only L2G row).
- Credible set cdcb1fce has lead variant rs34232196, an intergenic variant near PCSK9, with p = 1.6e-13. It gives PCSK9 an L2G of 0.829 (BSND scores 0.161).
- Both scores are >=0.8, so the claim holds.

(4) Timing: the paper was published online 2018-08-13 (print September 2018). That is about 10 months before phase 2 entry on 2019-06-20. The paper states that SAIGE summary statistics for all 1,403 PheCodes were released publicly and shown on the Michigan PheWeb, so the association data existed before entry.

Caveat: the credible set and L2G scores themselves are retrospective Open Targets computations. The GWAS Catalog files for GCST90435754 are dated 2024-07-31 (metadata) and 2025-01/02 (files). This analysis did not exist in 2019, but the claim is worded around the study's publication date.

(5) Sponsor authorship: all authors are at the University of Michigan, Vanderbilt and NTNU, and the paper declares no competing financial interests. No Hengrui authors.

The PCSK9-LDL genetic link itself is much older, but this check only covers the credible set named in the claim. WebSearch was unavailable (session search budget exhausted), so all facts come from direct API and PubMed/EuropePMC queries.

evidence_source: Germain M et al., "Meta-analysis of 65,734 individuals identifies TSPAN15 and SLC44A2 as two susceptibility loci for venous thromboembolism", Am J Hum Genet 2015;96(4):532-42, epub 2015-03-12 (PMID 25772935, GWAS Catalog GCST002808). Open Targets credible set 903e8e17ad2374b8f7ec99bf659a1b36 sits at lead variant rs1799963 (F2 G20210A, 11:46739505) and gives F2 an L2G score of 0.836.
outcome_summary: Ichorcumab (JNJ-64179375 / JNJ-9375) is a human IgG4 antibody that binds exosite 1 on thrombin. Janssen's first and only Phase 2 trial in VTE prevention was TEXT-TKR (NCT03251482), which started 2017-11-13. In it, 308 patients having knee replacement got a single post-operative IV dose (0.3-1.8 mg/kg) or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily. The drug was engaging its target: thrombin time lengthened with dose. But it did worse than apixaban on the primary efficacy endpoint, total VTE on venography: 59/190 (31.1%) on the antibody versus 6/49 (12.2%) on apixaban (OR 3.2, P=.011). Higher doses did not help. Bleeding was similar and there were no major bleeds. The authors call it "safe but less effective than apixaban". The JTH editorial reports that because of these results, Part 2 of the trial (the dose-response study) was never started. It also gives possible reasons: blocking exosite 1 only weakly inhibits thrombin; the drug was given after surgery, so it may not stop clots that have already formed; and knee surgery exposes a lot of tissue factor, while the rat shunt model that showed efficacy is driven by contact activation. ClinicalTrials.gov and the EU register show no later trial in any indication, so the program stopped after Phase 2 for efficacy. I found no company press release or SEC filing announcing a discontinuation; 'stopped' rests on the missing Part 2 and the absence of any later trial. The failure code is F2: the target was hit (thrombin time prolonged) but the biology did not carry over to the clinic, with timing and tissue context as the likely causes.

Open Targets credible set 903e8e17ad2374b8f7ec99bf659a1b36 sits at lead variant rs1799963 (F2 G20210A, 11:46739505) and gives F2 an L2G score of 0.836.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: JNJ-64179375 (JNJ-9375, ichorcumab) is a recombinant human IgG4 monoclonal antibody that binds the exosite I region of alpha-thrombin, which F2 encodes (KD 0.8 nM). It prolongs TT, ECT, PT and aPTT, and blocks thrombin-induced platelet aggregation (Janssen, JPET 2019, PMID 31451508; Wilson et al., Cardiovasc Res 2019, PMID 30184110). A 2017 review, PMID 28952381, calls ichorcumab a parenteral thrombin inhibitor. So "F2 inhibitor" is correct. It inhibits substrate binding at exosite 1 rather than the catalytic site, and these mechanism papers are dated after Phase 2 entry, but the mechanism does not depend on timing.

(2) Disease: NCT03251482 (TEXT-TKR, Janssen R&D, actual start 2017-11-13, which matches the recorded Phase 2 entry date) lists the condition "VTE Prophylaxis With Anticoagulation After Total Knee Replacement Surgery". Its Part 2 primary endpoint is total VTE (DVT on venography or symptomatic, PE, or death). Mapping to venous thromboembolism (MONDO:0005399) is appropriate. The trial population is post-surgical prophylaxis, not general VTE.

(3) Claim: confirmed with the Open Targets GraphQL API. Credible set 903e8e17... (GCST002808, Germain 2015, trait "Venous thromboembolism", PICS, p=2e-9, rs1799963) gives F2 L2G 0.836. Credible set d576e001... (GCST003390, Hinds DA et al., Hum Mol Genet 2016, epub 2016-02-09, PMID 26908601, self-reported "Thrombosis" in 23andMe, mapped to VTE, DVT and PE among other traits, p=1e-24, rs1799963) gives F2 L2G 0.873. The Germain 2015 abstract says F2 was one of nine loci at genome-wide significance. Across the GWAS Catalog v2 associations for rs1799963, the earliest VTE-type study is Germain 2015, followed by Hinds 2016 and Klarin 2017 (GCST004256, also before entry). Open Targets lists no F2 VTE credible set from an earlier publication. Caveat: the L2G score is computed retrospectively by the current Open Targets model. What existed before entry is the GWAS association itself, not the 0.8 score. The F2 G20210A to venous thrombosis link is much older in candidate-gene form (Poort et al., Blood 1996, PMID 8916933), but that study is not a GWAS.

(4) Timing: both GWAS papers (2015-03-12 and 2016-02-09) predate the 2017-11-13 Phase 2 start.

(5) Sponsor: neither GWAS has an author affiliated with Janssen or J&J. Germain 2015 is an academic consortium paper with one Novo Nordisk affiliation. Hinds 2016 has 23andMe and Pfizer affiliations. Clinical outcome was not assessed or used.
