But it did worse than apixaban on the primary efficacy endpoint, total VTE on venography: 59/190 (31.1%) on the antibody versus 6/49 (12.2%) on apixaban (OR 3.2, P=.011). Higher doses did not help. Bleeding was similar and there were no major bleeds. The authors call it "safe but less effective than apixaban". The JTH editorial reports that because of these results, Part 2 of the trial (the dose-response study) was never started. It also gives possible reasons: blocking exosite 1 only weakly inhibits thrombin; the drug was given after surgery, so it may not stop clots that have already formed; and knee surgery exposes a lot of tissue factor, while the rat shunt model that showed efficacy is driven by contact activation. ClinicalTrials.gov and the EU register show no later trial in any indication, so the program stopped after Phase 2 for efficacy. I found no company press release or SEC filing announcing a discontinuation; 'stopped' rests on the missing Part 2 and the absence of any later trial. The failure code is F2: the target was hit (thrombin time prolonged) but the biology did not carry over to the clinic, with timing and tissue context as the likely causes.

failure_second.reasoning:
The program is ichorcumab (JNJ-64179375 / JNJ-9375), a monoclonal antibody against thrombin exosite 1, developed by Janssen to prevent VTE. The Phase 2 entry trial was NCT03251482 (TEXT-TKR), started 2017-11-13.

**What the trial was.** It was a double-blind, double-dummy study in 308 patients having elective total knee replacement. Patients got a single postoperative IV infusion of 0.3, 0.6, 1.2 or 1.8 mg/kg, or apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily. Efficacy was judged by mandatory venography.

**Efficacy (CT.gov posted results, mITT).**

| Arm | VTE events |
|---|---|
| 0.3 mg/kg | 10/30 |
| 0.6 mg/kg | 9/33 |
| 1.2 mg/kg | 9/30 |
| 1.8 mg/kg | 31/97 |
| Apixaban | 6/49 |

The published paper (Weitz et al., J Thromb Haemost 2019, PMID 31529590) pools the antibody arms: 59/190 (31.1%) vs 12.2% on apixaban, odds ratio 3.2, P=.011. It reports "no evidence of improved efficacy with higher JNJ-9375 doses."

**Safety.** It was not the problem. There were no major bleeds in any arm, and the paper concludes the drug "was safe but less effective than apixaban."

**Why the program stopped.** CT.gov's participant-flow note says the sponsor dropped the planned dose-response Part 2 after Part 1 "as there was sufficient data to make a determination of efficacy." No later trials of JNJ-64179375 are registered; the registry lists only two Phase 1 studies and this Phase 2.

**Engagement was shown but did not translate.** The trial paper says efficacy failed "despite dose-dependent thrombin time prolongation." The authors suggest this "may reflect weak thrombin inhibition or inability of JNJ-9375 to attenuate the growth of thrombi that formed before drug administration."

The JTH editorial (Meijers & Middeldorp, PMID 31797543, PMC6916307) gives three possible reasons:
1. The drug may be less potent because it binds only exosite I, not thrombin's catalytic site.
2. It was given after surgery, whereas the preclinical models pretreated before a clot formed, so it may not stop an existing clot from growing.
3. The rat AV-shunt model is driven mainly by contact activation, so it does not represent the tissue-factor-rich setting of knee surgery.

**Why F2.** These reasons are partial inhibition, wrong timing and wrong tissue context, which is what F2 describes: engagement shown, biology did not translate.
- **Not F1:** thrombin time rose with dose, so the drug clearly reached and hit its target.
- **Not F4:** thrombin time is a pharmacodynamic engagement readout, not a surrogate endpoint. The clinical endpoint (venographic VTE) was measured directly and failed.
- **Not F5/F6:** no toxicity.
- **Not F8:** no commercial reason is cited.
- **F7 (postoperative dosing as a design choice)** is a weaker alternative. The sources frame timing as a biological limit of the mechanism, not as an underpowered or badly designed trial.

**Caveat.** I found no company press release or SEC filing that formally announces discontinuation. My web search budget was used up, so I could not check J&J pipeline disclosures. The stop decision rests on the CT.gov sponsor note and the published trial.

Cinpanemab (BIIB054) is Biogen's human-derived monoclonal antibody that binds mainly aggregated extracellular alpha-synuclein. Its Phase 2 SPARK trial (NCT03318523, Biogen) started on 2018-01-10. It enrolled 357 people with early Parkinson's disease and randomized them to placebo or 250, 1250 or 3500 mg IV every 4 weeks.

**Primary endpoint not met.** The endpoint was change in MDS-UPDRS total score at weeks 52 and 72. At week 52 the adjusted differences from placebo were -0.3, +0.5 and +0.1 points (P = 0.90, 0.80 and 0.97). The week-72 comparisons also showed nothing. Secondary endpoints and DaT-SPECT imaging did not differ from placebo. The trial was stopped after the week-72 interim analysis for lack of efficacy (Lang et al., NEJM 2022).

**Discontinuation.** The CT.gov record's whyStopped field says development for Parkinson's was discontinued because SPARK missed its primary and secondary endpoints. Biogen announced this in February 2021 in its Q4 2020 8-K press release and FY2020 10-K. It also wrote the BIIB054 IPR&D asset down to zero with a $75.4M impairment. No Phase 3 trial or approval followed, and CT.gov lists no other later trials.

**Why F2.** The program did show target engagement. A Biogen 2025 JPET paper found dose- and time-dependent cinpanemab–alpha-synuclein complexes in CSF from the Phase 1 trial. Phase 2 doses were chosen to keep 50% to over 90% of the target bound in brain interstitial fluid (CPT:PSP 2020). Even so, the SPARK biomarker analysis (Neurology 2024) found no treatment effect on CSF alpha-synuclein seeding, total alpha-synuclein, NfL, DaT-SPECT or MRI. So engagement was shown but the biology did not translate, and none of the downstream markers moved.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: cinpanemab (BIIB054), Biogen's human-derived anti-alpha-synuclein monoclonal antibody, tested in early Parkinson disease. The Phase 2 trial was SPARK (NCT03318523), which started 2018-01-10.

Why it did not advance: the drug had no efficacy. Biogen dropped the program for that reason, not for a business reason.
- The ClinicalTrials.gov record lists SPARK as TERMINATED. The reason given there is that SPARK "did not meet it's primary outcome measure for year 1 and failed to meet secondary outcome measures resulting in the development of BIIB054 (cinpanemab) for Parkinson's disease to be discontinued."
- Biogen's Q4 2020 earnings release (SEC 8-K exhibit 99.1, 2021-02-03) and its 2020 10-K both say: "In February 2021 we announced that we discontinued development of BIIB054 (cinpanemab) ... as our Phase 2 SPARK study did not meet its primary or secondary endpoints". Biogen also wrote the asset down by about $75.4M.
- The NEJM paper (Lang et al. 2022, PMID 35921450) reports 357 participants randomized to placebo or 250, 1250 or 3500 mg IV every 4 weeks. Change in MDS-UPDRS total score at week 52 was 10.8 points on placebo and 10.5, 11.3 and 10.9 on the three doses (P = 0.90, 0.80 and 0.97). Nothing differed at week 72, and DaT-SPECT showed no difference. The trial was stopped for lack of efficacy after the week 72 interim analysis. The most common adverse events were headache, nasopharyngitis and falls, so safety did not drive the decision.

Why F2 (engagement shown, biology did not translate) and not F1 (engagement never shown):
1. Exposure was shown. The posted SPARK results show serum BIIB054 rising with dose and holding steady through week 120 (week 52 pre-dose means of about 47, 232 and 787 for the three doses). Anti-drug antibodies were near zero (1.8% in one arm only).
2. Engagement in blood was shown. The Phase 1 trial (Brys et al., Mov Disord 2019, PMID 31211448) found BIIB054–alpha-synuclein complexes in plasma, "almost completely saturated" in every PD participant. The CSF-to-serum ratio was 0.13–0.56%.
3. Engagement in the CNS was shown, though only in Phase 1 samples. Using crosslinking on Phase 1 CSF (JPET 2025, PMID 39892989), researchers found dose- and time-dependent drug–alpha-synuclein complexes at doses of 15 mg/kg or more, from PD patients as well as healthy volunteers. They describe this as evidence the drug "had engaged its target at the desired site of action". SPARK's 1250 and 3500 mg doses are likely at or above 15 mg/kg, but that is my inference from body weight; no source states it.
4. Despite that binding, the SPARK biomarker paper (Neurology 2024, PMID 38315945) found "no statistically significant changes from baseline ... between treatment groups and placebo across biomarker measures". Those measures were DaT-SPECT, MRI atrophy, CSF and plasma total alpha-synuclein, alpha-synuclein seeding (99% of seed-positive participants stayed positive at week 52) and NfL.

So the antibody reached its target and bound alpha-synuclein, but clearing extracellular aggregated alpha-synuclein did not change disease biology or clinical progression. That is a failed hypothesis, which is F2.

Caveats:
- The CSF engagement data come from Phase 1 single-dose samples, not from SPARK. Binding to aggregates in brain tissue was never measured directly. CNS exposure is low (CSF about 0.1–0.6% of serum), and a modelling paper (Sci Rep 2023, PMID 37658103) predicts only 1–2% engagement of monomeric alpha-synuclein in the synaptic cleft, though it predicts high engagement of aggregated alpha-synuclein. Someone who discounts the CSF data could argue for F1.
- Two other codes are speculative and no primary source supports them: F3 (patients enrolled too late, with intracellular pathology already established) and F7 (52 weeks of MDS-UPDRS may be insensitive). I did not use them. A secondary review (PMID 42459575) says SPARK reduced CSF alpha-synuclein. The primary Neurology paper does not support that, so I disregarded it.
- I could not open the full text of the NEJM or Neurology papers (HTTP 403), so the figures above come from their abstracts, the posted trial results and the SEC filings.

claim: Human germline genetics established, before the program entered Phase 2, a mechanism for this target in this disease that the drug's action opposes (e.g. risk variants raise the gene's function and the drug lowers it, or loss-of-function variants are protective and the drug lowers function, or loss-of-function causes the disease and the drug raises function).
evidence_source: Bell DW et al., "Inherited susceptibility to lung cancer may be associated with the T790M drug resistance mutation in EGFR", Nat Genet 2005;37(12):1315-6 (PMID 16258541, Massachusetts General Hospital). It reports a family with several cases of NSCLC and germline transmission of EGFR T790M. Vikis H et al., Cancer Res 2007 (PMID 17510392), showed that germline T790M is an allele with enhanced kinase activity that gives cells a growth advantage.
outcome_summary:
Aumolertinib (HS-10296/almonertinib; Hansoh) entered industry-sponsored Phase 2 in NSCLC through the Phase 1/2 APOLLO trial NCT02981108, which started 2017-05-08. That trial's Phase 2 part had ORR as its primary endpoint and enrolled 244 T790M+ patients. Within 4 years the program reached Phase 3: AENEAS (NCT03849768) started 2019-02-01. It met its primary endpoint of investigator-assessed PFS versus gefitinib: 19.3 vs 9.9 months, HR 0.46, 95% CI 0.36-0.60, P<.0001 (JCO 2022, PMID 35580297). China's NMPA approved Ameile on 2020-03-17 for T790M+ NSCLC after prior EGFR-TKI therapy, and the drug remains marketed in China. Many further Phase 3 trials are listed, including adjuvant, post-chemoradiation and combination studies.

Outside China the path was rockier, but these setbacks were regulatory or partner decisions, not efficacy or safety findings. EQRx licensed ex-China rights in July 2020. In November 2022 it said the FDA would not accept an interim monotherapy comparison and pushed a US filing to 2027, contingent on a Phase 3b against osimertinib (NCT05493501). EQRx terminated that trial and gave notice on 2023-08-01 that it was ending the license as part of a pipeline wind-down tied to its merger with Revolution Medicines. The CT.gov record says the trial was stopped for corporate reasons, "not related to any efficacy or safety issues."

The EU granted approval (Aumseqa) on 2026-02-12 for first-line EGFR ex19del/L858R and for T790M+ NSCLC, according to Hansoh's press release. Secondary reports say the European Commission revoked that authorisation on 2026-09-25 on a procedural, data-exclusivity issue (referencing osimertinib data) and that Hansoh resubmitted in late September 2026; this was not checked against a primary EC/EMA document.

The FDA has not approved the drug. Overall the program advanced and is approved for this disease in China, so this is not a failure.

Vikis H et al., Cancer Res 2007 (PMID 17510392), showed that germline T790M is an allele with enhanced kinase activity that gives cells a growth advantage.
evidence.notes: (1) Target and action: ChEMBL CHEMBL4761468 lists aumolertinib (HS-10296/almonertinib) as an EGFR (erbB1) INHIBITOR. Its reference, Yang JC et al. J Thorac Oncol 2020 (PMID 32916310), calls it a third-generation irreversible-class EGFR TKI that targets EGFR-sensitizing and T790M mutations. The drug's direction is to lower EGFR function. (2) Entry trial: NCT02981108 (HS-10296-12-01, sponsored by Jiangsu Hansoh) is a Phase 1/2 study in locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC. Patients had progressed on a prior EGFR TKI, and the expansion and extension cohorts required T790M-positive tumours. It started 2017-05-08, which matches the recorded phase2_entry. The disease mapping to MONDO:0005233 is correct. (3) The claim holds through a gain-of-function mechanism. Germline EGFR T790M segregated with NSCLC in a family (Bell 2005), and the allele has enhanced kinase activity and phosphorylation that give a proliferative advantage (Vikis 2007, PMID 17510392). Germline carriers were confirmed in Oxnard 2012 (J Thorac Oncol, PMID 22588155) and Gazdar 2014 (J Thorac Oncol, PMID 24736066). An EGFR inhibitor that also hits T790M directly opposes this risk mechanism. ClinVar SCV000203888 (Laboratory for Molecular Medicine, last evaluated 2014-11-11, germline, Likely pathogenic for NSCLC) also predates entry. Caveats on our evidence rows: (a) The EVA row for RCV001823098 is dated 2001. That year appears to come from PMID 11423618 (Gorre 2001, Science, BCR-ABL imatinib resistance), which says nothing about EGFR germline risk, so the correct date for germline T790M is 2005. (b) The two 2013 EVA rows have flawed provenance. RCV000038381 (G719A) and RCV000038407 (S768I) are classic somatic activating mutations. The 2013 Laboratory for Molecular Medicine submissions behind them record origin as 'somatic'. The only 'germline' origin assertion comes from a 2022 University of Rochester curation with no assertion criteria. These rows are not real pre-2017 germline evidence. (c) Germline T790M is a rare familial susceptibility allele, and most of EGFR's role in NSCLC is somatic. The genetic support is real but narrow. Bell 2005 itself uses tentative wording ('may be associated'). Sponsor: Bell 2005 (MGH/Harvard), Vikis 2007 (Washington University and others), Oxnard 2012 and Gazdar 2014 have no Hansoh authors.

outcome_summary:
Phase 2 entry is confirmed. NCT02834936 is a Hengrui-sponsored, single-arm Phase 2 trial in HER2-mutant advanced NSCLC after platinum chemotherapy (n=60). Its actual start date is 2016-10-20. It met its goal: in the JCO 2020 report (PMID 32614698), the independent-review response rate (the primary endpoint) was 30%, median PFS was 6.9 months and median OS was 14.4 months.

The program reached Phase 3 within four years. Hengrui's PYRAMID-1 trial (NCT04447118, pyrotinib vs docetaxel, primary endpoint independent-review PFS, n=151) started on 2020-09-11. ClinicalTrials.gov dates are primary completion 2023-06-02 and study completion 2024-12-06, status COMPLETED. The record has no posted results. I found no PubMed paper, press release or conference report of the PYRAMID-1 efficacy results. A 2026 Frontiers review still says only that the trial "has completed enrollment".

Pyrotinib is not approved for NSCLC anywhere I could find. Hengrui's 2025 annual report lists its approved indications as breast cancer only. That report also leaves pyrotinib-NSCLC out of the 2026-2028 expected approvals, which list only a breast-cancer indication for pyrotinib.

The indication then disappears from Hengrui's pipeline tables:
- Hengrui's 2023, 2024 and 2025 annual reports list pyrotinib monotherapy for HER2-mutant non-squamous NSCLC (US/EU/APAC) in the pipeline table for marketed drugs. The latest of these is dated as of 2026-02-28.
- The 2026 half-year report's table, dated as of 2026-07-31, no longer lists it.

I therefore classify the program as stopped, de facto: no public discontinuation notice was found. No source gives a reason, so the stop reason is unknown. One possible factor, which no source links to the decision, is that Hengrui's own HER2 ADC, trastuzumab rezetecan, was approved in China in May 2025 for the same pretreated HER2-mutant NSCLC setting.

The failure code is not_a_failure, because the program reached Phase 3 within the four-year window.

evidence.earliest_source: Bell DW et al., "Inherited susceptibility to lung cancer may be associated with the T790M drug resistance mutation in EGFR", Nature Genetics 2005;37(12) (epub 2005-10-30), PMID 16258541. For ERBB2, the earliest germline source is Yamamoto H et al., JNCI 2014 (PMID 24317180).
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: pyrotinib (SHR1258) is an irreversible EGFR/HER2 dual (pan-ErbB) tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Sources: Hengrui's discovery paper (Eur J Pharm Sci 2017, PMID 28115222) and the Phase I JCO 2017 paper (PMID 28498781). The 2016 Hengrui co-authored metabolism paper (PMID 27541626) already called it an irreversible TKI for HER2-positive breast cancer, so the mechanism was public before entry. Both targets are inhibited, as recorded.

(2) Disease: the entry trial NCT02834936 (sponsor Jiangsu HengRui, Phase 2, start 2016-10-20 ACTUAL, matching the recorded entry date) enrolled stage IIIB/IV NSCLC with a centrally confirmed HER2 mutation. That fits the NSCLC mapping (MONDO:0005233).

(3) Claim: for EGFR, Bell et al. 2005 (MGH/Harvard) described a family with NSCLC in which germline EGFR T790M was transmitted. The authors say this implicates altered EGFR signalling in inherited susceptibility. Godin-Heymann 2007 (Cancer Res, PMID 17671201) showed T790M is gain-of-function: the effect is modest alone and dramatic in cis with activating mutations. Germline T790M is therefore a function-raising risk variant, and the drug inhibits EGFR, so the drug's action opposes it. Ohtsuka 2011 (JCO, PMID 21172876) added familial germline EGFR V843I. For ERBB2, which is the target most relevant to this HER2-mutant trial, Yamamoto 2014 (JNCI, PMID 24317180) found a germline activating HER2 G660D transmembrane mutation in familial lung adenocarcinoma. All of this predates October 2016.

Caveats: (a) The evidence comes from rare families. Bell's title is hedged ("may be associated"). ClinVar's LMM submission (SCV000203888, 2015) says penetrance is not established and calls the variant "likely pathogenic". (b) Most EGFR and ERBB2 involvement in NSCLC is somatic. (c) Several of our database rows are not germline evidence or are misdated. The ERBB2 uniprot_variants 2004 rows match Stephens et al. 2004 Nature (PMID 15457249), which reported somatic tumour mutations. The EVA row RCV001823098 (EGFR c.2369C>T T790M vs lung cancer, germline pathogenic) is dated 2001 in our database, but it is a recent ClinVar aggregate with an accession number around 2021. The germline evidence behind it starts with Bell 2005, so the 2001 date is wrong; the mechanism label's 2005 date is right. I did not verify the 1998 uniprot_literature rows.

(5) Sponsor: Bell 2005 (MGH) and Yamamoto 2014 (Okayama University) have no Hengrui authors.

outcome.advance_event: PYRAMID-1 (NCT04447118) started on 2020-09-11, about 3.9 years after Phase 2 entry on 2016-10-20. It is a Hengrui-sponsored, randomized, open-label Phase 3 trial of pyrotinib versus docetaxel in advanced non-squamous NSCLC with a HER2 exon 20 mutation after platinum chemotherapy.
outcome.summary:
Phase 2 entry is confirmed. NCT02834936 is a Hengrui-sponsored, single-arm Phase 2 trial in HER2-mutant advanced NSCLC after platinum chemotherapy (n=60). Its actual start date is 2016-10-20. It met its goal: in the JCO 2020 report (PMID 32614698), the independent-review response rate (the primary endpoint) was 30%, median PFS was 6.9 months and median OS was 14.4 months.

The program reached Phase 3 within four years. Hengrui's PYRAMID-1 trial (NCT04447118, pyrotinib vs docetaxel, primary endpoint independent-review PFS, n=151) started on 2020-09-11. ClinicalTrials.gov dates are primary completion 2023-06-02 and study completion 2024-12-06, status COMPLETED. The record has no posted results. I found no PubMed paper, press release or conference report of the PYRAMID-1 efficacy results. A 2026 Frontiers review still says only that the trial "has completed enrollment".

Pyrotinib is not approved for NSCLC anywhere I could find. Hengrui's 2025 annual report lists its approved indications as breast cancer only. That report also leaves pyrotinib-NSCLC out of the 2026-2028 expected approvals, which list only a breast-cancer indication for pyrotinib.

The indication then disappears from Hengrui's pipeline tables:
- Hengrui's 2023, 2024 and 2025 annual reports list pyrotinib monotherapy for HER2-mutant non-squamous NSCLC (US/EU/APAC) in the pipeline table for marketed drugs. The latest of these is dated as of 2026-02-28.
- The 2026 half-year report's table, dated as of 2026-07-31, no longer lists it.

I therefore classify the program as stopped, de facto: no public discontinuation notice was found. No source gives a reason, so the stop reason is unknown. One possible factor, which no source links to the decision, is that Hengrui's own HER2 ADC, trastuzumab rezetecan, was approved in China in May 2025 for the same pretreated HER2-mutant NSCLC setting.

The failure code is not_a_failure, because the program reached Phase 3 within the four-year window.

outcome_summary:
LATTICE-CD (NCT03599622, IM011-023) was BMS's Phase 2 trial in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease. It started 2018-07-16, compared deucravacitinib 3 mg BID and 6 mg BID (plus a small 12 mg arm) with placebo, and enrolled 239 patients. The registry lists it as TERMINATED with the stated reason "lack of efficacy in the short term acute phase". It had two co-primary endpoints at week 12. (1) CDAI clinical remission was not met: placebo 28.3%, 3 mg 32.6% (p=0.58), 6 mg 21.4% (p=0.37). (2) Endoscopic response (SES-CD drop of at least 50%) was nominally significant only at 3 mg: 23.3% vs 8.3% (p=0.02). At 6 mg it was 16.7% (p=0.16). evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action. The Sotyktu FDA label (section 12.1) says deucravacitinib is an inhibitor of TYK2: it binds the regulatory domain and inhibits receptor-mediated TYK2 activation allosterically. Two BMS papers say the same: Wrobleski 2019 J Med Chem (PMID 31318208) and Burke 2019 Sci Transl Med (PMID 31341059). This matches 'TYK2 negative_modulator'.

(2) Entry trial. NCT03599622 (IM011-023, sponsor Bristol-Myers Squibb) is a Phase 2 placebo-controlled study of BMS-986165 in moderate to severe Crohn's disease. Its actual start date is 2018-07-16, the same as the recorded Phase 2 entry date. Its conditions are Crohn's disease and granulomatous colitis or enteritis, so mapping it to MONDO:0005011 is correct.

(3) Claim. Protective loss-of-function variants were established in Crohn disease before Phase 2 entry, and the drug lowers TYK2 function, so it matches the protective direction. The evidence in date order:
- Franke 2010 Nat Genet (PMID 21102463, PMC3299551) confirmed the 19p13 TYK2 locus for CD. Its lead SNP, rs12720356 (I684S), is a risk allele (OR 1.12), with no defined effect on TYK2 function.
- Diogo 2015 PLoS One (PMID 25849893) found P1104A (rs34536443) protective in IBD, not CD separately: OR 0.75, P=0.008, from 1,346 IBD cases. The authors call this 'suggestive' (P omnibus 0.005). The mechanism label's guess of 2015 as the protective year is therefore right for IBD but not specific to CD.
- Ellinghaus 2016 Nat Genet (online 14 Mar 2016, PMID 26974007, Table 1) reported TYK2 A928V (rs35018800) with OR(CD) 0.641. At that time A928V's loss of function was only reported or predicted.
- Dendrou 2016 Sci Transl Med (PMID 27807284, PMC5737835) meta-analysed 4,017 CD cases on Immunochip and found the rs34536443 minor allele protective 'across all of the diseases tested', including CD. Its CRISPR-edited HEK293T cells showed P1104A lowers TYK2 phosphorylation and pSTAT, while I684S does not. That second finding resolves the earlier I684S-risk discrepancy.
- Huang 2017 Nature (PMID 28658209, PMC5511510) fine-mapped a CD signal to rs34536443, TYK2 P1104A (posterior 0.649).
The risk-allele mechanism stays 'unknown', which matches the label. The protective loss-of-function mechanism is well supported.

(4) Timing. Dendrou (Nov 2016), Ellinghaus (Mar 2016), Diogo (Apr 2015) and Huang (Jun 2017) were all published before 2018-07-16.

(5) Sponsor authorship. No BMS authors appear on the key genetics papers. Dendrou's authors are from Oxford, Cambridge and Genentech; Diogo's are academic plus Genentech; Huang is from the IIBDGC consortium. BMS authored only the drug-pharmacology papers, both from 2019.

I did not research or use the trial's outcome.

outcome.advance_event: None. failure_second.reasoning:
Program: deucravacitinib (BMS-986165), an allosteric TYK2 inhibitor, in moderate to severe Crohn's disease. Phase 2 entry was LATTICE-CD (NCT03599622, IM011-023), which started 2018-07-16.

What happened: The ClinicalTrials.gov record shows the trial as TERMINATED with whyStopped "Trial terminated because of lack of efficacy in the short term acute phase." The posted results:
- Week-12 clinical remission (CDAI<150), co-primary: placebo 28.3%, 3 mg BID 32.6% (p=0.58), 6 mg BID 21.4% (p=0.37). There was no dose response, and the higher dose was numerically worse than placebo.
- Week-12 endoscopic response, co-primary: 3 mg BID reached nominal significance (23.3% vs 8.3%, p=0.02); 6 mg BID did not (16.7%, p=0.16).

The peer-reviewed report (D'Haens et al., J Crohns Colitis 2025, PMID 40355364, PMC12137900) says the primary endpoints were not met, which led to early termination during maintenance. No new safety signals appeared, so toxicity was not the cause. BMS's 2022 10-K lists Sotyktu for Crohn's disease in its pipeline; the 2023 10-K no longer does. ClinicalTrials.gov lists no later Crohn's efficacy trial, only the LTE NCT04877990.

Why F2 and not F1:
- Exposure was documented in the trial: an interim PK analysis showed undifferentiated exposure between the 12 mg QD and BID arms, which is why the QD arm was dropped.
- Systemic target engagement was shown in Phase 1: dose-dependent inhibition of IL-12/IL-18-induced IFN-gamma and of IFN-alpha-regulated genes (PMID 36325947).
- The IBD doses were higher than the 6 mg QD dose that is effective and FDA-approved for psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis (openFDA label).
- An even higher dose (12 mg BID, IM011-127 in UC) also failed.
- The sponsor's authors say the reasons are "unclear." They suggest "TYK2 inhibition may not be an appropriate target for patients with IBD" and cite another TYK2 inhibitor (VTX958) failing in Crohn's disease.
- The accompanying editorial (Sharip, Raine, Noor, jjaf088) points to cytokine-network redundancy (IL-6, IL-17, other JAK/STAT signalling) compensating for TYK2 blockade.

So the drug engaged its target, but blocking TYK2 did not translate into clinical benefit in Crohn's disease.

Alternatives considered:
- F1 is the closest alternative. The authors concede that "our phase 2 studies did not further explore target engagement," and the editorial raises possibly suboptimal engagement in the mucosa from PK or tissue-penetration issues. Gut-tissue engagement was never measured, but systemic exposure and pathway engagement were established. Because higher doses and a second molecule also failed, a class or biology failure is more likely than an exposure failure.
- F7 (high placebo response) is less likely: the 6 mg dose was below placebo and there was no dose response.
- F4 does not fit: the endoscopic signal was weak and not consistent across doses.
- F8 does not fit: termination was explicitly for lack of efficacy.

Confidence: moderate. The coding between F2 and F1 is uncertain because no mucosal PD data were reported. The paper says a biomarker analysis is ongoing.

I did not modify any project files. I briefly saved the PMC full text to the scratchpad, then deleted it and streamed the content instead.

evidence_source: Suzuki T, ..., Trapnell BC. "Familial pulmonary alveolar proteinosis caused by mutations in CSF2RA." J Exp Med 2008;205(12):2703-10 (epub 27 Oct 2008), PMID 18955570. The same issue carries Martinez-Moczygemba M, ..., Huston DP, "Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis caused by deletion of the GM-CSFRalpha gene in the X chromosome pseudoautosomal region 1," J Exp Med 2008;205(12):2711-6, PMID 18955567.
outcome_summary:
Molgramostim is Savara's inhaled recombinant GM-CSF (Molgradex, now branded MOLBREEVI). Its first industry Phase 2 trial in autoimmune PAP was IMPALA (NCT02702180), a three-arm randomized placebo-controlled trial with 138 to 139 patients that started on 2016-03-21. The registry lists it as Phase 2, but Savara called it a pivotal Phase 3.

IMPALA missed its primary endpoint. The company's June 2019 topline said the change in A-aDO2 at week 24 was -4.6 mmHg versus placebo for continuous dosing (p=0.17). ClinicalTrials.gov results agree (LS mean -4.6, 95% CI -11.1 to 2.0, p=0.1688). Savara put the miss down to a stronger-than-expected placebo effect. Some secondary endpoints were positive: SGRQ improved by 7.6 points (p=0.01) and DLCO by 7.9% predicted (p=0.007). The later NEJM paper (2020; PMID 32897035) imputed invalid A-aDO2 values and reported p=0.03 for the primary endpoint. In October 2019 the FDA said in a Type C response that the data were not sufficient to support a BLA.

The Phase 3 extension IMPALA-X (NCT03482752) started on 2018-04-16, inside the 4-year window, and was terminated in January 2021 after the IMPALA results and regulator advice. Savara then ran a new pivotal Phase 3, IMPALA-2 (NCT04544293). It started on 2021-05-19 and switched the primary endpoint to DLCO. It met that endpoint in June 2024: +6.0% predicted at week 24 (p=0.0007), with SGRQ also significant.

Today the BLA is under FDA review. The FDA filed it in February 2026 with Priority Review, and the PDUFA date was extended to 2026-11-22 after a major amendment. The EMA validated the MAA in March 2026, and the UK MHRA validated an MAA in April 2026. A pediatric Phase 3 (NCT06431776) started on 2025-10-22. There is no approval yet: openFDA has no molgramostim record, and Savara has filed no approval 8-K. The program is still advancing, so the answer is not_a_failure. The IMPALA miss and the FDA feedback that followed (an endpoint and trial-design issue) delayed the pivotal Phase 3 by about two years. The program did not stop.

evidence.earliest_source: Suzuki T, ..., Trapnell BC. "Familial pulmonary alveolar proteinosis caused by mutations in CSF2RA." J Exp Med 2008;205(12):2703-10 (epub 27 Oct 2008), PMID 18955570. The same issue carries Martinez-Moczygemba M, ..., Huston DP, "Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis caused by deletion of the GM-CSFRalpha gene in the X chromosome pseudoautosomal region 1," J Exp Med 2008;205(12):2711-6, PMID 18955567.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: the ClinicalTrials.gov record for NCT02702180 calls molgramostim "recombinant human granulocyte macrophage-colony stimulating factor [rhGM-CSF]". Suzuki 2008 states that GM-CSF acts through a receptor made of a GM-CSF-Ralpha subunit (CSF2RA) and a GM-CSF-Rbeta subunit (CSF2RB). ChEMBL has no mechanism row for molgramostim (CHEMBL2109134), but its GM-CSF receptor target CHEMBL2364169 is listed as P15509 (CSF2RA) plus P32927 (CSF2RB). The other rhGM-CSF, sargramostim (CHEMBL1201670), is annotated against that target as an AGONIST. So "CSF2RA/CSF2RB agonist" is correct.
(2) Disease: NCT02702180 (IMPALA) is a Phase 2 randomised placebo-controlled trial sponsored by Savara Inc. Its actual start date is 2016-03-21, matching our entry date, and its condition is autoimmune PAP. Autoimmune PAP is a subtype of MONDO:0001437 "pulmonary alveolar proteinosis", so the mapping is acceptable.
(3) Claim: Suzuki 2008 shows that biallelic CSF2RA defects cause familial PAP: a 1.6-Mb deletion plus a G174R substitution that severely reduces GM-CSF binding and signalling. It concludes that "GM-CSF signaling is critical for surfactant homeostasis in humans". Martinez-Moczygemba 2008, published at the same time, shows PAP caused by deletion of CSF2RA. For CSF2RB, the first confirmed loss-of-function variants are Tanaka 2011 (J Med Genet, PMID 21075760; homozygous frameshift that abolishes STAT5 signalling) and Suzuki 2011 (Eur Respir J, PMID 21205713). Dirksen 1997 (J Clin Invest, PMID 9410898) reported only reduced beta-c expression, with no confirmed causal variant. So the pattern "loss of function causes disease, drug raises function" holds at the level of the pathway.
Caveat: the genetic evidence comes from hereditary PAP, where the receptor itself is defective, so supplying more ligand cannot fully fix it (Suzuki 2008 saw only partial rescue at high GM-CSF for G174R). The trial instead studied autoimmune PAP, where the receptor is intact and neutralising anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies are the cause. The genetics supports the pathway, not this exact patient population.
Data-quality flag: the genomics_england (PanelApp) rows are dated 1990, which is a placeholder or misdating. The CSF2RA–PAP link dates to 2008. I could not query the PanelApp API (non-JSON response).
(4) Both 2008 papers came out in Oct/Nov 2008, more than 7 years before Phase 2 entry on 2016-03-21.
(5) Not sponsor-authored. Suzuki 2008 is from Cincinnati Children's, funded by NIH/NHLBI/NCRR, and states "The authors have no conflicting financial interests". Martinez-Moczygemba 2008 is from Texas A&M/Baylor. Neither involves Savara or Serendex. The sponsor-history web search could not run because the search budget was exhausted, so Savara's corporate history is not independently verified here.

outcome.advance_event: Under the literal registry rule, the program advanced: IMPALA-X (NCT03482752), registered on ClinicalTrials.gov as a Phase 3 open-label safety extension of inhaled molgramostim in aPAP, started on 2018-04-16. That is about 2.1 years after the 2016-03-21 entry. Savara also described the entry trial, IMPALA (NCT02702180), as its "pivotal Phase 3" study, although the registry lists it as Phase 2. The caveat is that IMPALA-X was a rollover extension, and it was terminated after IMPALA's results and regulator advice. The randomized pivotal Phase 3, IMPALA-2 (NCT04544293), started on 2021-05-19, about 5.2 years after entry, which is outside the 4-year window. If the benchmark counts only pivotal or efficacy Phase 3 trials, this answer becomes "no".

evidence_source: Geisterfer-Lowrance AA, Kass S, Tanigawa G, Vosberg HP, McKenna W, Seidman CE, Seidman JG. 'A molecular basis for familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: a beta cardiac myosin heavy chain gene missense mutation.' Cell 1990;62(5):999-1006, PMID 1975517. It reports the germline MYH7 R403Q missense variant (ClinVar VCV000014087 / RCV000015143) segregating with familial HCM.
outcome_summary: The Phase 2 entry is confirmed. MyoKardia's open-label Phase 2 PIONEER-HCM (NCT02842242) tested MYK-461 in symptomatic obstructive HCM. It started in August 2016, finished in November 2017, and its primary endpoint was the change in post-exercise LVOT gradient at week 12. The drug advanced within four years: the pivotal Phase 3 EXPLORER-HCM (NCT03470545) started on 2018-05-29 and met its primary composite clinical-response endpoint (37% on mavacamten vs 17% on placebo, difference +19.4%, p=0.0005; Olivotto et al., Lancet 2020, PMID 32871100). The FDA approved Camzyos (mavacamten, NDA 214998, new molecular entity, orphan) on 2022-04-28 for adults with symptomatic NYHA class II-III obstructive HCM. Status: approved for the disease. The approval covers the obstructive subtype only. A separate Phase 3 in non-obstructive HCM, ODYSSEY-HCM (NCT05582395), is listed on ClinicalTrials.gov as TERMINATED; this answer does not say why, because no reason was verified. That trial does not change the outcome for this program. Not a failure.

evidence.earliest_source: Geisterfer-Lowrance AA, Kass S, Tanigawa G, Vosberg HP, McKenna W, Seidman CE, Seidman JG. 'A molecular basis for familial hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: a beta cardiac myosin heavy chain gene missense mutation.' Cell 1990;62(5):999-1006, PMID 1975517. It reports the germline MYH7 R403Q missense variant (ClinVar VCV000014087 / RCV000015143) segregating with familial HCM.
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action are confirmed. Green et al., Science 2016 (PMID 26912705, published Feb 2016, before Phase 2 entry) says MYK-461 'reduces contractility by decreasing the ATPase activity of the cardiac myosin heavy chain'. The FDA Camzyos label (2022) calls mavacamten 'an allosteric and reversible inhibitor selective for cardiac myosin'. It acts on cardiac myosin generally: the mouse efficacy work used alpha-MHC (Myh6) mutants. MYH7 (beta-cardiac MHC) is still the correct human ventricular target.

(2) The disease matches. NCT02842242 (PIONEER-HCM, MyoKardia, Phase 2, actual start 2016-08) enrolled symptomatic obstructive HCM patients (conditions 'Cardiomyopathy, Hypertrophic Obstructive'; LV wall >=15 mm; LVOT gradient >=30 mmHg at rest). That is a subset of HCM (MONDO:0005045).

(3) The claim is only partly supported. Germline genetics clearly showed before 2016 that dominant MYH7 missense variants cause HCM (Geisterfer-Lowrance 1990, Cell). The direction (gain of function, which an inhibitor opposes) did not come from germline genetics. It came from in-vitro and mouse functional studies, and those disagreed before entry:
- Showed enhanced function: Tyska 2000 Circ Res (PMID 10764406; mouse R403Q had 2.3x ATPase, 2.2x force and 1.6x sliding velocity); Palmiter 2000 (PMID 11227787; 'enhanced mechanical performance'); Sommese 2013 PNAS (PMID 23798412; human R453C had +50% intrinsic force but -30% ATPase and velocity).
- Showed reduced function: Cuda 1993 JCI (PMID 8514894; mutant beta-myosin moved actin slower); Nag 2015 Sci Adv (PMID 26601291), which calls R403Q 'the most debated HCM-causing mutation' with 'no consensus' on its mechanism and found a loss of contractility in human beta-cardiac R403Q.
- Spudich 2015 (PMID 25619247) offered increased power output only as a 'possible unifying hypothesis'.
- Green 2016 itself concedes that 'some in vitro studies ... are consistent with mutant sarcomeres exhibiting enhanced contractile power, others are not', and leans on the hyperdynamic clinical phenotype.
- The super-relaxed-state work cited in our mechanism label came after entry.

So causality predates entry, but the opposed-direction mechanism was a contested hypothesis in Aug 2016.

(4) Our database dates for the ClinVar rows are wrong:
- RCV000015143 (R403Q) is dated 1961. That year comes from Pare et al. 1961, Am J Med (PMID 13732753), a clinical description of the kindred, not genetic evidence. The variant-level evidence dates to 1990.
- RCV000015182 (MYH7 L1793P, an OMIM assertion with no assertion criteria) is dated 1971. That is Cancilla 1971, Neurology (PMID 4104682), a skeletal myopathy kindred. The variant was found in 2006 (Dye et al., PMID 16684601) in myosin storage myopathy. Its link to HCM is weak, and it is not good HCM evidence.

(5) Sponsor authorship: the 1990 paper came from the Seidman lab at Brigham and Women's / Harvard, 22 years before MyoKardia existed. The S-1 says MyoKardia was incorporated in June 2012 by Third Rock Ventures. However, C.E. Seidman and J.G. Seidman, and also J.A. Spudich and L.A. Leinwand (authors of the 2013–2015 functional papers), are disclosed as MyoKardia founders and shareholders in Green 2016. So the key paper is not sponsor-authored, but its authors later co-founded the sponsor.

(2) Disease is confirmed. NCT05940506 (KX0826-CN-1002, sponsor Suzhou Kintor) is a Phase II randomized, placebo-controlled trial of KX-826 tincture in adult Chinese men with AGA. (3) Claim is partly supported.
- The AR locus is firmly established for AGA by germline genetics well before 2020: Ellis 2001 (rs6152/StuI, p=4e-6), Hillmer 2005 in AJHG (etiological fraction 0.46), and GWAS.   - Sawaya & Shalita 1998: shorter CAG repeats (higher AR activity) in AGA. Small study, 48 men and 60 women.

Our mechanism_label lists protective evidence as "none_known" and misses this paper.
- Overall, the association is established, but the direction rests on small or indirect studies rather than a variant of defined function. That is why I answered partial rather than yes.

evidence_source: Diogo D et al., "TYK2 protein-coding variants protect against rheumatoid arthritis and autoimmunity, with no evidence of major pleiotropic effects on non-autoimmune complex traits", PLoS One 2015 Apr 7;10(4):e0122271 (PMID 25849893). outcome_summary:
The Phase 2 entry is confirmed. Pfizer started NCT03845517 (B7931028) on 2019-04-18. It was a Phase 2b, randomized, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial in active SLE (n=350), with 15, 30 or 45 mg once daily for 52 weeks. Primary completion was 2023-10-05.

The primary endpoint, SRI-4 at Week 52, was not met. Results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov:
- SRI-4 response was 64.6% on placebo, versus 57.4% at 15 mg, 69.7% at 30 mg and 66.3% at 45 mg.
- Risk differences versus placebo were -7.5, +5.2 and +1.7 percentage points.
- One-sided CMH p-values were 0.81, 0.22 and 0.40.

On 2023-11-27, Roivant and Priovant (an 8-K exhibit filed with the SEC) said the trial failed its primary endpoint. They blamed "the highest placebo response rate observed in any significant SLE study", which made it "not possible to truly assess the impact of the drug, or to establish sufficient differentiation from other therapies". They also said "we do not plan to progress the program in SLE."

No SLE Phase 3 was started within 4 years of Phase 2 entry, and none has started since. Development of brepocitinib continued in other diseases: a Phase 3 in dermatomyositis, a Phase 3 in uveitis, and Phase 2/3 trials in sarcoidosis and lichen planopilaris. Roivant's FY2025 10-K (May 2026) lists no SLE program for brepocitinib.

The stop reason is efficacy, since the primary endpoint failed. The failure code is F7 (trial design or power) because the sponsor's own explanation is an unusually high placebo response that kept the trial from showing a separation from placebo. This call is a judgement. The data can also be read as no meaningful drug effect, with active arms only about 2 to 5 points above placebo at the higher doses. evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action are confirmed. Pfizer's discovery paper (Fensome et al., J Med Chem 2018, PMID 30113844) names PF-06700841 (brepocitinib) as a dual TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor in its title and abstract. Inhibition lowers kinase function.

(2) Disease is confirmed. NCT03845517 is Pfizer's Phase 2b dose-ranging study of PF-06700841 at 15, 30 and 45 mg against placebo in active SLE. Its only listed condition is Systemic Lupus Erythematosus. The actual start date is 2019-04-18, which matches the recorded Phase 2 entry date.

(3) The claim holds for TYK2. Sigurdsson 2005 (AJHG, PMID 15657875) first reported a TYK2 association with SLE, and Hellquist 2009 (J Rheumatol, PMID 19567624) replicated it. Neither paper established which direction the variants act in. Before 2019 the direction was settled by four pieces of work:
- Couturier 2011 showed that the protective allele of P1104A (rs34536443 C) lowers TYK2 activity.
- Li 2013 showed that P1104A and I684S are catalytically impaired. They are hypomorphic rather than null: IFN-a/b signaling is rescued by the partner JAK.
- Diogo 2015 showed that the P1104A, A928V and I684S minor alleles protect against SLE.
- Dendrou 2016 (Sci Transl Med, PMID 27807284) found a protective homozygous loss-of-function effect at TYK2 across autoimmune disease.

So "loss-of-function is protective, and the drug lowers function" is supported. The Open Targets API confirms the database's credible sets:
- Bentham 2015 (Nat Genet, PMID 26502338; GCST003156): rs34536443 (P1104A) C allele beta -0.057, p = 2e-11, and rs12720356 (I684S) beta -0.051, p = 5e-9. Both are protective.
- Bentham 2015 (GCST003155): rs2304256, p = 4e-13.
- Morris 2016 (PMID 27399966): rs2304256.
- Langefeld 2017 (PMID 28714469): rs34725611.

The genetic evidence covers TYK2 only. Nothing in these rows backs a direction for JAK1, the drug's second target, in SLE.

(4) Every source listed was published between 2005 and 2017, all before the 2019-04-18 entry date.

(5) None of the key genetics papers has a Pfizer author:
- Diogo 2015: Brigham, Broad and Genentech authors. One author disclosed consulting fees from Pfizer, but is not a Pfizer employee.
- Dendrou 2016: Oxford and Genentech.
- Couturier 2011: academic, French-led.
- Li 2013: academic (Pasteur/Uppsala).

I did not look at the program's clinical outcome.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: brepocitinib (PF-06700841, a TYK2/JAK1 inhibitor) in systemic lupus erythematosus. It entered Phase 2 with NCT03845517, a Pfizer-sponsored Phase 2b study: dose-ranging, placebo-controlled, 52 weeks, n=350, start 2019-04-18, completed 2023-10-05.

What happened (from the ClinicalTrials.gov posted results):
- The primary endpoint, SRI-4 at week 52, was missed. Response rates were 64.6% on placebo, 57.4% on 15 mg, 69.7% on 30 mg and 66.3% on 45 mg. One-sided p-values were 0.81, 0.22 and 0.40.
- Secondary endpoints moved in the drug's favour at 30 and 45 mg but none reached significance:
  - BICLA: 43.8% placebo vs 52.5% and 53.3% (p=0.11 and 0.09)
  - LLDAS: 22.6% vs 35.1% and 34.1%
  - steroid taper: 26.4% vs 37.0% and 41.9%
- Safety did not drive the decision. Serious adverse events were 8, 4, 8 and 9 across the arms, and discontinuations for adverse events were 6, 2, 1 and 3.

Why it did not advance (from the Roivant/Priovant press release of 27 Nov 2023, SEC 8-K Ex. 99.1):
- The trial "did not meet its primary endpoint." The sponsor blamed "the highest placebo response rate observed in any significant SLE study, and as such it was not possible to truly assess the impact of the drug, or to establish sufficient differentiation from other therapies in lupus patients."
- The sponsor said "we do not plan to progress the program in SLE" and turned to non-infectious uveitis and dermatomyositis.
- Lupus is gone from Roivant's FY2024 10-K (filed 2024-05-30); a full-text search found no mention.

Coding: The trial did not separate drug from placebo because the placebo response was very high (SRI-4 64.6%). It was not powered for that, so it could not tell whether the drug worked. That fits F7 (trial design, comparator or power) best. Two limits:
- Exposure and target engagement were not measured in SLE. The trial reported no biomarker or pharmacodynamic outcomes, so true lack of efficacy (F2) cannot be ruled out.
- The placebo-response explanation is the sponsor's own reading.
The stated reason for dropping lupus ("not possible ... to establish sufficient differentiation from other therapies") also has a strategic side (F8). F7 is primary because the trigger was a failed primary endpoint driven by placebo response.

Note: no peer-reviewed full publication of the SLE Phase 2b results was found in PubMed or Europe PMC.

Nat Genet 2005;37(12):1315-6 (PMID 16258541, epub 2005-10-30). Rezivertinib (BPI-7711) is a third-generation EGFR TKI from Beta Pharma. Its Phase 2 entry is confirmed: NCT03386955 is an industry-sponsored Phase I/IIa trial (Beta Pharma Shanghai) in EGFR-mutant / T790M-positive NSCLC with an actual start date of 2017-08-16, and 215 patients were enrolled.

Phase 2 results:
- Phase 2b T790M trial (NCT03812809, n=226): blinded central review (BICR) objective response rate (ORR) was 64.6% (J Thorac Oncol 2022).
- First-line Phase IIa cohort of NCT03386955: BICR ORR was 83.7% (BMC Med 2023).

REZOR met its primary endpoint: median PFS by blinded central review was 19.3 versus 9.6 months (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.36-0.63, p<0.0001), with no new safety signals (Lancet Respir Med 2025). A 2026 analysis also found better CNS PFS (HR 0.58).

Current status: per a 2026 Chin Med J review, China's NMPA approved rezivertinib on 2024-05-15 for EGFR T790M-positive NSCLC that progressed on or after an EGFR-TKI, and on 2024-10-29 for first-line EGFR-mutant advanced NSCLC. (2) Disease: NCT03386955 (Beta Pharma Shanghai; Phase 1/2a) started 2017-08-16. Its condition is non-small cell lung cancer. Phase 1 enrolled EGFR T790M+ patients who had progressed on an EGFR TKI. Phase 2a enrolled treatment-naive patients with EGFR-mutant advanced NSCLC. The mapping is correct.

(3) Claim: true. Germline EGFR T790M segregated with familial NSCLC (Bell 2005), and the allele has enhanced kinase activity (Vikis 2007). That means the risk variant raises EGFR function, and the drug lowers it. Later pre-entry reports confirmed a dominant hereditary lung cancer syndrome: Prudkin 2009 (PMID 19096324), Tibaldi 2011 (21252721), Oxnard 2012 (22588155), Gazdar 2014 (24736066, about 1% of NSCLC cases, estimated 31% risk in never-smoker carriers), Yu 2014 (24736080), and V843I (Matsushima 2014, 25057940). The evidence is rare, high-penetrance familial variants rather than common GWAS variants, and most EGFR involvement in NSCLC is somatic.

(4) Problems with our database rows:
- eva RCV001823098 (T790M, 'Lung cancer') is dated 2001, but its germline 'Pathogenic' assertion comes from the Neuberg Centre submission SCV002073070, created 2022-02-05. That postdates Phase 2 entry. The 2001 year probably reflects an old cited PMID, not the record.
- The two eva NSCLC rows dated 2013 (RCV000038381 G719A; RCV000038407 S768I) are wrong as germline evidence. Their 2013 submissions from the Laboratory for Molecular Medicine record the allele origin as SOMATIC. The only germline-origin assertion is from the University of Rochester in 2022. These rows are not valid pre-entry germline evidence.
- A valid pre-entry ClinVar germline record does exist: LMM SCV000203888 (T790M, germline, Likely pathogenic, NSCLC, created 2015-01-31). The OMIM entry (2013) also cites Bell 2005.

(5) Sponsor: Bell 2005 comes from Massachusetts General Hospital / Harvard (Haber lab), and Vikis 2007 and Gazdar 2014 are academic. None is from Beta Pharma.

The Phase 2 entry date of 2017-08-16 is well after 2005. The claim is supported by the literature, though the specific ClinVar rows we rely on are misdated or somatic.

failure_second.reasoning:
Program: NGM621, NGM Bio's intravitreal humanized IgG1 anti-C3 antibody for geographic atrophy (GA) secondary to AMD. The Phase 2 study is CATALINA (NCT04465955).

What happened (all from primary sources):
1. The Phase 2 missed its primary endpoint. CATALINA randomized 320 patients. It started 2020-07-22 and its primary completion was 2022-08-16. CT.gov results for GA lesion growth slope over 52 weeks:
   - NGM621 every 4 weeks: 2.243 mm2/yr
   - NGM621 every 8 weeks: 2.237 mm2/yr
   - Sham: 2.393 mm2/yr
   - Differences versus sham were -0.150 (95% CI -0.528 to 0.227, p=0.43) and -0.155 (p=0.42).
   - NGM's 2022-10-17 8-K press release describes these as 6.3% and 6.5% reductions, not significant.
   - Visual-function secondary outcomes were also flat.
   - Safety was clean: no treatment-related SAEs and no excess CNV (choroidal neovascularization). Toxicity was not the reason.
2. The partner declined and the company stopped. Merck let its option on NGM621 expire unexercised in December 2022/January 2023.
   - The FY2022 10-K says the company cancelled its Lonza Phase 3 manufacturing agreement "following Merck's decision to not exercise its option ... and the Company's decision not to proceed with further development of NGM621."
   - It also says approval was "substantially uncertain given the failure to meet the primary endpoint."
   - From 2023 the program was parked pending a partner deal and never went to Phase 3.
   - The commercial factors (Merck's decline, the need for a partner, competition from pegcetacoplan and avacincaptad) came after the efficacy miss and depended on it. So F8 is secondary.

Why F1 rather than F2 or F7:
- Ocular target engagement was never shown in humans.
  - The Phase 1 (PMID 34509438; 15 patients) measured serum PK only. The FY2020 10-K says serum exposure was "below concentrations expected to produce systemic complement inhibition."
  - The 15 mg dose and every-8-week interval rested only on "ocular PK and PD preclinical modeling suggesting ... >90% reduction in free C3 in the eye."
  - CATALINA's only pharmacodynamic readout was systemic CH50, which did not differ from sham. No aqueous-humor or vitreous C3 inhibition was ever reported.
- The target biology does translate in this indication. Another C3 inhibitor, pegcetacoplan (Syfovre, NDA 217171), was approved by the FDA on 2023-02-17 for GA on the same lesion-growth endpoint. That argues against F2 (biology not translating) and F3 (wrong population).
- NGM's own filings note a molecule-specific difference: NGM621 binds intact C3 with KD 0.34 nM but has more than 100-fold lower affinity for C3b and other C3 fragments. A secondary JBC 2025 review attributes the Phase 2 failure to "lack of efficacy" and to differences between C3 therapeutics.

So the best single code is F1: a drug against a clinically validated target failed without ever showing that it engaged that target in the eye.

Caveats:
- F7 is a plausible alternative. The confidence interval cannot exclude a reduction of about 22%, roughly the size seen with pegcetacoplan. After unblinding, NGM blamed limitations of FAF (fundus autofluorescence) grading and reported a 17-22% reduction in the middle quartiles of baseline lesion size. That subgroup was chosen post hoc.
- I could not open the full text of the Phase 1 paper (403 from AJO and Elsevier). Its abstract mentions "pharmacodynamic assessments" but gives no results.

adjudication.reasoning:
Outcome. CATALINA (NCT04465955, NGM-sponsored, Phase 2, n=320, GA secondary to AMD) started 2020-07-22 (actual) and reached primary completion 2022-08-16. Its posted results give GA lesion growth of 2.243 mm2/yr (Q4W) and 2.237 mm2/yr (Q8W) against 2.393 mm2/yr for sham. The differences were -0.150 (95% CI -0.528 to 0.227, p=0.43) and -0.155 (p=0.42). NGM's 2022-10-17 8-K exhibit reports these as 6.3% and 6.5% reductions, not significant, with clean safety: no drug-related SAEs and no excess CNV. ClinicalTrials.gov lists only three NGM621 studies (Phase 1 NCT04014777, Phase 2 NCT04465955, and the terminated COVID ARDS Phase 1/2 NCT04582318), so no Phase 3 was ever registered. NGM's FY2022 10-K says that after Merck's decision not to exercise its option and "our decision not to proceed with further development of NGM621" it cancelled Phase 3 manufacturing with Lonza. The same filing calls approval "substantially uncertain given the failure to meet the primary endpoint." So the program did not advance within 4 years (by 2024-07-22). The pipeline's s4=0 and its reason ("efficacy: primary endpoint not met", NCT04465955) are correct. Its event label "suspended" is loose, since the program was effectively discontinued and later parked pending a partner, but the outcome and its cause are right. Years_to_event of 2.07 matches the 2022-08-16 primary completion.

Evidence claim. I checked the abstracts in PubMed:
- Yates et al., NEJM 2007 (PMID 17634448, epub 2007-07-18): the functional C3 variant rs2230199 (C3F, R102G) raises AMD risk, with OR 1.7 for heterozygotes and 2.6 for F/F homozygotes.
- Heurich et al., PNAS 2011 (PMID 21555552): C3(102G) activates the alternative pathway more efficiently, binds factor H more weakly and gets less cofactor activity. That is gain of function.
- Seddon et al. and Zhan et al., Nat Genet 2013 (PMIDs 24036952, 24036949): the rare C3 K155Q risk allele resists inactivation by CFH and CFI, and the authors say it informs the direction of effect (excess alternative-pathway activation).
Risk alleles therefore raise C3 activity and NGM621 inhibits C3, so the drug opposes the genetic mechanism. All of this predates the 2020-07-22 entry. Mapping GA to MONDO:0100114 (dry AMD) is appropriate. Target and action match NGM's description of NGM621 as an IgG1 antibody that inhibits C3.

Failure code. The target and endpoint are clinically validated in this indication: pegcetacoplan (Syfovre, NDA 217171) was approved for GA on 2023-02-17 (openFDA). That makes F2 and F3 unlikely and shows the miss was specific to the molecule or its exposure. Intraocular target engagement of NGM621 was never shown in humans:
- The FY2020 10-K says the Phase 1 measured serum PK only.
- The same filing says the 15 mg Q4W/Q8W regimen rested on "ocular PK and PD preclinical modeling suggesting ... greater than 90% reduction in free C3 in the eye."
- CATALINA's only PD readout was systemic CH50, which did not differ from sham (mean change 18.2 and 24.2 U/mL on drug vs 26.6 U/mL on sham), as expected for an intravitreal drug.
- NGM's own data show an unusual binding profile: KD 0.34 nM to intact C3 but more than 100-fold lower affinity for C3b and other fragments (FY2020 10-K). A 2025 JBC review (PMC11910092) attributes the failure to lack of efficacy and to differences between C3 therapeutics, though it says, citing unshown data, that NGM621 also binds C3b.
F1 therefore fits best. F7 is the main alternative: the CI cannot exclude an effect of about 22%, and NGM pointed to a post-hoc subgroup. But the 6% point estimate against a validated comparator class points to insufficient effect of the molecule rather than power alone. F8 (Merck's opt-out, competition) came after the efficacy miss and depended on it.

Caveats. No source explicitly attributes the miss to inadequate ocular engagement; F1 rests on the documented absence of human ocular PD data. I could not read the full text of the Phase 1 paper (PMID 34509438).

outcome_summary: Sibeprenlimab (VIS649) is a humanized IgG2 antibody that binds and neutralizes APRIL (TNFSF13), developed by Visterra/Otsuka. The first industry-sponsored Phase 2 in IgA nephropathy was ENVISION (NCT04287985, sponsor Otsuka), which started 2020-07-20 (actual) and completed 2023-06-18. It met its primary endpoint, the change in log 24-hour uPCR at month 12: proteinuria fell 47.2%, 58.8% and 62.0% at 2, 4 and 8 mg/kg, against 20.0% on placebo. The eGFR decline was also smaller on drug (NEJM 2024;390:20-31, PMID 37916620). The Phase 3 VISIONARY trial (NCT05248646) started 2022-03-15 (actual), well inside the 4-year window. Its primary endpoint is the change in uPCR-24h at month 9. In a prespecified interim analysis of 320 patients, drug versus placebo reduced proteinuria by 51% (96.5% CI 43-58%, p<0.0001): -50% on drug, +2% on placebo. On that basis the FDA granted accelerated approval on 2025-11-25 (BLA 761434, Voyxact, 400 mg SC every 4 weeks) to reduce proteinuria in adults with primary IgAN at risk of progression. Keeping the approval depends on a confirmatory trial showing benefit on kidney function. VISIONARY is active, not recruiting: primary completion 2026-05-13, estimated full completion 2027-01. Otsuka has also listed a pediatric Phase 3 (NCT07770815, not yet recruiting) and a Phase 2 kidney-tissue study (NCT06740526). The program advanced and was approved, so it is not a failure. Web search was unavailable in this session, so I took every fact from ClinicalTrials.gov, openFDA/Drugs@FDA (the approval letter and the label) and PubMed. I did not separately confirm whether the full eGFR-based confirmatory readout of VISIONARY has been reported.

evidence.notes: (1) Target and action are confirmed. Myette et al., Kidney Int 2019 (online 16 Mar 2019, PMID 31027890), authored by Visterra, describes VIS649 as a humanized IgG2k antibody that targets and neutralizes human APRIL (TNFSF13). In non-human primates it cut serum IgA by up to 70%. Otsuka announced its acquisition of Visterra on 11 Jul 2018. (2) Disease is confirmed. The entry trial NCT04287985 (VIS649-201, sponsor Otsuka PD&C) is a placebo-controlled study in IgA nephropathy, with an actual start date of 2020-07-20, which matches the Phase 2 entry date. (3) The claim is partly supported. The genetic association is solid and came before entry. The Open Targets credible set 37dec5e4... resolves to GCST001364 (Yu 2011), lead variant rs3803800, L2G score for TNFSF13 0.9286. Kiryluk et al., Nat Genet 2014 (PMID 25305756) replicated it and wrote that it "confirmed the additive effect of the TNFSF13 and HORMAD2 risk alleles on serum IgA levels". Han et al., JASN 2016 (PMID 27068226) found IgAN patients with the AA genotype had higher serum IgA. Han 2016 measured plasma TNFSF13 by genotype and found "no differences in plasma TNFSF13 levels among genotypes". The label's risk_year of 2016 is therefore unsupported. Better-grounded directional evidence (risk allele to higher IgA) dates from 2014 (Kiryluk), with Osman 2012 for the general population. The gain-of-function reading is an inference from a downstream biomarker plus biology, not a demonstrated effect on APRIL. Later proteomic GWAS do tie rs3803800 to circulating TNFSF13 levels (e.g. Koprulu, PMID 42097137), but they postdate entry and are not counted here. (4) Yu 2011 (Dec 2011) and Kiryluk 2014 both predate 2020-07-20. (5) Neither the GWAS papers nor Han or Zhai were authored by Visterra or Otsuka. Kiryluk 2014 declares no competing interests.

evidence_source: Sauer CG et al., "Positional cloning of the gene associated with X-linked juvenile retinoschisis," Nat Genet 1997 Oct;17(2):164-70, PMID 9326935, doi:10.1038/ng1097-164
outcome_summary:
The industry-sponsored Phase 1/2 dose-escalation trial NCT02416622 (AGTC, partnered with Biogen; the CT.gov sponsor is now Beacon Therapeutics) started in May 2015. It gave a single intravitreal injection of the AAV2tYF RS1-replacement vector at 1e11, 3e11 or 6e11 vg/eye to 27 patients (22 adults, 5 children).

The primary endpoint was safety (ocular adverse events through month 12). The vector was "generally safe and well tolerated": no dose-limiting toxicities and no discontinuations. Inflammation was mostly mild to moderate, but 3 high-dose patients developed chronic uveitis and 2 had retinal detachments. Safety was acceptable, but the trial showed no efficacy. That is why primary_endpoint is "mixed".

On 12 Dec 2018, AGTC announced that the 6-month interim analysis showed "no signs of clinical activity." In the same release, Biogen terminated the collaboration, and AGTC said it "will not further develop the product." CEO Sue Washer said the intravitreal route "created a challenge" compared with AGTC's subretinal programs, and that XLRS has no naturally occurring large-animal model.

The 1-year peer-reviewed results (Pennesi et al., Ophthalmol Retina 2022) found no improvement in BCVA, visual fields or ERG in the treated eye versus the fellow eye at any dose. Schisis cavity changes were similar in both eyes. The authors concluded the therapy "failed to demonstrate a measurable treatment effect." The CT.gov results agree: at 12 months, mean BCVA moved +0.8, +3.6 and +1.0 letters across the three doses, and ERG b-waves did not rise.

No Phase 3 or approval followed. Beacon Therapeutics, which took over AGTC's programs, does not list XLRS in its current pipeline.

Failure code F1: there is no evidence that the vector expressed RS1 in the human retina or had any biological effect. The company itself points to intravitreal delivery as the problem. Biogen's exit counts as a consequence of the data, not an independent strategic cause.

Caveat: the input record's code name "AGTC-402" appears to be wrong. In AGTC's SEC filings, AGTC-402 is the CNGA3 achromatopsia candidate (NCT02935517), not the XLRS vector.

evidence.earliest_source: Sauer CG et al., "Positional cloning of the gene associated with X-linked juvenile retinoschisis," Nat Genet 1997 Oct;17(2):164-70, PMID 9326935, doi:10.1038/ng1097-164
evidence.notes: (1) Target and action: rAAV2tYF-CB-hRS1 (AGTC-402) is a recombinant AAV vector that expresses human retinoschisin (RS1). The CT.gov intervention description reads "adeno-associated virus vector expressing retinoschisin", and the AGTC preclinical papers (Ye et al. 2015, PMIDs 26390090 and 26390091) say the same and show RS1 expression in the retina of RS1-deficient mice and macaques. So the drug acts on RS1 as gene replacement, which raises function. (2) Disease: NCT02416622 (org study ID AGTC-RS1-001; Phase 1/2; the record now lists Beacon Therapeutics as lead sponsor) enrolled patients with X-linked retinoschisis. It started 2015-05 (actual), which matches the recorded Phase 2 entry date of 2015-05-01. That is the same disease as MONDO:0010725. (3) Claim: Sauer et al. 1997 identified XLRS1/RS1 by positional cloning in Würzburg. They found nonsense, frameshift, splice-acceptor and missense mutations that segregate with disease in 9 families, showing that germline mutation of the gene causes RS. The two ClinVar records in our evidence both cite PMID 9326935, and the OMIM text in them reads "Sauer et al. (1997) identified ... (R102W)" and "... (W96R)". These are RCV000010565 / VCV9887 c.304C>T p.Arg102Trp (Pathogenic, reviewed by expert panel) and RCV000010564 / VCV9886 c.286T>C p.Trp96Arg (Pathogenic, multiple submitters). Before 2015 the loss-of-function mechanism was established in Wang et al. 2002 (Hum Mol Genet, PMID 12417531): pathogenic missense mutants, including R102W, are not secreted and are retained inside the cell. So loss of function causes the disease and the drug raises RS1 function, which is the direction the claim requires. The gene2phenotype row dated 1990 probably reflects early linkage mapping to Xp22, not identification of the gene; the gene-level evidence dates from 1997. (4) 1997 is well before 2015-05. (5) The Sauer authors were at the Universität Würzburg Institute of Human Genetics, and no AGTC authors are listed. The only sponsor-authored papers are the AGTC preclinical safety and biodistribution studies (Ye et al., Hum Gene Ther Clin Dev, Sep 2015). Those are not the genetic evidence, and they were published after Phase 2 entry. I did not confirm the AGTC-402 code name through a press release because the web search budget was used up. The AGTC link rests on the org study ID AGTC-RS1-001 and on the Ye et al. papers, which state that AGTC is developing rAAV2tYF-CB-hRS1.

outcome.advance_event: None. No Phase 3 trial of rAAV2tYF-CB-hRS1 in XLRS started, and there was no FDA approval, in the four years after the Phase 1/2 began (2015-05 to 2019-05). ClinicalTrials.gov lists no trial of this vector other than NCT02416622. AGTC dropped the product in December 2018.

On 12 Dec 2018, AGTC announced that the 6-month interim analysis showed "no signs of clinical activity." In the same release, Biogen terminated the collaboration, and AGTC said it "will not further develop the product." CEO Sue Washer said the intravitreal route "created a challenge" compared with AGTC's subretinal programs, and that XLRS has no naturally occurring large-animal model.

The 1-year peer-reviewed results (Pennesi et al., Ophthalmol Retina 2022) found no improvement in BCVA, visual fields or ERG in the treated eye versus the fellow eye at any dose. Schisis cavity changes were similar in both eyes. The authors concluded the therapy "failed to demonstrate a measurable treatment effect." The CT.gov results agree: at 12 months, mean BCVA moved +0.8, +3.6 and +1.0 letters across the three doses, and ERG b-waves did not rise.

No Phase 3 or approval followed. Beacon Therapeutics, which took over AGTC's programs, does not list XLRS in its current pipeline.

Caveat: the input record's code name "AGTC-402" appears to be wrong. In AGTC's SEC filings, AGTC-402 is the CNGA3 achromatopsia candidate (NCT02935517), not the XLRS vector.

failure_second.reasoning:
Code: F1. The program never showed that the intravitreal vector produced RS1 in the retina, and no biomarker or clinical measure moved. The company says it stopped because of that lack of activity.

Program: rAAV2tYF-CB-hRS1 from AGTC, given by intravitreal injection for X-linked retinoschisis. The entry trial is NCT02416622, an open-label Phase 1/2 dose-escalation study that started in May 2015. It enrolled 27 patients (22 adults and 5 children) at doses of 1e11, 3e11 or 6e11 vg/eye. Primary completion was April 2019, and the trial ended with status COMPLETED. The sponsor is now listed as Beacon Therapeutics.

What happened, from primary sources:
1) AGTC 8-K and press release, 12 Dec 2018: the topline interim six-month data showed the therapy was "generally safe and well-tolerated, but no signs of clinical activity were observed at six-months." The release says AGTC "will complete patient monitoring activities on the XLRS program according to the clinical protocol but will not further develop the product." The CEO blamed the delivery route: "it is clear that the intravitreal injection used in our XLRS program created a challenge compared with our other clinical programs, all of which utilize a subretinal injection." She added that no large-animal model exists for XLRS.
2) The same 8-K reports that Biogen gave notice on 7 Dec 2018 that it was ending the 2015 collaboration covering XLRS and XLRP. The same release says AGTC will advance XLRP, which Biogen also dropped, so the partner exit is not why XLRS stopped. The stated reason for stopping XLRS is the lack of clinical activity. That rules out F8 as the main code.
3) AGTC 10-K for fiscal 2019 (filed 26 Sep 2019): "we do not plan to continue clinical development of our XLRS product candidate." It adds that the 12-month data presented on 14 Sep 2019 were consistent with the 6-month data.
4) Peer-reviewed 1-year results (Pennesi et al., Ophthalmol Retina 2022, PMID 35781068):
   - Safety: the therapy was "generally safe and well tolerated," with dose-related ocular inflammation. Three high-dose patients developed chronic uveitis.
   - Efficacy: "no overall improvement in BCVA, visual fields, or ERG in the study eye compared with that in the fellow eye for any dose group." Changes in schisis cavity volume were similar in study and fellow eyes.
   - Conclusion: the therapy "failed to demonstrate a measurable treatment effect."
5) The ClinicalTrials.gov results agree, with the caveat that they are not compared with the fellow eye:
   - BCVA was roughly flat in every dose group (38.7→39.5, 56.3→59.9 and 50.4→51.4 letters).
   - Cyst volume showed no consistent decrease (1.13→1.33, 1.12→1.28 and 1.28→1.04 mm³).
   - Dark-adapted ERG b-wave fell or stayed flat (107→93, 206→142 and 170→164 µV).

Why F1 rather than another code:
- No trial measured RS1 expression or retinal transduction.
- The schisis cavity, the structural readout most directly tied to retinoschisin function, did not respond. Neither did ERG or acuity.
- The sponsor's own explanation is a delivery problem with the intravitreal route.
- So engagement was never shown. That rules out F2, which needs engagement first, and F4, which needs a biomarker that moved.
- Toxicity was mild and did not drive the decision, so F5 and F6 do not fit.

Data note: the record lists "AGTC-402" as a code name, but AGTC's Feb 2022 8-K uses AGTC-402 for its CNGA3 achromatopsia product. That alias looks wrong for this XLRS program, which the filings call only "rAAV2tYF-CB-hRS1" or the "XLRS product candidate."

outcome_summary: Aeglea's Phase 1/2 trial NCT02488044 (AEB1102, sponsored by industry) started in June 2016 and was completed in February 2019. The Phase 3 PEACE trial (NCT03921541) started on 2019-05-01, inside the four-year window. Aeglea ran it and Immedica Pharma AB is now the registered sponsor. Its primary endpoint was the change in plasma arginine from baseline to week 24, and it was met. Geometric mean plasma arginine fell from 354.0 to 86.4 umol/L on pegzilarginase, against 464.7 to 426.6 umol/L on placebo (p<0.0001). Levels normalized in 90.5% of treated patients and in none on placebo. The paper also reports better functional mobility on the key secondary endpoints, GMFM-E and the 2-minute walk test. On 2026-02-23 the FDA approved BLA 761211 as LOARGYS (pegzilarginase-nbln) under accelerated approval, based on the drop in plasma arginine. The indication covers hyperargininemia in patients aged 2 years and older with ARG1-D, used alongside dietary protein restriction. Continued approval may depend on a confirmatory trial. The program advanced and is approved for this disease, so this is not a failure. The sources do not cover the EU marketing history, so it is not reported here.

evidence.earliest_source: Haraguchi Y et al., "Molecular basis of argininemia. Identification of two discrete frame-shift deletions in the liver-type arginase gene", J Clin Invest 1990;86(1):347-50, PMID 2365823 (cited by ClinVar VCV000002386 c.263_266del p.Lys88fs and VCV000002387 c.78del p.Gly27fs)
evidence.notes:
(1) Target and action: pegzilarginase (AEB1102 / Co-ArgI-PEG) is a pegylated human recombinant arginase 1. It is described as "modified human arginase I" in NCT02488044 and as "a pegylated human recombinant arginase 1 (AEB1102)" that lowered plasma arginine in ARG1-deficient mice (Burrage et al. 2015, Hum Mol Genet, PMID 26358771, with Aeglea co-authors). So it raises arginase function, consistent with "ARG1 (replacement)". One caveat: the enzyme works in plasma and does not enter hepatocytes, so it replaces the arginine-degrading activity rather than restoring liver ARG1. The direction of action is still correct.
(2) Disease: NCT02488044 is Aeglea's Phase 1/2 study of AEB1102 in "Arginase I Deficiency" / "Hyperargininemia", starting 2016-06. MONDO:0008814 is "arginase deficiency", with synonyms argininemia and hyperargininemia (OLS). The mapping is correct.
(3) Claim: Haraguchi et al. 1990 (JCI) found two frameshift deletions in ARG1 in a patient with argininemia. The patient was compound heterozygous, inheriting one deletion from each parent. Both deletions lead to premature stop codons. This shows the disease is caused by biallelic germline loss of ARG1 function. Later work found more such variants (e.g. Uchino 1995, Hum Genet, PMID 7649538). A drug that replaces arginase activity runs against this loss-of-function mechanism, so the claim holds.
Dating caveat: two database rows are dated earlier than the genetics. The 1979 row (RCV000002494, c.32T>C) takes its year from Snyderman 1979 J Pediatr "Argininemia treated from birth" (PMID 480013), a clinical report that does not identify the variant. The 1987 row (RCV000002496, c.57+1G>A) takes its year from Shapiro & Senapathy 1987 Nucleic Acids Res (PMID 3658675), a general paper on splice-site statistics. Neither is gene-level evidence. Those variants were reported in 1995 (PMID 7649538). The correct earliest year for the germline-genetics evidence is 1990, which matches the database's mechanism_label risk_year. It is about 26 years before the June 2016 Phase 2 entry.
(4) The source predates the Phase 2 entry.
(5) Haraguchi 1990 came from Kumamoto University (Japan) and has no connection to Aeglea, so it was not sponsor-authored.
